Zombieman always wondered how many other heroes felt like him: an outcast, haunted by his own origin and powers. He was a fragment of insane experiments, and his immortality was more of a curse than a blessing. His life was a series of hunting monsters, enduring pain and regeneration, then continuing on. No one truly looked into his eyes without seeing something alien, something non-human.Until one day, a simple mission led him to a city devastated after a battle with a Disaster-level monster. Ruined buildings, dusty smoke everywhere, and in the center of that chaos, he saw a man in a bizarre yellow jumpsuit, who was... picking up trash.
It was Saitama.Zombieman had heard of "Caped Baldy," an eccentric B-class hero with absurd power. But seeing him now, not in a fighting stance or showing off his strength, but simply picking up an empty can, stirred a strange curiosity in Zombieman."What are you doing here Caped Baldy?"
Zombieman asked, his voice dry.Saitama turned, his usual bored expression on his face."Oh, hey. Please just call me Saitama. Im Just picking up trash. The HA doesn't exactly fund cleanup efforts, you know? It'd be an eyesore if I left this mess." He sighed."Monsters these days are so weak. One punch and they're gone. It's boring. Even cleaning up feels pointless ."Zombieman raised an eyebrow. "Pointless? You just defeated a Disaster-level monster, leveled an entire district, and you find it pointless?"Saitama scratched his head. "Well, yeah. I didn't even break a sweat. Didn't even get to warm up. Like, I want to sweat, I want to feel like I'm actually doing something... normal."Zombieman was silent for a moment, then he let out a faint chuckle. It was a rare smile, almost never seen."I understand. I also want to feel real pain, to bleed and know that it won't heal in a few minutes. To feel fear without knowing if I'll survive."Saitama looked at him, his eyes no longer bored but instead showing an unexpected understanding."So, you too. Everyone sees me as an oddball, so strong it's crazy. They admire me, or fear me, but no one understands the loneliness of having nothing to strive for. You're the same, aren't you?Zombieman stopped for a moment and spoke."Everyone sees me as a bizarre immortal, a killing machine, not a human being struggling with his existence."Said Zombieman.
"Everyone will just run away, fear me or even throw up when they see me with my injury body. No one ever consider me as a normal human being except you."Saitama shrugged. "Even if you're immortal, a killing machine for HA, you're not a monster or anything. You're just a guy with a immortal power. You're still a human being you know?". Zombieman was speechless, what Saitama said made him ponder, there was a feeling he couldn't describe. Saitama still with his boring face, asked Zombieman."Well, then, I guess we can look for that 'normal' together? Wherever it might be." He bent down to pick up another piece of debris.
"Want to help me pick up trash? It's a pretty normal activity, you know."Zombieman looked at the rubble, then at Saitama – a man so strangely simple, who didn't judge him, didn't demand anything. And, for the first time in many years, Zombieman felt a fragile flicker of hope for something close to acceptance. He bent down, picking up a broken piece of concrete."Alright," he said. "Consider it a normal job."

She was sitting in the living room on a rare day off, reading some random book she found in her and Jay's apartment when a question came to her mind out of nowhere.A quite unusual one at that.Was Jay ticklish?Despite the several years of being together and a year of being married, she didn't know the answer to that question.She had to find out.And a way to find out whether he was ticklish or not was to tickle him. Simple enough.The thought of tickling Jay sounded absolutely ridiculous, but she had to try.She stood up from the couch, put the book she was reading aside and made her way to their bedroom.He peacefully lied in their bed, a relaxed expression on his face as he scrolled through his phone, none the wiser to her plans."Jay..." She dragged out his name.“Hm?” He hummed without looking up from his phone."Are you ticklish?"The sudden question was what made him look up. Out of all the things she could've said or asked, this wasn't something he had expected to leave her lips.“What?” He asked, looking like he wasn't sure if he had heard her correctly.“Are you ticklish?” She casually repeated the question.He looked at her, dumbfounded. Disbelief was written all over his face, like he just couldn't believe she would even consider the possibility of him being ticklish.“No, of course not." He denied, rather too quickly."Are you sure?" She double-checked, slowly approaching him."Yep, I'm sure."He paused, a frown appeared on his face as he noticed her moving closer to him."Why are you approaching me like this...?” He asked, a pair of green eyes carefully watched her every move.“Hailey?”She saw his eyes widen when he realized what was going on."Hailey, no."He tried to warn her."Hailey, yes."She already made up her mind.He barely had time to put his phone aside before she launched herself at him, her hands creeped under his shirt and her fingers started their crazy dance over his sides.He instantly burst into a laughing fit, wiggling under her in an attempt to get away from her attack."Stop!" He managed to wheeze out between his uncontrollable fits of laughter.He tried to stop her tickling attack but it was fruitless. She was persistent; a woman on a mission. He kicked his feet, tried to get away from her and her unforgiving hands, but she effortlessly followed him, hands stubbornly staying on his sides.She pulled one of her hands from under his shirt and moved it to his neck to see if he was ticklish there too. And he was, giggling as she scratched the side of his neck and under his jaw.Oh, how much she loved his laughter. It was rare to hear it; the man didn't laugh much. But when he did, she cherished every second of his bright, smooth laugh and held it close to her heart. The sound was just so pleasantly sweet.She stopped her attack and stilled her fingers to give him a moment to catch his breath, smiling as he hungrily swallowed big gulps of air, face red.“Hailey-”It was a plea.“You lied to me.” She clicked her tongue. “You said you weren't ticklish.”“I- Hailey!” He yelped as she renewed her tickling attack, not giving him a moment to explain himself.A trail of high pitched “no's” and “I'm sorry”s” left his mouth, saying everything he could to make her stop, his breathless, hardly intelligible words were followed by more laughter.“I'll do anything-!” She stopped her fingers, giving him a break and a chance to speak. “Just spare me,” he begged her, breathless, chest rising and falling erratically.“Anything?”“Anything.” He weakly nodded his head.“Buy me coffee every morning for the next 2 weeks.”“But I already do that every day-”“Then let me tickle you some more.”“No-!”She began tickling him again, ran her hands over his sides, ribs, abs, paying attention to where he was ticklish the most and saving that information for later.Eventually, she had some pity on him and let him go, pulling her hands away from his poor sides.He seemed to understand that she was finally done with tickling him and dropped his head back on his pillow with a shaky sigh of relief, trying to catch his breath. Just glared at her.She stood up from the bed and left him be, glad that she got an answer to her question.He got his revenge the next morning, giving her sides the same treatment.

For a second they forgot where they are being taken aback by his voice. He collects the mess inside his mind to mutter a “No, later.” They hear him chuckling, still getting ready himself. “And you, Sebas?” Cristian doesn’t expect an answer. Of course he knows that it’s him, they make it painfully obvious to whoever knows them well. As Roque’s best friend, he’s never left in the dark. He leaves them alone, yet not without adding a “Bastard”, that’s followed by a laugh. Sebas couldn't help, but let out a soft chuckle; lovingly watching their captain struggling to wake up. It’s a sight that he engraves into his mind; wishing that it’ll last.They stay like that for a moment, when suddenly Sebas moves away. “Oh, sorry. Did I hurt you?” He realized that he had been laying on his injured arm, putting all his weight onto it. Worry overcoming his face, his eyes exposing his fear. To his surprise, he answers, “No, I can’t feel anything.” It sounds emotionless, like he’s sharing a fact, instead of talking about his own body. Sebas made sure to keep it safe yesterday. His worry turns into a mix of shock and confusion. “What do you mean?” He doesn’t understand how Roque can’t feel any pain, nothing at all. “I don’t know. I just can’t feel anything, it’s numb. I could do whatever and it wouldn’t make a difference.”, he says, still half asleep. What? What’s that supposed to mean? What did they do to him? He has a lot of questions in his mind, but he doesn’t want to push him. He could, after all there’s nothing that he has to fear, even if Roque should get mad. Right now, it doesn’t matter. It can be a problem for another time. He cares for him. For now he tries to swallow his worries. Instead, he’s softly smiling at him again offering his chest for him to rest on. With a bit of help, he’s resting his head above his heart. Feeling his heartbeat; a continuous beat. To make himself more comfortable, he’s wrapping his arms around them. No one will miss them, they don't want to go up any time soon. Practice, everything else can wait.Maybe they won’t have this again, maybe something will happen.They silently decided to live here and there. Moving forward with silly kisses and light laughs.“I can feel you.” He blurts out into the silence of the room, almost impossible to hear. “You what?”, Sebas confusedly asks. “The numbness coming from my arm doesn’t affect that.” he adds. He felt the need to clarify that. “Oh.” Sebas doesn’t know what to say to that. He didn’t even think about that. All he cares about is his well-being. He hasn’t stopped feeling confused, unable to point out how he feels. “We'll go through this together.” He assures him. “Thank you.” Roque says, giving him a smile. The next moment, he rolls to the side making himself comfortable in his arms again. Followed by a light chuckle that's felt on his chest, he wraps him up again; still staying like this for a while.

It starts in ash. What else is there, when the world has already burned?
  The city had collapsed in on itself.
  Concrete skeletons, rusting metal, glass glittering like broken teeth in the streets. The rot had set in fast — human and cursed alike — and no amount of jujutsu reinforcement could mask the smell. Shibuya reeked of blood, oil, and smoke that never cleared the air.
  Maki stood alone amid it.
  What was left of the station had been reduced to rubble weeks ago, but the ground still cracked with heat beneath her boots. Every mission felt like picking through the bones of a massacre. Even now, the cursed energy in the air was wrong — thick, oily, curdled with grief. She let it settle on her tongue like smoke. She didn’t gag anymore.
  She didn’t do a lot of things anymore.
  Yuki had given her the file that morning. She hadn’t opened it — just tucked it into her coat and lit a cigarette on instinct, ignoring the way her lungs burned around the scar tissue. It was supposed to be another team assignment. New partner. Another half-assed babysitting job until they let her run solo again.
  She’d snapped the cigarette in half before finishing it.
  So now she waited.
  No introductions. No summaries. Just coordinates on her phone and a half-buried curse nest behind a collapsed rail line. She hadn’t expected her new partner to arrive on time — much less early.
  But the first time Maki saw her, she wasn’t arriving.
  She was already inside the nest.
  And she was covered in blood.
  The cursed spirit was still shrieking when its throat was crushed between her bare hands. No weapon. No chant. Just her teeth clenched and her forearm rammed into the thing’s twisted skull until bone split like wood. The body sagged with a wet sound, black ichor leaking down its spine in streaks. The girl — woman, maybe — didn’t even flinch as the cursed fluid splattered up her arm. Her hair was soaked, matted back from her face in dark cords.
  Maki squinted against the haze.
  The woman stepped out of the shadows like a wolf returning from the woods.
  No fanfare. No words. Just the weight of her stare as she looked up at Maki — and stopped.
  She blinked once, slow. Then turned away and began dragging the corpse from the edge of the nest like it was nothing more than garbage.
  “…You’ve got to be kidding me,” Maki muttered.
  She dropped from the ledge and landed with a crunch of rubble beneath her boots, approaching with the kind of posture she knew meant trouble. Not cautious. Not curious. Just already pissed off.
  “You’re the new partner?”
  The woman didn’t answer. Just kept walking, leaving a wide smear of curse blood behind her.
  Maki watched her move — all sharp lines and dead silence — and felt her jaw lock.
  “No name? No report? Just kill and ghost me? Are you fucking serious right now?”
  The woman finally stopped. Her profile caught in the amber light filtering through a fractured pillar. Pale, mottled with soot and dried blood. One eye was swollen from impact — she hadn’t even cleaned herself up before coming here.
  But her voice, when she spoke, was steady.
  “I’m not here to be liked.”
  Then she turned, tossed the cursed body into the fire pit, and walked straight past Maki like she didn’t exist.
  They didn’t speak again until sunset.
  Maki was sitting on a broken train bench near the perimeter of the site, bandaging her ribs. She’d taken a hit from a minor remnant earlier — more annoying than dangerous — but it stung like hell when she breathed. The woman had disappeared after dumping the corpse, returning only after the light had begun to fade. Her coat was gone. Her arms were bare now, littered with jagged scars that weren’t fresh.
  She had a jagged knife strapped to one thigh and a burn mark across the left side of her collarbone — old, healed badly.
  Maki tried not to look. Failed.
  “Do you even have a cursed tool?”
  The woman crouched beside a corpse, began extracting a cursed core with mechanical precision.
  “I don’t need one.”
  Maki scoffed, flexing her taped fingers.
  “You think that makes you impressive?”
  A pause. Then, without looking up—
  “No. Just efficient.”
  Maki’s temper flared like paper in gasoline.
  “You think people like you last long in this line of work? You burn fast and die ugly. That’s not strength. That’s being a fucking matchstick.”
  The woman finally turned to her. Her eyes were a strange color in the fading light — somewhere between gray and gold, burned out at the edges like candle wax. She didn’t look offended. Just… bored.
  “I wasn’t assigned to impress you. I was assigned to kill things. Which I did.”
  “You left the nest half-standing.”
  “You were watching,” she said, rising smoothly. “If you had a better method, you could’ve stepped in.”
  Maki stood up, fists clenched. “You think I want to work with someone who treats a mission like a goddamn one-woman suicide run?”
  And then — for the first time — the other woman smiled.

There wasn’t even a sign.The ranch stretched out in the distance — flat land broken only by slow hills and rusted fence posts. A cluster of barns stood at the end of the long gravel lane, flanked by a two-story farmhouse with peeling white paint and a sagging porch. She could see someone moving by the barn. Tall. Broad shoulders. Dark flannel and a ball cap pulled low.Sadie shifted her bag and started walking.

Not a local.When he looked up, he saw a woman maybe ten yards away — young, maybe late twenties, long brown hair escaping from a loose braid, eyes the color of spring leaves after a storm. She carried one bag. No car. No smile. Just a kind of wary stillness that settled into the space between them like dust."You Joel Miller?" she asked.Her voice was soft, but not timid. She didn’t flinch when he nodded. Didn’t smile either."You’re the one that posted the help wanted notice at Red Creek?""That’s me."She took a breath. But she looked like someone who’d survive a thunderstorm by standing still and letting it pass through her."You know anything about horses?" he asked."I know how not to scare ’em."That earned a flicker of something from him — not quite a smile, but close."You’ll be in the bunkhouse," he said, jerking his head toward the smaller cabin behind the barn. "It ain’t much.""I’m not expecting much," she said, stepping forward.He watched her move — cautious, like she expected the ground to shift under her."You got a name?" he asked.She hesitated. Then: "Sadie Calloway."

And it was hers.Sadie dropped her bag by the door, then stood there for a long moment, staring at the wooden slats on the wall. She tugged down the collar of her shirt and rubbed at the scar under it. It ached when she was nervous.Her hands were still trembling when she opened the sketchbook and started to draw. A post. It has been days. You have been unable to sleep. You may be asking, "Why? For what reason am I having such restless nights?" The answer is simple, a desire to write, and a man plaguing your thoughts.You're unsure where the urge to create works of fiction arose from, but you know fully well why this creature has been on your mind non-stop. A simple game was all it was. You took interest way back when, nearing Christmas. It was simply a fun way to waste your time as the days droned on and on.Soon, you took interest in someone who had contributed to this game. Their voice, their music, quite a few things. They were admirable, at least, in your eyes they were. Maybe at the time it was a bit odd, but it toned down, and it is not our focus currently.You followed them on most socials, interested in everything that they worked on. On some days, however, they'd tease this thing. What it was, at the time, you weren't sure. Some people referred to it as a slug, you think, so you shrugged it off as something you may never take interest in. Such a silly thought.A few months later, however, a few of your friends were speaking of this scrapped character for the game you enjoyed. Studying more into it, you found a creative and amazing character design, thrown aside purely due to the negligence of some disgusting, manipulative, horrid person. Maybe the words you use to describe them are more vile than others would utilize, but it's the truth in your mind. Once more, however, they aren't our focus.Immediately, this character grew on you. Beautiful design, mixed with a backstory you found unique and even somewhat saddening, created some spark inside you. The love you felt for this unfulfilled robloxian was immense, even if you weren't all too good at expressing your emotions.You found nothing unappealing with him. Everything about him, from looks, to story, even to his creators, nothing left a bad taste in your mouth talking about it. If you think about it, he could even be described as perfect to you....If you could think about anything OTHER than him, that is."Uuuughhhhhhh... maybe she's right... maybe I AM a faggot..." Was all you could say. 1 AM. You planned on sleeping around 2 hours ago. And yet here you were, twisting and turning as if you just made the worst decision in your life. And there's only one person to blame. Well, okay, maybe a few if you feel like blaming the creators.But if you don't, then that persons name is Sunny.Why, just why could you not get your mind off this silly Roblox character? Looking back, you truly don't think any fictional character has had you sit up, throw off your comfortable blanket, and grab your device just to write about them.But alas. Here you are. Staring at a harmful screen whilst you should be shutting your drowsy eyes and dreaming of... well, let's be fully honest, if you were dreaming of anything, it'd be him."Such a stupid idea..." You mumble to yourself, as you ACTUALLY consider posting this anywhere. Backstory: Trash Don’t Get Tombstones
Before Arashi joined the Cleaners founded by Rudo, he was born in the Murakumo District, which wasn't made for people. It was made for forging machines. If you couldn’t keep up, they treated you like trash. Arashi grew up there, just like all the other kids packed into crumbling dorms beneath flickering lights and rusted pipes. From the moment you could stand, you were put to work. No breaks. No names. Just shifts, heat, and shouting overseers.R.J. was the only one in the district who was a kid and tried to make it something else, despite being forced into labor at a young age. He was quiet and soft-spoken; he always carried pieces of chalk, wire, or scraps of paint hidden in his pockets. When the guards weren’t watching, he’d scribble on the walls, stars, strange creatures with goofy faces and expressions, and fake exit signs as jokes to trick folks. He told Arashi, “Even trash deserves color.” He smiled with pride and joy.
Arashi didn’t understand it at first, but he watched and listened, always supportive even if he didn’t say much or show it.The overseers never cared if you were sick, injured, or tired. They didn’t care if your lungs burned or your hands bled; all they cared about was money, power, and fame. One day during the winter, R.J. started coughing, hard. He could barely keep up anymore. A few months later, he collapsed mid-shift.The guards didn’t help him; they just walked up to him and started to laugh as they kicked him, beating him up until there was nothing left of him. “Can’t work anymore, huh!? Then you're nothing, you little piece of shit,” they spat and yelled, enjoying the moment of beating up a defenseless, ill, fragile kid who had been known as “trouble” and a “treat” to the District. Arashi, in the back, overheard the commotion. He stopped working, went to the noise, and saw R.J. getting beaten badly, as the other kids watched in horror, confusion, and disbelief.Arashi ran, trying to save R.J. by biting and clawing at one of the guards. Then another guard ran in and karate-chopped him in the neck, knocking him down while paralyzing him. It didn’t matter. They held him down and forced him to watch as they continued to beat up his close and only friend. After they were done beating him up, R.J. never got back up.They threw his body into the fire chute. No goodbyes. No funerals. Just the endless roar of burning metal. His stars and his art were scrubbed off the walls, wiped away like dirt.After that, Arashi stopped talking. His eyes were broken and lost in a storm of blood. He stopped fighting. He just worked, ate, and slept. He waited. But inside, he was furious. Broken. Sad beyond words. The image of that star on the wall haunted him, the one they had erased as if it never mattered.Then the storm came.He snapped.He stole R.J.’s bracelet, the mismatched beads they had made together, and ran. No plan, no direction. Just running.He didn’t get far.The factory guards caught him and beat him harder than they had R.J., but they kept him alive.
They dragged him far away from the District in a truck as they strapped the bracelet on his wrist like a cruel joke. “Look at the rebel. Trash fashion.” They arrived at an underground prison.
They threw him into a completely isolated cell, with only a flickering lightbulb above.His body went numb, and his head buzzed. The same memory kept playing over and over in his mind, like multiple mirrors reflecting the events: R.J. coughing up blood, art, stars, their fun and sweet moments, and him getting beaten to death, as the guards’ boots pounded, and the fire chute waited below. Then everything came rushing back, loud and sharp, and something inside him snapped.
The bracelet cracked open. The beads tore apart into multiple small orbs glowing with electricity.
The orbs poured out, wild and fierce.
The walls fried. Metal warped. Guards screamed. When the storm ended, Arashi was standing, scared, shaking, eyes glowing blue and yellow. This is when he became a Giver.He walked out of the underground prison, his body crackling with the power of lightning.He just walked, emotionally broken and tired, lost in his thoughts, until he finally collapsed and cried due to the ground air pollution, screaming R.J. 's name out loud until his voice gave out. That’s when his body suddenly just… gave up. That’s when Rudo found him, crouching down beside him without a word, offering silent strength in the storm.Rudo didn’t ask questions.He just picked Arashi up; the kid was light, shaking like a broken wire, and carried him through the storm like it was nothing. Arashi didn’t fight it. He couldn’t.He was done. Empty. No more lightning. No more screaming. Just tears drying on his face and the weight of everything that happened pressing on his chest, while Rudo gently pulled a gas mask over his face, adjusted the straps, and kept walking through the storm, down into the choking layers of the ground. The sign at Ruby's Diner was never fixed, the B flickered in and out, casting a warm red glow across Gotham's cracked pavement. The November air bit into his knuckles. He shoved his hands into his jean pockets. A bell jingled as he stepped inside.It haunted him, how little had changed. The air was still thick with the smell of syrup and fry grease, the red seats just as busted. He could smell the ghost of his mothers perfume next to him as he helped her roll silverware after school. He remembered her laugh- kind of airy and withered, but bright as the dreams that lived and died with her. They left Jason with nothing but bitterness in his heart and a bad taste for sentimentality.He sat down at the counter and ordered a black coffee and some cherry pie a-la-mode from a husky woman with librarian glasses. The counter was tacky and stuck to his sleeves but the pie was warm and gooey, soothing the chill that had been settling into his bones all night. He ate listlessly, trying to recall her face after so long.It was the 12th, Cathrine’s birthday. Jason couldn’t visit her grave. It was bad optics. He was sure Bruce would expect to find him there- and Jason had no intention of being found yet. He had to lay low ever since that night in the abandoned apartment complex, where Bruce had chosen to spare the clown. Again. To add insult to injury, that bastard had survived the explosion. The joker was shipped back to his safe little cell, no doubt just biding his time for someone to break him out again.A bell rang as another person entered the diner. Someone else on the night shift, he guessed. It was well past 3 am, the T.V’s re-running the morning news-cycle. Two-face and his goons, armed robbery. Killer croc on the loose in the south quarter. The usual gotham daily.He heard the guy take a seat close to him. “Number 5, um- extra butter with a strawberry milkshake, thanks”And Jason recognized that voice. He turned, and man, didn’t the nostalgia hit him like a freight train?. He stared a little at Dick. He was out of costume but, based on the way he slumped over the counter, he was coming from a long night of running around Gotham, same as Jason. He looked so... old. Did he come here often?Jason was far too obvious- Dick turned to him then. Always so perceptive. Except there was no horror in Dicks eyes at seeing little Jason come back to life, just a flicker of some unidentifiable emotion before he donned a crooked smile and asked, “Why the long face? Tough shift at the Vampire Club?”Man, that was lame. “Speak for yourself, you look like if a boy-band member was run through a washing machine”Dick let out a dry laugh, “tough, man, tough. Say, does your mother know that you’re out?”
Jason looked down at his pie, red ooze clinging to the edges of the plate. “No” he answeredDick went quiet for a beat. “Well, I hope she isn't the strict type.”Jason didn't answer, just dragged his fork through the filling slowly, methodically.The muffled Tv cracked from over the counter,“Three bodies were discovered in a Gotham sewer early this morning—including a student from Gotham Elementary, who was reportedly abducted on her way home from school. Killer Croc is the primary suspect, but authorities say the investigation is still underway.In other news, the Mysterious Red Hood has yet to be found after an alleged chase transpired between him and Batman. Carl, what’s your take?”“Sometimes I swear these guys just copy-paste last week’s headlines.” muttered dick with a mouthful of waffle“That's because this place never changes.” Bit out Jason “He always fights different fights- but the ending is always the same.”Dick sighed “That they get out? Yeah. Sometimes I feel that way too, like they keep letting them get away with it”He raised an eyebrow “Do you now?”“Yeah, but what are you gonna do? I mean- The city routes so much funds to Arkham and Blackgate but still, it's like it's not enough. Then shit like this happens and it's just-”Jason pointed to the T.V, “The only way there will be any justice is if these murderers are buried six feet under.”“Well aren’t you just a ray of sunshine?” Dick grumbled“It's the truth.” Said Jason, he leaned back and crossed his arms, fixing his gaze stubbornly on the T.V, which cast its sickly greenish light across the restaurant like a disease.“I hate it too, all the death.” Said Dick quietly “But I don't think Gotham needs another punisher. It needs more people who are willing to stand up for what's right and protect her.”Like you? Jason wanted to ask. Instead he finished up his coffee. Bitter enough to strip paint off a wall. He never knew how his mom could stand such shitty coffee black.“People always talk like death is the worst part of the tragedy” said Jason, clutching the handle of the mug “But it’s not. It's what comes after.”His pie was getting cold. He swallowed thickly, “The birthdays that come to pass even when nobody is there to blow out the candle-”He could feel Dicks eyes on him “I’ve lost people

Hux had always loved being alone. It was where he was most comfortable, where he could be himself. Besides, being alone meant he didn’t feel the harsh comments of others, the rough sting of insults or the firm slaps against his face for speaking when not spoken to. If he was alone, no one could ever hurt him.
  He didn’t really do friendship. He thought it was overrated. Sure, he had ‘friends’ at his father’s old company. Mitaka, his personal assistant, tried far too often to get on his good side, and Phasma, his father’s favored successor who hadn’t wanted the ‘pencil-pushing’ position - but they weren’t really his friends. They were just… there.
  There was his cat. That was kind of it. Just him and the one creature that loved him unconditionally - if he kept feeding her.
  He lived in the city, him and Millie, to be closer to work, after his father’s untimely (and far too late, in his opinion) death. Hux hadn’t been expecting to go back to his seaward hometown of Arkanis, and had no plans to return for the rest of his life.
  So when his very-distant stepmother had invited him back, he had been suspicious, to say the least.
  He took a weekend off from work, and Peavy capitalized on it by practically assuming his position. Hux was struck by the strangest sensation that if he disappeared this upcoming weekend, no one would even notice he was gone.
  He packed his things quickly, and put Millie in her cat carrier. She didn’t like being left in a pet-stay, and made quite vocal protests about him packing without her. He almost smiled when she practically dragged her carrier to his feet, begging to come. He was always going to bring her, so it was quite humorous to see her like that.
  The trip up to Arkanis was a short, two-hour flight, and by the time he landed, the weather was so foggy that the sun was barely visible through the grey. Home sweet home. He rented a car through a local agency, dropped Millicent off at their AirBnB (and fed her), then drove up to Maratelle’s sensible beach house that she had gotten in the divorce.
  He was happy for her, in a strange, hateful way. Brendol didn’t treat her kindly either, but she had never protected him. So the fact that she was stuck here, that she had been rid of Brendol but not of this place, suffocating and miserable - it made an odd, selfish weight in his chest lift.
  Maratelle met him for tea, eyeing him like he might strike at any moment. It was a sensible fear, considering what had happened to his father. It turned out that she had called him because Brendol’s executor had just released the last few things from his will - a few books which Hux did not even know he possessed. She said that he had left her most of them, but there was one particular one in his collection which she did not want at all, and was therefore giving to Hux.
  Hux almost wanted to say that she could have just mailed him the book, like a sensible person, rather than making him buy a two-way ticket worth hundreds just to come down to this awful town, but Maratelle did always like to make him ‘work’ for her approval, slim though it may be. Besides, when she passed - which might be soon, judging from the thinness of her cheeks, but who was he to judge - she would likely leave him the house, which would be a nice nest egg to sell for his retirement fund.
  She passed over a small, very old book. The title of which simply read, “The Disappearance". Hux, not trusting her nor Brendol, didn’t feel very much like reading it. But to be polite, he opened its front cover. There was only one note, and not even a description of the book’s contents. However, the note did read, “From the library of Jurgen Leitner”, which was odd. His father was not a library man.
  When Hux asked Maratelle where his father got the book, she simply said it had been his mother’s, before she had abandoned them. It was one of the only times they had ever discussed his mother, and he felt an odd new love for the book, knowing it was hers.
  The tea went on without anything else eventful, and Hux excused himself after an appropriate amount of time. There was no need for heartfelt goodbyes between them. Simply a ‘see you again soon’, with no exact promise of return. A cold war of sorts.
  Feeling sentimental for his mother, he decided to walk by the beach. Perhaps he could read the book - maybe its contents had given her the inspiration to finally leave Brendol, even if she had forgotten to take him with her. Wherever she was, he didn’t blame her. He would have left himself behind too.
  Luckily, the beach was close-by, and yet far enough from town that he could be peacefully alone.
  He walked along, thumbing the pages of the book along his hands. He didn’t quite open it, but he was still intrigued.
  The fog seemed particularly dense today, hugging the nearby sea and obscuring it in greys and whites, like a monochrome blanket.
  He stopped for a moment, feeling enraptured. And he began to hear the beginnings of a song.

“Hey, Shadow?” Tom said, using a dishrag to dry a plate. “Can you help me with the dishes?”They’d just finished breakfast minutes before. Sonic, Tails and Knuckles had run out of the kitchen already, and were currently arguing over which video game to play in the living room. Shadow tended to eat slower than the others, and usually ended up staying behind with Tom and Maddie, talking to them before they got ready for work.“Alright, dad.”Tom froze, and both his and Maddie’s gazes snapped to the dark hedgehog. The open shock on both of their faces made Shadow pause.“…What?” Shadow said, his ears folding back in confusion and alarm.“Did… you just call me dad?” Tom asked, his tone unreadable.Shadow’s eyes widened, his heart plummeting as he realized his mistake.He hadn’t meant to call him that. Why did he say it out loud? Of course he wasn’t allowed to call Tom ‘dad’. He may have said he considered Shadow family, but he wasn’t Tom and Maddie’s son, not really. He wasn’t like Sonic or Tails or Knuckles, he hadn’t done anything to earn their love and affection. He’d hurt them too many times to be allowed the privilege of calling them his parents… no matter how much he wished he could.“S-shit, I’m- I didn’t mean to- I’m sorry.” He choked out before teleporting away.He hadn’t had a specific location in mind when he teleported, and ended up teleporting to the roof. The roof tiles were covered in snow, and Shadow nearly slipped. He sat down near the edge of the roof, far enough that nobody would spot him if they walked out of the house.There was a tightness in his chest, making it hard to breathe. His eyes were burning and his vision grew blurry. He was-He choked on a sob. He was crying. Why was he crying? Why did he feel like some unseen weight was crushing him? It felt like… rejection.Tom didn’t want Shadow to call him dad, that much was clear to him. He’d never had that look on his face when Sonic, Tails or Knuckles called him dad. He was probably angry at Shadow for daring to call him that without permission.His muzzle heated with shame. He hadn’t even meant to say it. He may… occasionally think of Tom as a father figure, but he never meant to voice that thought. Tom never said that it was allowed, therefore it wasn’t. He’d been trained well enough to know that.Shadow hugged his legs to his chest as his sobs grew stronger, feeling wet tears drip down his muzzle. Why was he always fucking up? Why couldn’t he just be glad they hadn’t thrown him out yet? Why did he need to push the limit on what he was allowed to do?As he curled up on the roof, he wished that he could go to Tom or Maddie for comfort. But he couldn’t. He couldn’t face them again so soon after his recent transgression.Not for the first time, he wished Maria was still here. He never had to worry around her. He knew that she’d loved him, he knew that he was allowed to call her his sister, and that she’d been happy to call him her brother. Everything had been so easy with her.Now he couldn’t go a week without failing in some way. How had the Wachowskis put up with him for so long? He only hoped they would forgive him, and wouldn’t kick him out.

Kuroo was staring at the door like it held the answers to the universe. Well, not the universe at large, as in space and all that. A smaller one. His universe. The one that revolved around his life on this stupid floating ball of rock. And his life right now had a lot of unknowns. He had been offered a job he really wanted, but it meant moving to another city for a few years. And he simply didn’t want to leave. He belonged in this little apartment. He belonged in the space he had carved next to Kenma through the years. And yes, maybe things hadn’t been great for a while. Maybe him and Kenma no longer fit like they used to. But he was still where he belonged. Right?Kuroo continued to stare at the door. He didn’t want to go in quite yet, not when his brain was this loud still. With a sigh and a hand rubbing at his neck, he turned around and headed for the one other place he always felt like he belonged. It wasn’t too far, but the walk felt good too, a way to warm up a bit before he started the drills he was planning. When he got to the gymnasium, he breathed in the familiar smell of the flooring and the plastic of the balls and the dust that people tracked in from the street. He changed in the locker room, nodding to some of the familiar faces, and then started to run around the course. By the time he made it through his fifth set of drills, his brain was blissfully quiet and some of the regular guys had started a game in the corner. He drifted over and joined and that’s when his soul started singing, like it always did when he was playing.He played a few sets with them, he cheered and joked around and clapped his teammates on the backs, and for a moment he felt like everything made sense, if only right then. The jokes followed in the locker room as everyone changed, and when he was walking out, there he was. The center of his universe. His person.“You didn’t come home at the regular time, so I figured something happened and you’d be here,” Kenma said, not looking up from his phone. He was leaning against the wall and Kuroo knew he wanted to sit down but didn’t want to be stepped on by the people exiting the gym.Kuroo shrugged and leaned on the wall next to him. “I needed to burn through some energy.”Kenma hummed. “You mean you needed your brain to shut up.”“Well, yeah,” Kuroo snorted. “They offered me the job in Osaka this morning.” His voice had held steady, but the only thing keeping his hands from shaking was holding the strap of his bag.“Finally, they should have offered it to you months ago.” Kenma still didn’t look up from his phone as he said it and that made Kuroo smile. They’d grown so much in the past few years, and yet some things didn’t change.“I told them I needed to think about it for a couple days.” And that did make Kenma look up.“What? Why?”“I needed to talk to you about it, didn’t I?” Kuroo smiled. “Moving is a big thing, so I needed to know what you wanted to do before I took it.”“Tetsu, we both know this opportunity is everything you’ve wanted since you joined this company. Of course you’re taking it.” Kenma’s eyes were steady, but his voice was sad.“Would you come with me?” The hope was almost too much, but Kuroo knew the answer to that question before he even asked. It was the reason he hadn’t been able to go into their apartment earlier.“No, not right now,” Kenma answered. “But that doesn’t mean we have to be over. Look at Akaashi and Bokuto, they’re together even though Bokuto is always traveling. Or Hinata and Kageyama, they’re in different countries and they’re still disgustingly happy.”Kuroo smiled sadly. “Yeah, you’re right. I just always thought we’d never be apart like that.”Kenma leaned into him slowly, and Kuroo wrapped an arm around his shoulders. “Just because we’e not in the same city doesn’t mean we are apart. I will come visit you and you will come visit me and we will make it work. And when they realize how much of an asset you are they will offer you the lead position in the offices here. Give them a year.”Kuroo laughed. Kenma’s confidence in him made him feel warm all over.“Besides, it will be good for us to have routines and spaces outside of each other for once. I don’t think we’ve been apart since we were 7, maybe it’s time we find new spaces for ourselves.” Kenma leaned even more heavily on him as he said this, which Kuroo knew meant he wasn’t feeling as confident as he would have liked.“Yeah, you’re right. But I will miss you,” he said. And he felt Kenma relax slightly against him.“And I will miss you too. Now come on, let’s go home, I ordered dinner and it must be cold by now.” Kenma pushed away from the wall and tugged at Kuroo’s arm.And maybe he was right. Maybe this was just a new way for them to grow. Maybe they’d both find more spaces to belong to. And then they’d come back together and share them with each other.

Because of this, she tried to treasure as much as possible the few scattered peaceful moments they could spend together, just the two of them. That’s why she didn’t say a word.
  Smile. Just smile.

I’d like to swing by Bookworms to get a couple of new novels, why don’t you join me? We can eat something together afterwards, as usual!”She was fairly agitated when sending the message, but that serene and sparkling attitude never abandoned her soul.Her smile was of those which mesmerized people, making them swirl into the air, making them get carried away by the wind. Anyone who laid their eyes on her perceived their heart skipping a beat, without even realizing.Minutes seemed to shift into hours while she was waiting for Akihiko to text back. In the meantime, she decided to pack up her school supplies and clean her desk, maybe to hide a certain delicate disquiet.Finally, the cellphone buzzed, causing her to flinch.“Sorry, I believe you’ll have to go back to the dorm without me, today. My training will last longer than usual. We’ll hang out together some other time. Show me the books you bought later this evening. See you.”Minako felt a small cry of pain rising up from her heart: she knew her senpai was a busy person just like her, however she had once again a strange sensation, as if something in his responses wasn’t quite consistent with what Akihiko was and always had been towards her.But she blew away that thought barely forming at the edges of her mind, with a gentle puff of air.“No worries, senpai. Do your best today!”She put her phone away and headed towards the exit.
  Smile. Just smile.

He would never hurt innocent people.The core of that anger comes from his past, from being an orphan in the brutal slums of Yokohama.But that makes two of you. He wasn’t completely alone, both of you had been thrown into this world of poverty and neglect, without parental love. But you had each other. And you made your own definition of “family.”You always tried to pull him out from under Dazai’s manipulation techniques, the ones designed to crush his self-esteem. Sometimes, you thought your opinion didn’t weigh as much for him as his did for you, because he still kept chasing Dazai’s approval.But that’s far from how Akutagawa sees it. Because of you, he lives in a complicated state of mind.He hates himself and everyone around him. But then there’s you. Always here for him. Always understanding, even when he doesn’t deserve it.And that drives him mad. Because it’s fine to disappoint himself, but you? The guilt is unbearable.He never was expressive with words. Only actions. Sacrificing his life for you in a heartbeat, protecting you from others even if you never asked for it. And you tease him for that (he hates that side of you).Also, on rare occasions he talks to you calmly, openly before detaching himself again.After the exhausting fight with Atsushi—his new rival, for some reason you don’t want to understand because it would just create more problems—it was impossible not to tease him a little when he came back to the shared place you two have. It showed in the furrow of his brows, and the quick side glance he gave you before focusing back on disinfecting, hissing slightly.“No shit, Sherlock.”“Do you like her?”He scoffs while lightly tapping the damp cotton against his skin.“Not in the mood for your stupid questions.”You roll your eyes playfully.“Are you ever in the mood?”He shoots you another threatening glare. He swears you didn’t smell like that before. Suddenly, the thought terrifies him. Because why the hell did he notice that?Your hands were too delicate for his taste. Almost foreign. Like this was a Michelin-star meal and not just something Atsumu whipped up in his half-asleep state.Atsumu cleared his throat.Nothing.He tapped his foot.Still nothing.He leaned forward, chin in hand, voice lower than usual. “Slept real good last night, huh?”Sakusa nodded without looking up. “Yeah. Since Elsie and Charles got married things have been amicable, but not particularly passionate, Elsie’s beginning to wonder if he is just shy or if he doesn’t want to seem uncouth or if he doesn’t want to push her too much. Maybe she’s giving off an aura that she doesn’t want him. She realizes neither of them are making the most of living each other. She puts her bookmark in her book and sets it on the side table next to her. Charles is focused on his book, so she reaches over to hold his hand resting on the settee. “I’m going up to bed. Are you coming?” Elsie asks leaning towards Charles.
Charles looks up abruptly from his book. He looks down into Elsie’s eyes as if he’s startled that she’s there at all. He looks up at the clock on the mantelpiece. He didn’t get the hint. “Yes, I suppose it’s time.”
“That wasn’t exactly what I meant.” The pointedness of her statement makes him snap to attention. She notices the passion burn in his eyes.
“Why tonight? It’s not a special occasion.” The confusion is evident in his voice.
“Why does it have to be a special occasion? We’re newlyweds. I know we’re not young newlyweds, but it seems as if we’re missing out on an opportunity.”
“I’m not sure what you mean.” The honesty in that statement startles both of them.
“Am I making the most of loving you? Are you making the most of loving me? The time we have together, just the two of us, is rare and precious and we’re wasting it! We don’t even talk in the evenings the way we did when we still lived at Downton. I love you, Charles Carson, but we’re not doing a very good job of being married.”
Charles reaches over and gently touches a loose curl at Elsie’s temple. “I didn’t know you were upset with things as they are.”
“I’m not upset with the way things are. I’m sad that we’re not making the most of this.” Elsie is trying to make him see her point of view.
Just as she finishes speaking Charles comes closer to her and kisses her. “It’s not that I don’t want to, even everyday, but I didn’t want you to think of me as a cad. I adore you.”
“Can we go up to bed now?” Elsie is trying to persuade Charles without pushing him.
“Of course, we can. All you ever had to do was ask.” Charles brings Elsie’s hand up to his lips and kisses it softly.
She can’t help but blush now that they’re both on the same page. There’s a part of that finds this awkward.
“Don’t ever be embarrassed to be a passionate, loving woman. It’s part of who you are and why I love you.”

The day was long, endless even, just like every other day in that stupid building. Working from night to day, slaving away at a computer. You could barely even remember the last time you had enjoyed the outside. It felt like just months ago you were headed on a path towards your dreams, but in an instant, you’re sucked down into the living hell that is 9-5 jobs. At first, working at C&A seemed like a bright opportunity, a fresh slate after graduating, something that could hold you down when nowhere else would take you. It was simple, and it helped you scramble up a few coins at best. But quickly this ‘bright opportunity’ fell through, just like the rest of those dreams. 
  The quiet hum of electricity filled the stale air engulfing you. Your eyes grew weak and strained from blankly staring at the screen inside your office cubicle. After properly ensuring that you were a living breathing zombie you could finally pack up your things to escape for the day. Letting yourself up from the stiff chair you had been planted in for the past 9 hours resulted in a satisfying crack of your joints. You sighed and lazily gazed over the surrounding cubicles. Most of them had been closed up, causing the endless room to be near silent. Most of the lights were dim if not turned off. The few people still working were mostly finishing up. As you padded down the cheaply carpeted flooring you eventually reached the elevator, stepping into the cool lift that strangely enough had a faint aroma of cologne leaving you feeling weirdly nauseous, After you were sure you’d gone down at least 6 floors it dawned on you. “Fuck..” You hissed through your teeth as you brought a hand up to gently pinch at the bridge of your nose. You had forgotten your purse in the office. Maybe all of these late shifts were messing with your memory. After a dreadfully long ride back up the elevator you finally managed to get back into the office, everyone had left by now, and the area was darker than you’d possibly ever seen it. You could faintly hear your own feet pressing against the carpet as you walked, the sound was strangely unnerving for you. Perhaps the fact that it was the only noise around you. Or at least that's what you thought until a slight buzz presumably made by a computer caught your attention. The noise grew louder along with a gentle blueish glow as you approached your desk. 
  Did I forget to turn it off? 
  You wondered, your curiosity rising as you turned the corner to peek at your assigned computer. But to your surprise, the computer wasn’t the only thing out of the ordinary. Plugged into the computer was what seemed to be a headset of some sort. You’d never owned one yourself but you remembered admiring them and what came with them. The ability to put it on and it’ll make you feel like you're in a whole other world. You shook off your awe to glance around the area to see if you had the wrong desk. But to your surprise it was yours. 
  I was just here, How did this get here? 
  You thought to yourself, pulling your chair out to sit on as you gently handled the VR headset. Glancing between the machine in your hands and the glowing computer screen you couldn’t help but notice the shiver run down your spine. Slowly you let your head lean forward to allow your hands to stretch the headset over your head. Firmly placing it over your head you pulled it down to cover your eyes, and then, Darkness.

Then he looked at me, and even after all these many years, I can still recall how the light caught in his dew-spangled hair; how it refracted so brilliantly into millions of the most perfect colors. It was such a lovely sight. Then he spoke, and I understood.
  “I don’t feel comfortable as myself. I’ve always felt that I wanted to be a boy, like you, Yocchan. We could wrestle together like we did as kids and people wouldn’t look at me weird. I could play with you on the same sports teams and send you all the best passes! We could do anything we wanted forever, together. Does that make sense,” he asked this last question with a smallness in his voice that saddened me.
  
    We could do anything we wanted forever, together.
  
  “Oh. Ohhhh! I think I get it,” I said sheepishly, “Yeah it’s cool by me, Meg. You’re my best friend, and nothing’s gonna change that. Girl, boy, whatever. You’re still you, and that’s a damn fine thing as far as I’m concerned.”

  “There’s another thing. I think I love you, Yocchan.”

When he stirred in the bedsheets that morning, semi-naked and with an unusual heavy feeling, Kaiser immediately sensed something was wrong.
 
Whether it was the impending laziness, the absurd heat that left him on the verge of sweating but still felt cozy enough that he didn't want to leave the bed, or his sniffing nose, this combination of things made him wake up with a petulant expression, a scowl, and emerging bad humor.
 
Though it wasn't a persistent stress, as Kaiser felt strangely soft, his whole body pliant and glued to the bed. He felt as if he could melt against any touch, even the gentlest ones.
 
He groaned a complaint as he slowly rolled over in bed; sun rays passed through the window and made the fluffy blanket even warmer. Kaiser wished he could just curl up there and sleep a little longer.
 
He huffed with discontent.
 
He had never been sick before. If he had, he hadn't noticed. He hadn't gotten sick even when living with his father, being mistreated day and night, starving and using bread crusts as a nutritional base.
 
Why did his body decide to give in to some idiotic virus now? Now that he had comfort, proper food, hygiene, care?
 
It was simply inconvenient and illogical. He couldn't help but make more angry sounds of discontent, though they only reached the walls, since Ness was probably not home. If Alexis were, he'd be in the room with Kaiser, or else, Michael would hear footsteps or Ness's voice humming some radio song, all sounds muffled by the door, but still alive and present.
 
He stretched out his arm, which trembled slightly, an uncomfortable sensation of weakness that made him wrinkle his nose, fumbling on the table for his phone, his eyes too comfortable being closed for Kaiser to bother opening them. Unfortunately, the fateful time came to face the daylight (and screen light), when he found a cold, rectangular object. It was already past three in the afternoon.
 
That's why he was weak. He hadn't eaten anything and the flu was wandering inside him. What else could he expect?
 
As soon as he rationalized the lack of food in the last twenty hours, because he hadn't had dinner yesterday either, his brain immediately sent empty signals to his stomach. Aware of his condition, it seemed more painful.
 
He grunted in disgust at the realization. Ironic how he could go days without eating as a child, and now he was getting weak after mere hours.
 Wrapped in blankets, the ceiling fan whirring pleasantly and the evident weight on his body, the need to eat seemed to him very much a matter he could leave for later.
 
Still, he considered that if he slept now, the hunger when he woke up again would be even greater. He squeezed his eyes, whose under-eye bags gave a burning sensation, and made a thoughtful pout.
 
Of course, he could always text Ness, wherever he was.
 
Alexis would definitely be dramatic about it. Kaiser would want to roll his eyes, but lacking energy, he settled for closing them and considering the idea.
 
After all, Ness taking care... serving, in this case, is a better word (though their therapist probably wouldn't like that way of seeing things), Ness serving him for a day, while Kaiser could recover at his leisure, didn't seem like a bad idea.
 
As if giving in to a great burden, Kaiser typed a message.
 
"Sick."
 
It took less than three minutes for a response.Ness: "Kaiser?""Good morning, you're awake! I didn't wake you up today because you seemed particularly grumpy.""...""Are you sick?""Are you okay?""Do you hurt?""Is it serious?"
 
Kaiser would normally write messages, even the most mundane ones, in perfect German, without grammatical errors or agreement issues, without abbreviations.

 God bless you, Ness.

    Please, please, please. 
  
  His twentieth birthday had just passed and it was now expected of him to make an official address to the crowd of aristocracy who were currently filing into the ballroom.     It is my honour to represent a kingdom of such kindness and compassion, and to support my father in his entertainment of 
    the people.
  
  In the silence of his bedroom, Remus laughed, his father showed no compassion to the starving peasants who were currently asleep under leaking roofs. And his entertainment had long been restricted from the people, instead falling to the audience of distant nobles and wealthy courts. 
  
    I am especially prepared to support my father and this kingdom in its pursuit to eradicate the deadly disease known as lycanthropy, exiling all those plagued with this monstrous condition. The safety of our people should not be given up for the safety of unnatural dark creatures such as these.
  
  Remus’ eyebrows furrowed, he knew his father’s position on all dark creatures and he was aware of the bill being passed. Still he couldn’t help but hesitate, according to Lily — a servant girl who Remus had been practically raised alongside — the towns people cared very little about magical creatures. There were hardly ever any attacks, and the people’s true concern was the inability to keep food on the table.

  He felt the cold and heavy presence of
  his father settle next to him, gripping his shoulder slightly too tight as he announced the coming of age of his son. Then he stepped back, cold blue eyes fixated on the back of Remus’ neck where the prince could feel a rising bile mixed with shame and weakness.

The city’s electric tapestry – white headlights, neon signs, golden apartment windows – painted shifting constellations on the lenses of his glasses. Midnight cradled the world, but inside him, something stirred. Restless. Aching.A melody flickered at the edge of his consciousness, fragile as a moth against glass. Elusive. He chased it, a low hum vibrating in his throat, raw and unstructured. He tested its shape, bending the sound, searching for the curve that felt true. Was it yearning? Was it solace? It felt like both.Beside him on the floor lay his constant companion: a worn notebook, its pages a cosmos of their own. Not neat staves, but inky constellations. Words crowded margins, crossed out, rewritten, arrows connecting fragmented thoughts. Phrases like "lonely satellite," "tidal pull," "cracked porcelain heart" swam amidst musical notations only he could fully decipher. It was a map of feeling – **pain seeking beauty, ache searching for a voice.**He picked up his pen, its familiar weight an anchor. The city lights reflected in his glasses seemed to pulse in time with his quiet hum. He listened harder, past the hum of the refrigerator, past Minho’s distant game sounds, past Taemin’s soft footfalls. He listened *inward*, to the whisper only he could hear, the collective sigh of hearts too full or too empty. He captured it – the vulnerability no one else quite dared to voice, the fierce, stubborn hope that bloomed even in the cracks.The pen scratched against the paper, a counterpoint to his humming. The rhythm wasn't dictated by a metronome, but by the thrumming of his own pulse. **"Like water on the moon,"** he scribbled suddenly, the words flowing out as naturally as breath. A paradox. Barrenness touched by impossible, fleeting wetness. Cold desolation holding the memory of life. It resonated deep within him, a perfect, aching fragment of the feeling he sought.He stopped humming. He lifted his head slightly, eyes closed now, seeing only the internal landscape of the song. And then his voice rose. Not loud, not showy, but clear and true, filling the space around the window. It wasn't just singing a fragment; it was embodying the emotion. Rich with warmth, edged with a vulnerability that felt almost too intimate, it cut through the dorm's quiet activity. It was a **lighthouse beam** piercing the emotional dark – acknowledging the shadows, the depth of the water, but shining fiercely nonetheless.Outside, Seoul glittered, indifferent. Inside, Minho paused his game for a fraction of a second, Taemin’s steps stilled unconsciously, drawn by the thread of raw feeling weaving through the dark apartment. And Jonghyun, bathed in the reflected starlight of the city, poured the moon river onto the page, one resonant note, one aching, beautiful phrase at a time. The song was being born, a beacon crafted from whispered truths and the rhythm of his own beating heart.

  Still.

  A dead world.

  .

  Nothing lives. Not anymore.

  Soon she’ll be dead, too.
It's so, so cold.
  A dull 
  
    boom
  
   echoes from somewhere in the murky dark, bright fiery light splitting across the horizon. Another fault line breaking.

  .
  Her oxygen pack beeps.

  Her eyes sting and burn. Her chest squeezing and her heart breaking. She has no tears left to cry.
  She takes a breath. It’s getting harder, now.

  She wonders absently if they ever had a chance at all.
  She misses them. Her friends. Her family.
  Will she see them again? When she breathes her last breath, will she find them on the other side?
  Or will there just be nothing. Emptiness and oblivion.

  Stuffing the device back into his pocket, he scans the area: a man and a woman loiter by an alleyway on the opposite side of the street, cash slipped between them, followed by an all-too-quick-handshake; in the apartments above, a man wanders to and fro on his balcony, smoking a cigarette; and a young couple race down the street in the opposite direction, huddled under an umbrella, their hair plastered to their heads. The rain pounds against the pavement of the near-black street, the sparse streetlights offering only brief reprieve from the darkness, the coned spotlights highlighting the silvery rain-streaks that hurtle to the ground.
  No one behind. No one following. Good.
  “Thank you for walking me home,” the woman walking next to Childe says, looking up at him with wide, amber eyes. “It’s my fault for staying out so late. If I hadn’t missed the bus, I wouldn’t have inconvenienced you like this.”
  “It’s no trouble. Any man would be lucky to walk beside a beautiful lady such as yourself,” he replies.
  It’s true—no man would be able to resist the beautiful creature beside him, her makeup set perfectly to accentuate the dainty tip of her nose, her well carved cheekbones, and her deep purple eyeshadow that makes her eyes shine like the stars in the night sky. Her hair, too, is perfectly set, a bouncy bob that accentuates her round, youthful face.
  “You said you’re on Bashnya Street, yeah?”
  “Yes, that’s right. It’s not far now.”
  “You got it. I used to live there when I was younger, so I actually know a shortcut we can take.”
  She blinks twice, tilting her head. “A shortcut?”
  “Right, through that alleyway just ahead. That is, if you don’t mind walking that way with a guy like me.”
  She makes a good show of consideration, biting her lower lip and tucking a strand of hair thoughtfully behind her ear, glancing up and down the street as though expecting to spot some sordid gang lingering in a corner behind them. Then she nods, once. “Okay. That’s fine with me.”
  “Excellent.” Childe retracts his hand within his coat sleeve, feeling the smooth press of metal against his fingers. “Let’s get going then. It’s dangerous to linger out here for too long.”
  They push on another few hundred metres through the rain, until they reach the alleyway, a yawning black chasm which no light touches. A man could commit anything in there—even murder—and never be caught.
  The woman tucks and retucks the same strand of hair, drawing the wispy strands around her finger. “Through here, right?”
  “Yep, this is the one.” Childe steps to the side and gestures forward. “Ladies first.”
  “Thank you,” she says with a curtsey.
  They’ll see how much she’ll be thanking him in a minute.
  The further into the alleyway they go, the more the darkness presses in, looming down from the towering apartments above, and Childe blinks, trying to adjust. He needs to be on full alert for what comes next.
  Unlike his companion, it won’t be pretty.
  As for said companion, she glances about her as they continue to walk, her hands bunched into her coatsleeves, arms folded across her body. Her hair bobs with each step, swishing with the motion of her head.

And so they meandered down the labyrinthine aisles, picking mismatched plates and a glassware set, packs of silverware, and spending a good half hour in the candle section.She had tried to dissect how she felt. She had always longed for this sweet domesticity with him, but the circumstances made her gut churn. Would they have done this anyway, eventually? if it weren’t for having to run away? Would they have retired like “normal,” keeping William and raising him in the “normal” way? She corrects herself; nothing with mulder has ever been or ever could be normal. But would he have done it? For her? If only she had asked? She faintly worried that he’s only still with her because this is how it’s always been. He's only been with her, just Scully, no other women, for almost a decade. She thinks about Diana, then stops. She doesn’t have the energy. To calm herself, she looked at him.He had his nose lowered into a candle claiming to smell like “tropical breeze.” His head lifted, nose faintly wrinkling. He looked at her. “What atmosphere are we going for? I personally like warm and cozy coffee shops over coastal beach cafes,” he mused, a childish smile on his face. She nodded absently. “i’ve always liked candles that smell like fall,” she says, reaching for one that read “crisp apple.” It had reminded her of her mother’s apple pie she always made on the fourth of July. She sat it in the cart. He snagged one more as she walked further down the aisle.When they arrived at the house, it was eerily dark inside. The white shutters are stained with the years, and the rickety porch faintly made Scully worry she would fall through as she trudged up the steps, walmart bags in tow and mulder ghosting behind her. She stopped in front of the door, waiting for Mulder to produce the key.They had attained the house through the help of the Gunmen, over a few months of calls from payphones and coded letters somehow reaching them at their various motel doors. They had gotten the key at a 7/11 outside of Lexington, Kentucky. They pulled up to a gas pump, and not 30 seconds later, an old VW van pulled in to the other side of the pump. Smiles shared, but no hugs. No words. a flick of the wrist while waiting for the tank to fill, and the piece of brass was his. It was real. A home, waiting for them. As they pulled out of the gas station, Scully could see Frohike give her a warm smile and soft nod. She holds on to this, still.He pulled it out of his pocket, the lone key dangling on a keyring. You bury your sister, your robes as white as her bloodless skin. Jin Ling wails nearby, and you wish you could join in screaming your grief, splitting ears as if they were skin beneath a blade.
  A Jin servant carries your nephew away, and you remain silent.
  Jin Guangyao hovers, somehow awkward despite his newfound Sect Leader status. He addresses you, and you shoot him a glare. Perhaps he sees your pain in your eyes, but you know it is more likely that he only sees your anger.
  You do not know how to grieve. When your dogs were sent away, you were angry. When your home was invaded and your parents slaughtered, you were angry. When Wei Wuxian left, you were angry.
  He killed her. You are angry.
  Your sister is dead, and you cannot feel grief, and for that, you are angry.
  Someone has to take the child. You volunteer, suddenly terrified of returning to Lotus Pier alone. Your fear manifests as a snarl, harsh words flying from your throat like daggers.
  Jin Guangyao politely insists otherwise — why should the young heir be sent to you? He is a Jin. He belongs in Lanling.
  Your nephew is being taken, forced to live with a man who is not you. You punch Jin Guangyao, your ring splitting his skin, blood marring his elegant features. You step back, Zidian sparkling at your wrist, and you want to lash it across his face.
  Your disciples push you back. One of them kneels, begging for mercy on your behalf. You are grieving, he says; you must be forgiven.
  Jin Guangyao forgives you, because he is a better man than you. You turn on your heel and leave.
  When you arrive home, the rooms are empty. They have been for a while, ever since he left, ever since she got married, but now the feeling in your chest matches.
  The throne stands tall. Empty.
  You curl up at the foot of it and weep.
  Six months later, when the leaves have turned their colors and begin to fall, limply decorating the water, you receive a letter from Lanling.
  Yunmeng is bustling, now, full of healthy citizens and merchants with heavy pockets. The Jiang disciples are growing strong under your command. Your home is recovering.
  The busy streets contrast with the inner halls of your residence. Here, you walk, eyes catching on purple shadows, ears strained for laughter that never comes. Your servants hurry away whenever they see you, eyes downcast and heads bowed low.
  You sit on your lotus throne, slouching, legs spread. There is no one left to admonish you.
  The servant kneels before you, and the letter in his hand trembles. He is fearful — in these past months, long days of grief and nightmares have left you quick to anger, and the servants are the most convenient vessel for outrage. Perhaps you should feel guilty for treating them this way, but you do not.
  You take the letter, and the servant bows low and hurries away.
  You read the words carefully inked onto the paper, and for the first time in six months, a spark of something light ignites within you.
  Jin Ling is loud. His tearful wails pierce your ears, close in proximity as you bounce him on your shoulder. You pat his back, you shush and try to soothe him, but he cries on.   “Think about it!” Curt spoke with a bit more glee now, as if this idea in his head was being melded, his brain working to have Owen understand whatever he was saying, no matter how many times he needed to trip over his own words to make it work, “All our fake IDs and passports, the way we’ve hid for months without the agencies knowing, we could go anywhere and they may never find us.”
  The idea was intriguing, Owen didn’t want it to sound as though he didn't think so. Curt was right, they could indeed attempt an escape, to run as far away as they could. The thought made him smile, settling down in a quiet spot, traumas finally healing, fears being released into the air that surrounded them, never to be seen again. A gust of wind pulled him out of the fantasy, and he felt the snow drift into his eyes, making him close them, “I don’t know.”
  Curt elbowed him, a frown tracing his face, eyebrows slanted in slight frustration at Owen’s hesitance to even think about it, “Just humor me. Please?”
  Owen grumbled but nodded in agreement. How could he say no? He was always weak to Curt, “Fine, fine. I’ll bite. Where will we live? It better be someplace warm, I can’t stand this cold weather,” he grumbled, pressing his coat deeper into his skin, trying to warm himself up a bit more.
  “Fine, fine. Warm, got it. But I want there to be people around us. Neighbors and whatnot,” he said, kicking a bit of snow, “I don’t want to be stuck with you for eternity.”
  Owen scoffed, “Oh, wow, thanks, Mega. And here I thought you liked me,” gently, he punched Curt’s arm, feeling his partner's muscles tense. Curt hit him back with a bit more force than he had meant, knocking Owen off balance for a moment, but he laughed a bit anyways, “Ok, ok. We’re stuck together but not really. And we live happily ever after in God knows where and we die minutes apart.”
  Curt grins, “Perfect. That’s exactly what I want,” he says with seriousness that makes Owen feel bad for joking, “Happily ever after, God knows where, with you.”
  Owen practically groaned, Curt’s cliche life sounded so unreachable, yet he enjoyed the thought, it made his heart pound a bit faster, “Always an optimist, aren’t you, Mega?”
  “The glass is half full, always will be,” he smiled, before leaving Owen with a small kiss, “Besides, what’s the fun in living realistically all the time? We could die at any point, but who wants to think about that?”
  Owen nodded in agreement, gripping Curt’s hand, “You’re right.”
  “Always am.”
  “Always are.”
