The hum in the old Kabasaki plant wasn’t fully mechanical, nor fully chemical. It had a pulse to it. Like veins running beneath the concrete and rust — like the bones of the place still remembered what it had seen.
Uru’s breath hitched as the restraints around his wrists loosened, just slightly.His fingers twitched. His vision was still sluggish, warped by the sedative, but the experience was over. He was awake. The girl was gone, and so was that damned detective. And yet, he didn’t stand. He  could. The sedative had faded enough, his body quickly getting over it. But something pressed on his chest like phantom weight. Not fear — he wasn’t a man who feared very easily anymore — but instinct. A cold, animal-brained warning:
   Wrong. Wrong. Leave. 
His mind struggled to catch up. He blinked. And in that half-second of darkness, through the slits in his mask—
A man. Standing near the rusted shelves across from the machine. Tall. Still. Poised like a knife. Platinum hair. Sharp symmetry. A face almost familiar. Not the detective, not quite. Something…  worse. The harder Uru tried to focus, the more the figure changed — subtly, impossibly — as if it was made from more than one person.He blinked again. A mistake. This time, the man wasn’t  there  . He was  behind  him. He could feel it. Uru’s pulse lurched. He  knew  this room — had studied every bolt and console before this situation even happened. He’d stumbled upon it half-by-accident, and would have tested the machine himself, had it not been rigged so  elaborately  to break if moved or used improperly. Nothing should have been able to sneak up on him here. And yet, something had. Watching.  Judging. The sense of scrutiny was so sharp it sliced through the air, prickling the back of his neck.“… Detective?  ” Uru rasped. His voice came out dry. Thin.  Stupid.
He hadn’t  meant  to say it. But those eyes — cold, vicious, calculating — they’d  reminded  him of something. Of that man. Detective Kaname Date. But more angular. Crueler. Like someone had sculpted that detective into a weapon.And something else. A feeling beneath the surface. Like this man had once lived behind  his  eyes. Walked the same paths. Stared into the same voids.
The eyes reminded Uru of his own.
“Who are you…” Uru muttered, staggering to his feet. The restraints clattered against the armrests like bones as they fully fell away from his wrists.No answer. Of course not. But the silence had weight to it. Like the very air refused to forget.  Forget what?  He turned, some deeper instinct tugging him toward the doorway. And sure enough—
There. The man. Standing in the entrance, still as death. Blocking the only exit. He wasn’t just a hallucination. Uru  knew  it. He had a  presence. Heavy. Real. That inhuman posture, shoulders too square, head just too still — like he didn’t wear his flesh the same way everyone else did. He was wrong.  Wrong  in the way the world sometimes made things that never should have existed.
Their eyes locked.
Uru had stared death in the face. Many times. He  had been  death.  Tearer.  But this wasn’t death. This was something worse. The man looked at him not with fear. Not with hatred. But with  recognition. Like he  knew  him. Not recently. Not from police reports or news clips. But intimately. Deeply. As if they’d grown up together — or  might  have, had the universe tilted just a  fraction  to the left. But the recognition was wrong, nonetheless. It felt hollow.“Stop it,” Uru hissed, without thinking. His voice was taut and clipped, akin to a thread ready to snap. Not rage.  Panic.  Like a child getting stared down by an older brother who’d long since learned how to hurt him without even lifting a hand.
   That thought made no sense.
The man smiled. Barely. No warmth. No amusement. Just that glint of recognition. And under it, unmistakable:  disappointment. Like Uru had failed some test. Like he was a younger sibling who hadn’t lived up to the blood he didn’t know he shared.
 That thought made no sense.  
 
… Or  too much sense. The feeling hit him like nausea. Like falling. Of course. He staggered forward, hand reaching out. As if to touch. As if to  confirm. But when he blinked again, unwillingly—
Gone. The man was gone. Only silence remained. Only the machine, purring softly in the gloom of the room. He turned back toward it. Breathing in the chemical sting still hanging faintly in the air. Expecting… something.
But nothing came.
And he had no time left to waste playing whatever  game  that man wanted to start.

Charlie kicks one of the cones he was told to collect for Mrs. Singh. He’s angry and frustrated with himself. Why did he agree to join the rugby team? Right, because of his stupid crush on Nick. He takes a deep breath and looks around, noticing the tackle bags.
  Maybe he could practice a little to overcome his fear. He runs towards the tackle bag and throws himself on it, standing up and putting the tackle bag into place again. Repeating the action a few times, with each tackle he gains a little more confidence. Sure, it’s not the same as tackling someone else, but it’s a start.
  “Hey, what are you doing?”
  Someone calls out to him as he's putting the tackle bag back into place. He turns around and sees Nick running towards him, still wearing his sports clothes.
  “Mrs. Singh told me I should commit to tackling. I should not worry about getting hurt and just throw myself in,” Charlie explains as Nick stands in front of him.
  “I see. Maybe I can help you practice?” Nick suggests with a smile.
  “You don’t have to do that.”
  “I think I do. After all, it was me who suggested you join the rugby team in the first place.”
  “You're still wearing your sports clothes,” Charlie points out.
  “Yeah… I noticed you didn’t come to the changing room, which made sense after the awful practice and… I was worried about you.”
  Charlie doesn’t know what to say to this. Nick’s worried about him and he wants to help him practice.
  “Can I have a hug?”
  “Of course.” Nick wraps his arms around him and pulls him closer.
  Charlie sighs and closes his eyes for a moment, wrapping his arms around Nick’s back, feeling a little better just from Nick being close to him.
  “I’d like it if you helped me practice,” he says into Nick’s ear.
  Nick pulls away from the hug and nods.
  “Okay. Can you do the tackling on the bag again? I want to see it.” Nick stands a few steps away, while Charlie runs in the opposite direction. “You’re ready?”
  Charlie nods and runs towards the tackle bag, sending it to the ground as he lands on top of it.
  “That was great, Charlie!” Nick compliments him and Charlie stands up. Together with Nick’s help they put the tackle bag into place. “Do you wanna practice on the bag again or do you think you’re ready to try to tackle 
  
    me
  
  ?”
  “I think I’m ready,” Charlie’s voice is shaky as he speaks. He might be comfortable tackling the tackle bag, landing on something that feels firm, but soft. Quite the opposite from tackling another human being, feeling muscles.
  Nick steps closer, seeing how nervous Charlie is. He places his hands on his shoulders.
  “Hey, it’s okay. You got this. We start easy. I stand here and you tackle me. Like the first time.”
  Charlie nods, still nervous, but with Nick’s encouragement he feels safe. He runs in the opposite direction again before turning around, facing Nick.
  “Come on, Charlie. You can do it,” Nick’s still encouraging and motivating him.
  With a deep breath, Charlie runs towards Nick, their bodies colliding together as Charlie sends Nick to the ground, lying half on top of him.
  “Great,” Nick says and Charlie stands up, reaching out his hand to help Nick up. Little sparks fly between them as they touch.
  Charlie does it a few more times, tackling Nick. Like the first time, they also practice it while Nick’s running around. Which feels difficult but not impossible. Nick smiles at him all the time, encouragement again and again, giving Charlie the confidence that he needs.
  Charlie lands on top of Nick after the tackle. Both boys are breathing heavily and smiling at each other. For a moment, they lay like this. Charlie wants to get up, afraid that someone might see them but is stopped by Nick’s hand, holding him in place.
  “Can I kiss you?” Nick asks.
  “Yes.” Charlie leans down and brushes their lips together in a gentle kiss. This is still so new to them.
  It’s a little dangerous, being out in the open on the field and kissing but Nick’s lips feel so good. After a while, they stand up and Charlie collects the cones like he was supposed to with Nick’s help. They go to the changing room and Charlie feels a little better.

“My name is Mattia Rossi. I was not given a middle name— or if I was, I haven’t been made aware. I am twelve years old, and have been homeless for two years. Ever since leaving my house back up in Maine, monster attacks have been getting worse and more often. I train myself with the daggers my mother gave me when I was seven. I still don’t know what I’m supposed to do with them— I don’t think I’m very good at it.I found this old unused book in an alleyway. Hopefully this wasn’t owned by anyone. It had a pen and none of the pages were used or even dirty. It just felt like fate to grab it up. To my knowledge, I’m in California. I’m very far away from my hometown, but I’d like to keep it that way.Right now, I’m outside of this absolutely giant building. It’s so loud even outside— I wonder what it’s like inside.”
  end entry
Mattia slowly approached the bright lights and neon lasers of the building. She’s never seen such a thing before. It was mesmerizing— like a magical being coaxing her to come forth. Her backpack sat low on her shoulders. Upbeat music blasted through the doors and windows from the inside. It was nothing familiar; all she’s ever heard were the quiet harps and chiming church bells. It was loud and felt like it vibrated her entire skeleton.With reluctance, she stepped forward and pressed her hand to open the door. It didn’t budge. She pursed her lips and looked around to make sure nobody saw before pulling the door instead and stepping through.Inside was ten times brighter and louder. Flashing pink lights immediately gave her vertigo. Her eyes instinctively squeezed shut. Within not even 30 seconds of Mattia stepping through, she was crowded by at least 3 people, likely workers, shoving plates with food in her face. Mattia immediately stepped back and held her hands out for them to back up.One, a younger woman with bright blonde hair and freakishly blue eyes, spoke up with a placating and soothing smile. Her plate of food lowered.“Hey, little girl. Where are your parents? You seem a bit… young to be by yourself.” The lady said. Mattia’s heart thumped with both the best of the music and her own apprehension. Prospero James Caruso knew far more about the man who sat across from him every day at exactly 3:15 in the cafe on the corner of his street than he cared to admit.
The man was incredibly… soft. His features delicate, eyes a soft dove color, skin a gentle tan. His hair was almost artfully messy, though it was obviously unintentional due to the amount of times he'd seen his slender hands run through it, musing it further.
He knew his name was William—it was written on his notebook, Prospero was not nosy for noticing, thank you very much. He was just… observant. Very observant.
He knew that he always ordered an iced latte and a chocolate croissant, and he always burned his mouth on the pastry. He also knew he got a peach tea on his way out, the brunette man's voice containing a soft southern lilt (which was oh so rare in a small town in Maine) as he apologized to whoever was working the counter for the inconvenience.
He knew that William would get a call from a woman named Winona—or was it Winnie? He heard both—every Tuesday. He knew that he always asked her how their mom (he always called her Mama) was doing.
He knew his nose was slightly crooked, and his teeth had a small gap between them that showed when he laughed at whatever the woman had said. He knows how many freckles were on his face (It was 53, Prospero had taken the time to count when his laptop died on a rainy day last summer).
And he knows that he writes.
Oh, he writes. A lot. And he always bites his bottom lip when he does, his eyes always slightly narrowed as his pen dances across the page, filling it with whatever it was that he wrote.
Some days, Prospero muses silently about what he might be writing about. A story, maybe. Or his life. A partner?
He always wears a pair of white headphones with a single The Smiths sticker on one side, the sound of their music often leaking slightly into the air. Prospero didn't mind, of course. How could he, really, when that small, mindless smile lit up William’s face every time the music started up?
He didn't know other things, though. He didn't know who had sewn careful patches onto the coat he wore. He didn't know how he had ended up in this little town (but he assumed it was because of college, it was for most). Hell, he didn't even know if he was gay.
He didn't know why his bag was so worn, or why he always furrowed his brows when someone texted him. He didn't know who had drawn on his sneakers, or what book he had tucked into the bag he carried.
But he wanted to know. He wanted to know more than he had ever wanted to know something in his life, and he couldn't quite puzzle out why.
Today was different. Very very different.
Prospero walked into the small cafe as he always did, frowning as he closed his umbrella, the cold water having already seeped into his jacket.
William was already there, when Prospero arrived. That was new. He had his same order, of course, but his headphones weren't on.
As he makes his way to the counter to pick up his usual (a small macchiato and a cannoli), his eyes linger on William. It seemed he had got caught in the rain, as he was shivering… and wet, of course. Soaked to the bone, really.
He was so lost in thought that he almost missed his order, snapping back to attention as the short, ginger barista handed him his order.
“Will, huh?” The girl said. Her nametag read ‘Morella’.
“...I don't know what you're talking about.”
He made sure to tip her extra.
“May I?” He murmurs as he approaches the small table, only to be met with a nod and a smile.
“Of course!”
That was also new.
William had never spoken to him outside of a simple “Can I sit here?” before. Prospero didn't really even know why he still asked, since he sat there every day.
He takes his seat as always, carefully setting down his own drink and pastry, watching as William opened his notebook (Was it new? He'd never seen that one before…) and pulled out his pen.
Before he could think, he (very stupidly, now that he thought about it), opened his mouth to speak.
“I’m Prospero.”
William looked up, startled, but smiled just as quick.
“Will."

It sought obliteration.That night, as Zin-Azshari drowned in its own tears, Illidan returned to the inner sanctum. The arcane sigils he had carved in secret pulsed with eerie green light. My flame shall forge you into something eternal."Illidan closed his eyes."And if I ask for more?" he said aloud, fingers tightening around his staff."More power? More than the stars themselves burn with? Speak your desire."“…I want to save this world.”Silence.Then laughter. Deep. Cosmic. Cruel."Then burn it first, and from its ashes, we shall rebuild it in your image."Illidan hesitated—longer than he should have. In that breath of doubt, the door behind him creaked open.He turned.And there she was.She stepped from shadow like a sigh caught on moonlight. Her armor bore the sigil of the resistance—a stylized crescent wreathed in arcane tendrils. Her eyes, brilliant amethyst, locked onto his fel-lit ones without fear.Thalyssra Moonsong."Stormrage," she said, her voice calm and biting. "Plotting the world's salvation through annihilation again?"Illidan lowered his staff but did not extinguish the flames around it. “You shouldn’t be here.”“I disagree.” She walked closer. “I saw the sky tearing itself apart and thought: ‘Surely Illidan Stormrage is behind this.’ And here you are. I have had approximately one million thoughts about HDG in the past few months. I think this is the only one that’s worth posting. All of the others are too cruel and spiteful, or would hurt me too much to write, or are beyond my ability to write.HDG is a fascinating setting but my relationship with it is not great. I have at times said that I hated it. I have at times said that I loved it, but in a way the lorets wouldn’t appreciate. I have tried very hard to love it in a more traditional way, and failed. I do not know why this is. It has things I like in it, kinks and such. I cannot pinpoint a specific thing that turns me away, not even the imperialism and rape. I just cannot love the whole. It takes up space in my brain and I don’t want it to.I have written little microessays, and then not posted them. I have thought about writing real criticism of the setting, like Drapetomania or Affini Recruitment Handbook, but the fact is other people have done better at that than I could. I have analyzed my own relationship with disability, which is perhaps the one good thing that’s come out of all this. Still the source of my emotions is unexplained.Then I listened to Blue Magic by Kelly Hogan and Bill Taft. I’d heard it before, but rediscovering it made something click, made me realize something that I knew but hadn’t internalized.It’s magic. It’s author fiat and deus ex machina, in the service of having something to believe in unconditionally. Expecting it to make sense is an exercise in futility. And that’s OK. It’s not morally wrong, or at least I hope it isn’t because I’m into stuff that’s just as author-fiat-y and ethically dubious. Even in light of that there are valid criticisms to make, but again, I don’t think I can say anything in that field that hasn’t already been said.Which brings me to my point. If the wiki had said that up front, instead of being half in-universe propaganda, I think maybe all of this would have been avoided. Maybe I would like it. It has things I like in it. Maybe I would move on. But I wouldn’t be trapped in this spiral like I am now. I know there’s a wiki rewrite in progress. I hope it goes well.(Also, Sheepwave is right. As long as you’re changing things you should rename it to the Human Domestication Guide Guide.)

Billy is pretty sure Joe only bought the single because of the band name.
Or maybe it hadn't just been the name he liked, but the hammers and sickles and red stars and other assorted commie paraphernalia on the record sleeve.
Joe's dad had been some big trade union guy, before he got sick and died, and Joe stuck with his dad's socialist politics out of blind loyalty to John Mulgrew as well as Joe Strummer.
No matter why Joe bought the record, he quickly became obsessed with the band, with the song. He played Dicks Hate The Police so much that it's burnt into Billy's brain, even now, almost 20 years later. Sometimes he wakes up in the morning with that opening guitar riff stuck in his head.
Joe even made a tape of the record so he could play it on the tour bus. Which he did. From Vancouver to Halifax, from Halifax to New York, from New York to Detroit, over and over and over.
In the end, Billy snapped and threw the tape out the window somewhere on the border between Ontario and Michigan. Billy was a lot less patient in those days.
Maybe he could have ignored it, if Joe hadn't always insisted on singing along and jumping around at the back of the tour bus while Billy or Pipe or John tried to drive, making a fool of himself, making Billy's teeth itch.
Billy can still see Joe, standing right at the back, his fat head blocking the rearview mirror, howling along: MOMMY MOMMY MOMMY LOOK AT YOUR SON, YOU MIGHT HAVE LOVED ME BUT NOW I GOT A GUN....
Even on the thousandth listen, Joe hadn't lost his pure, childlike enthusiasm for that song, even though it was about becoming a monster.
And something about the delight in Joe's eyes made Billy rip the cassette out of the tape deck and throw it on the floor and jump up and down on top of it until it was broken.
It all got kind of ugly after that. Pipe pulled Joe off Billy, then John made Billy get back in the driver's seat and keep going despite his bloody nose.
Thank God they were only a couple hours away from Detroit, and they had a gig at the Greystone the next day. If they'd had a day off, the band might have broken up then and there.
At the end of the tour, Billy bought Joe a copy of the new Dicks album to say sorry for trashing his tape. That was probably the last time Billy ever apologized to Joe for anything.

“It’s best we get out of this wall first but after that we need to find a ship so I can get you to the City. Oh and don’t worry about ammo, as long as we have glimmer I can make us some.”

You wake up, the sun just above the horizon. Gold light streams in through the trees, through your window, and lay on your covers like a blanket of light. Your eyes feel foggy from sleep, and you feel as though you were tied onto the bed. The bed sheets are soft and warm from your body heat. Slowly sitting up you run your hand through your hair, tucking loose hairs in place. Looking out the window you see the forest, it seemed sometimes to be filled endlessly with trees. You hear soft murmurs from the kitchen, and the soft songs of a rock dove from outside. Yawning, you place your feet on the cold wooden floor. You take a second to steady yourself, a hand on the wall as you look around the room. It wasn't yours, but it felt like home. So many nights you've stayed here. Safe. You can barely remember when you first came. It was like you've always known of this little cabin. You've memorized everything, the old fashioned lamp on his nightstand, the book laying next to it, the ash tray on the windowsill, his old acoustic guitar, his electric next to it collecting dust, the wooden dresser from the thrift store, the box filled with his medication on top of it. You take a moment to look through the window once more, absorbing the moist morning air before you start to move. Walking to the kitchen you finally see him. His head was resting on his shoulder as he leaned on the counter, his hair curved around his features, his clothes wrinkled, his calloused hands holding a cup of coffee, smoke rising. He was smokey, and warm like a fire. There was nothing in the world that you would want more, then to lay in his rays like he was the sun. To hold him when his mind is ablaze, and to be held when you're a wreck. He was a man who made you feel loved. You loved him as deep as the ocean, and he loved you as tall as the sky. If that had any meaning, you believed it did. His eyes meet yours, he smiles still tired“Good morning.”“Morning” you respond smiling. You walk up to him as he asks you how you slept, if you dreamt, if you did what it was, what you wanted to eat for breakfast, a form of beautifully simple small talk. You give him your soft replies, throwing back your own questions. His deep eyes lost you, the best part was that you could tell he was looking at you, not through you. There was something so beautiful about it, you weren't seen as lower then him, nor better then him. Only with him you feel as though you are an equal, and there's something so human, so beautiful about that. You lean on his side, a hand around the back of his waist trying to be as close as possible to him. You felt his soft clothes, the warmth of his body. In response he pulls you closer to him. Holding coffee in his other hand, every now and then taking a sip. You let yourself fall into him, you let him absorb himself in you. You hear the rock dove again, its song still singing.“It's beautiful.” you say to him looking out the window.“What is?”“Everything.”

Osgood glanced up as Kate pushed into the lab holding two steaming mugs.
‘Take a break?’ Kate suggested, nodding to the adjoining office.
‘Uh, yeah! I’ll be there in a minute.’
Osgood found Kate sitting in the deserted courtyard, her collar pulled up against the chill.
‘I brought you coffee.’ Osgood offered, sitting beside her.
Kate smiled, taking it.
Blinking lights flickered to life. Osgood gazed at the twilight, sipping lukewarm tea from her thermos.
‘Enjoying the last of the early evenings?’ Kate approached.
Osgood nodded, handing her the thermos.
The rain was peaceful, Osgood found. Her tea was warm, and the tower was quiet. Kate glanced over from her computer. She picked up her own mug, sipping it silently.
Late spring brought nicer weather, which brought Osgood better drinks. Kate made the short trip to the café nearby, getting Osgood her complicated favourite. A simple routine, but they liked it.
The barracks offered a bird’s-eye view of the bustling courtyard. Osgood and Kate sat side by side, a shared lunch between them and a thermos of black coffee half drunk.
Rain clouds were few and far between. The ground was baked, and the air was dry. Osgood spotted Kate hiding in the shade, hurrying over to hand her a water bottle.
They were far from home, on an island in Greece. Osgood had found a mocktail she rather enjoyed, relaxing in the shade beside a sunbathing Kate. It was almost a holiday.
Skyfall events led to long nights outside. Osgood’s thermos was empty, the hope of something warm a distant dream. Kate entered the tent with two cups and a kind smile.
Osgood didn’t like Halloween; too illogical she thought. Kate kept her company in the lab, providing a supply of sweets and hot chocolate with discussions of satellite readings and telescope images.
‘Would you like to get drinks some time?’ Kate asked late one evening.
‘We already do.’ Osgood frowned.
‘I meant- Forget I said anything.’ Kate dismissed before leaving the lab.
It was a date. Osgood hadn’t realised Kate meant that. They sat across from one another: whiskey for Kate, a mocktail for Osgood. To end, they said goodnight with a kiss.

  Lois’s voice was muffled as she reached past Clark’s broad frame, trying to grab her toothbrush from the cluttered cup by the mirror. He was hunched over the sink, brushing his teeth with methodical slowness, hair still damp from his lightning quick shower. Water dripped down the strong column of his neck onto the old and worn Metropolis Meteors t-shirt that was stretching tight across his chest.
  He glanced sideways at her reflection, foam spilling a little at the corner of his lips as he spoke around his toothbrush. “You could…wait…a second.”
  She gave him an unimpressed glare, her hair piled in a wild bun on top of her head, sleep lines still creasing her cheek. “We’re already running late. I’d like to get to work without Perry threatening to fire me before my first coffee.”
  Clark spit out his toothpaste, rinsing with a quick gulp of water, and smiled at her in the mirror. “Technically, he threatens to fire you 
  
    after
  
   your first coffee.”
  “Details,” Lois muttered, squeezing her way into the narrow space beside him.
  The apartment bathroom wasn’t exactly built for two, but they’d made it work, with her hairbrush balanced on the edge of the counter, his razor tucked on the windowsill, her face cream nestled between his cologne and deodorant. She picked up her toothbrush and paused, squinting at his reflection.
  “What?” he asked, reaching for his deodorant. “You’ve got…” She gestured to her own jaw, mirroring the streak of shaving cream he’d missed near his ear. “Hold still.”

  “Thanks,” he murmured softly.
  “Don’t mention it,” she said, just as softly, and turned back to brush her teeth, cheeks flushed.
  Clark smiled to himself as he finished getting ready, running his fingers through his damp curls until they sat in soft waves against his forehead. Lois rinsed her mouth and spat, wiping her lips with the back of her hand.
  “You done?” she asked, elbowing him aside to reach for her cleanser.
  He glanced just right at her. “Depends.”
  “On what?” Lois exclaimed, raising an eyebrow at him.
  “On whether or not you’re gonna let me make you breakfast.” Clark replied, and she shot him a withering look, though the corner of her lips twitched. “Look, the last time you made me breakfast, you burned the toast so badly the smoke alarm went off and the fire department showed up.”
  “In my defense, I was distracted by you walking around in nothing but my flannel.” He grinned back.
  “Well now, whose fault is that?” She slapped his chest lightly as she pushed past him into the bedroom.
  He followed her, laughing under his breath, watching as she rifled through her wardrobe for something clean. She emerged with a grey pencil skirt and a silky teal blouse, tossing them onto the bed before stripping off his old t-shirt.
  Clark swallowed hard, eyes lingering on the sweep of her bare back as she reached for her bra. Even after everything, after nights spent tangled in sheets and mornings pressed close in sleepy warmth, she still made his chest ache with a kind of awed, boyish wonder.
  “Eyes up here, Kent,” Lois said without turning around, her voice warm with laughter.
  “Sorry,” he replied sheepishly, though he wasn’t. He grabbed his suit trousers from the dresser and tugged them on quickly, tucking in his white shirt before grabbing his tie.
  Lois finished buttoning her blouse and turned to face him, one brow arched as she watched him struggle with his Windsor knot.

  “I can tie a knot,” he defended, ducking his head as she pulled the fabric snug against his collar. “It’s just… your way looks better.”
  “Flattery will get you nowhere,” she said, smirking, though her cheeks pinked slightly as she tugged the knot tight and smoothed it down his chest. “There. Now you look like an actual reporter instead of a lost farmhand.”
  He caught her wrist gently before she could step back, leaning in to press a soft kiss to her lips. “Thank you.”
  “Mm.” She kissed him back, lingering for a moment, savouring the warmth of him, the gentle press of his mouth. When they pulled apart, her eyes sparkled with mischief. “Now go make coffee before I murder someone.”
  “Yes, ma’am.” He said, then Clark immediately padded barefoot into the kitchen, while Lois slipped on her skirt and hunted for her heels under the bed. He let Paul in, like he always has.When Paul knocked, John quickly made his way to the door, unlocking it. Without ceremony, Paul stepped into his home, taking off his jacket and hanging it on one of the hooks next to the door. “Is Yoko here?” he asked. John shook his head.He didn’t ask why Paul was there, in New York, in his house. He didn’t ask what had happened, if he was okay. “Want a drink?” he offered. Paul accepted. John brought him whisky. He didn’t like whisky. Neither did Paul. They both drank of the brown liquid, grimacing at the sweet taste. Paul sat on the small sofa, legs crossed. John joined him, taking the spot furthest away from him. They sat in silence for a moment, sipping at their distasteful drinks. A car alarm went off outside, startling John from his thoughts. He looked to Paul, noticing he was already observing him. John set his glass on the coffee table, leaning away from his seat. “I liked your song.” he pauses, “The one about me,” John said passively (and possibly agressively), staring at the wall.“Which one?” Paul responds, worrying the thin fabric of his sleeve between his fingers as he keeps his eyes harshly trained on John.“The, uh,” John taps his fingers on the table, humming the tune of the song, like he hadn't listened to it obsessively, tediously analysing every word.“Oh. Yes.” Paul says, following John’s example and setting his glass on the table.“Suppose- suppose you’re getting out of the muzak phase. Though the vocals could be a bit, well, better,” John slips his finger around the rim of the glass sitting on the table.“I quite liked the vocals. Soft, they were soft. Gentle. I think yours was rather a bit much, don’t you think?”“Mine was accurate, is what it was.” John argued, removing his hand from his glass and brushing it through his hair.“Ritchie told me you were about to go through with much more.” Paul said, almost conversationally, folding his hands across his lap. John turned to him then, eyes brushing over his face. It was still Paul, it was Paul sitting there in his living room, it was Paul who was drinking his whiskey, it was Paul with whom he was arguing. It was Paul, the boy from Liverpool, the boy he took to Paris, the man he worked with for all those years. But it wasn’t that Paul. The man in front of him was Paul, of course, but not his Paul. Not the Paul he wrote love songs with, not the Paul with whom he shared his hotel room, not the Paul who he saw that day in 1957. No, this was a new Paul, a Paul who wrote love songs about him, a Paul who only ever saw this John, not the old John.“I was.” John confirmed.

Molly observed from the corner of her eye how intently Sherlock worked at his microscope, murmuring softly to himself.
“You’re a bit like my dad,” she finally said, then hesitated before continuing,
“He’s dead… oh. I’m sorry.”
Molly sighed inwardly. Why was it always so hard to find the right words around Sherlock? She constantly felt like a child, unable to express herself properly. No wonder Sherlock probably found her annoying.
“Please don’t feel obliged to make conversation. It’s not your area of expertise.”
His words stung – precisely because they were honest. That was what Molly liked about Sherlock: he never lied.
Despite his dismissal, she kept talking:
“You know, before my dad was dying, he was usually cheerful and loving – except when he thought no one was watching.”
She glanced at Sherlock. “I saw him once. He looked… sad.”
Sherlock frowned. “Molly…,” he said, audibly irritated.
“You look like that, too. Sad. When you think no one can see.”
She glanced briefly over at John. Sherlock followed her gaze without moving away from the microscope, then turned slightly toward her.
Molly continued undeterred:
“Are you okay? And please don’t just say ‘yes’… I know what it looks like when someone’s sad and thinks no one notices.”
Sherlock replied mockingly,
“You can see me…”
“I don’t count,” she answered quickly, bitterly.
Sherlock looked at her in surprise.
“What I’m trying to say is: if you ever need anything… if there’s anything I can do – no matter what – I’ll be there for you…”
She stammered, blushing. “I mean, not like that… I just meant, if you need help…”
She felt his gaze and turned away, embarrassed.
“It’s fine…”
Sherlock blinked in confusion.
“But… what could I possibly need from you?”
Molly shrugged, smiling sadly.
“Nothing. I don’t know. Maybe just a thank you. Just like that.”
The corners of his mouth twitched – he always did that when he didn’t know how to react.
A mumbled “Thank you” escaped his lips.
Molly didn’t respond.
“I’m going to get some crisps. Would you like some too?”
She regretted the question the moment she asked it.
“It’s okay, I know – you don’t want anything.”
“Well, I would…”
“I know, you don’t want anything,” she interrupted quickly and rushed out of the lab.
On her way to the vending machine, she scolded herself – for her insecurity, her impulsive words.
What could an intelligent, brilliant man like Sherlock Holmes possibly want with her – the small, awkward pathologist who couldn’t even hold a proper conversation?
When she finally returned to the lab with a bag of crisps in hand, it was empty.
Sherlock and John were gone.

It spoke of hurt and longing, the kind that could only be spoken when the other person was away or deep in the throes of a dream. It spoke of passion that had seemingly fizzled out due to one party feeling like they weren’t allowed to speak their mind.
It was one that he had dedicated to his wife, ever since the drift in their marriage.

His wings hadn't detected the man's presence, and a smirk played across his lips."You don't mind."The man huffed, emerging from the shadows to join him at the railing. Keigo grinned, sliding beneath Shouta's arms until they were pressed together. The older hero's cheeks reddened slightly as he gazed down, his expression a mixture of annoyance and affection."I missed you," Keigo murmured, tilting his head as he looked up at the man. Shouta exhaled softly, giving a subtle nod before leaning down to brush his lips against Keigo's forehead."Missed you too."Keigo leaned into the touch, savouring the rare moment of affection. Their stolen meetings on rooftops had become the highlight of his chaotic life, precious moments hidden from the world.They'd been sneaking around for months now, their relationship a carefully guarded secret. The 8 year age difference between them was part of the reason, it would raise eyebrows in certain circles, where traditional values still held sway. But Keigo couldn't bring himself to care about societal expectations. He'd spent his whole life following someone else's rules; his heart was the one thing he refused to let others dictate.And if that meant falling for a perpetually exhausted hero with dark circles and a heart hidden behind layers of logic, so be it.Shouta's shoulder bumped against his, drawing Keigo back from his wandering thoughts."Rough day?" he murmured, dark eyes searching his. Keigo responded with a weary nod, his usual brightness dimmed but still present in the curve of his lips."The Commission expects perfection," Keigo admitted with a half-hearted shrug, letting his wings droop slightly behind him. "Sometimes I just want to fly away from it all." He glanced up at Shouta, his amber eyes reflecting the city lights below. "But then I wouldn't get to see you, would I?"Shouta hummed, calloused fingers brushing Keigo's cheek as if touching something priceless. "You're such a hopeless romantic."Keigo let out a soft laugh, his eyes crinkling at the corners as he wrapped his arms around Shouta's waist. "Only for you," he whispered, burying his face against the thin fabric of Shouta's capture weapon. The steady rhythm of Shouta's heartbeat beneath his ear was more comforting than any safety net could ever be.Shouta's fingers threaded through his windswept hair, the touch tender and soothing against his scalp.Deep down, a part of Keigo longed for something more open with Shouta. He dreamed of walking hand-in-hand without glancing over their shoulders, of using the front door instead of slipping through windows like thieves in the night. The secrecy wore on him sometimes — a silent weight he carried willingly. For Shouta, he'd continue as long as necessary, but in quiet moments like these, he couldn't help but imagine a future where their relationship could exist in daylight.Shouta sighed, his breath ghosting over Keigo's forehead as his arms tightened around the winged hero. "I know it's hard," he murmured, as if reading Keigo's thoughts. "But we can't risk the Commission using this against you." His dark eyes searched Keigo's face, a rare vulnerability flickering in their depths. "Not yet."Keigo nodded slowly. “I know.”Shouta must have caught the longing in his eyes, because one heartbeat later, his lips found Keigo's in a kiss that felt like coming home, tender yet reassuring. Keigo's breath caught as he responded to Shouta's kiss, his body melting completely into the warmth between them.When Shouta finally broke the kiss, his whispered words against Keigo's lips sent a flutter through his chest — something totally unexpected."I love you."Keigo froze, eyes widening as the words registered. It was the first time either of them had said those words aloud, though the sentiment had been growing between them for months. His wings fluttered involuntarily, betraying the rush of emotion that surged through his chest.“You do?” he squeaked.Shouta huffed out a soft laugh, his eyes warm despite his attempt at playing it cool. "Of course I do." His voice dropped lower, full of something that made Keigo's heart ache. "I wouldn't be risking everything if I didn't."Overwhelming emotion swelled in Keigo's chest, so warm and all-consuming. His usual quick wit failed him as he gazed up at the man who had somehow become his entire world. After a moment of stunned silence, he managed to find his voice again."I love you too," Keigo whispered, the words feeling both foreign and completely natural on his tongue. "More than flying. More than freedom." His wings curled forward instinctively, creating a feathery cocoon around them both as he pressed closer to Shouta's chest.Shouta's arms tightened around him in response, his usual facade softened in the private moment between. For once, Keigo didn't feel the need to fill the silence with chatter or jokes. This was enough.

Chuuya stood in the middle of the front yard with his tiny fists stuffed into his jacket pockets, watching the moving van roll away down the narrow street. Their old neighborhood had been louder, busier — kids yelling down apartment halls, radios playing through open windows, Kouyou stomping her feet on the upstairs landing just to annoy him. This place was too quiet. Everything here sounded like breathing.Behind him, the screen door creaked as his mother stepped out. “Go explore, sweetheart,” she said, brushing a loose curl out of his face. “There’s a little path that leads straight to the sea.”He squinted at the road ahead. The sidewalk didn’t quite reach the horizon — it curved, just a little, before it dropped into dunes and brush and something blue far away.“I don’t wanna get sand in my socks,” he mumbled.“You won’t,” she said. “If you take your shoes off first.”Before he could think of a reply, she pressed something into his hand. A paper boat — folded from recycled stationery, the faint lines of a grocery list running sideways across the hull. It smelled faintly like oranges and chamomile.“Launch it for me,” she said. “Make a wish.”Chuuya blinked at it, then at her. “That’s dumb.”“Mm, maybe,” she said with a smile. “But it’s tradition. And we’re starting fresh, aren’t we?”He didn’t argue again.The air was crisp, a little wet, when he followed the narrow footpath down past tall grasses and telephone poles with peeling stickers. The town was smaller than he remembered from their first visit — or maybe just quieter today. The only sound was the wind brushing the reeds and the sharp cry of gulls drifting far above.The sand started soft and dry, then turned damp and clumpy the closer he got to the water. His sneakers squeaked with each step, and he regretted not taking them off after all. Still, the sight of the sea — endless, gently glittering — made his chest squeeze with something almost like excitement.He stepped close to the edge, past a line of half-buried shells, and crouched in the wet sand. Holding the boat in both hands like it was fragile, he placed it gently in the shallow, foamy tide. The water rocked it once, twice——and then a sudden gust of wind pushed it sideways, toppling it onto its side and soaking the paper through in seconds.Chuuya let out a low, frustrated noise and scowled at the water like it had betrayed him personally.“...You’re not supposed to push it like that,” said a quiet voice behind him.Chuuya jumped.A boy was standing a few feet away — about his height, pale and thin, with a mop of dark hair that looked like it hadn’t been brushed in a week. He wore a big coat that didn’t fit right and stared at the paper boat like it had insulted him, too.“You have to wait until the tide goes out a little,” the boy said, expression unreadable. “Otherwise it’ll flip over.”Chuuya stared. “...Who are you?”The boy didn’t answer. Instead, he crouched beside Chuuya, still keeping a little space between them, and reached out toward the ruined boat. Chuuya flinched — but instead of grabbing it, the boy gently pulled it free of the water and set it upright again on the damp sand.“See,” the boy said softly, “it’s not really broken yet.”Chuuya didn’t know what to say to that. He watched as the water crept back in and gently lapped at the paper again, but didn’t flip it this time.“I’m Chuuya,” he muttered, still frowning. “We just moved here.”“I know,” the boy said. “You live in the yellow house now.”That made Chuuya blink. “...You’re spying on us?”The boy shrugged. “You’re loud.”“I’m  not —”“You stomped down the stairs this morning.”Chuuya flushed. “That was my sister.”The boy didn’t answer. He just kept watching the boat.They stayed like that for a long moment, the two of them crouched by the water like mismatched stones. Chuuya tried not to shift too much, not to let on that his socks were cold, not to feel too weird about this silent boy who appeared from nowhere and apparently watched houses for fun.“Do you even  live  around here?” he finally asked.The boy just nodded. “Up that way.” He gestured vaguely over his shoulder. “Second house with the broken mailbox. The one that always has the cat outside.”Chuuya glanced behind him but couldn’t see anything beyond the brush and the bend in the path.“What’s your name?” he asked, eventually.The boy shrugged again. “You can just call me whatever.”Chuuya scowled. “That’s not how names work.”There was the smallest twitch at the edge of the boy’s mouth. Not quite a smile — more like the ghost of one.“You can call me Dazai, then,” he said. “If you want.”Chuuya opened his mouth to say something — something annoyed, something clever — but the tide caught the boat again. This time, it tugged it gently forward, further out toward the rippling blue.The boat tilted once, twice, then quietly gave up. It was a quiet winter night, two o'clock in the morning, when I was woken up by a strange noise. First, a series of crackling and thudding sounds, followed by heavy footsteps that stopped right outside my door. After a long pause, the clattering footsteps resumed, and by the time they halted again, I was wide awake.I didn't dare move, my own breathing the only sound I could hear. Fumbling around, I groped for my phone on the nightstand and, trembling, typed a message in our family group chat: "There's someone in the hallway!" Naturally, no one replied at that hour. I curled up in bed, terrified and anxious. Who could be outside the door? I tried to suppress those terrifying thoughts, but it was impossible. My parents, usually the chattiest, most argumentative people in the world who bickered nonstop in the group, were eerily silent. Could they have... My mind raced to the worst possible conclusion.Suddenly, another loud bang echoed, like the sound of gunfire in a war movie. I was on the verge of tears. After what felt like an eternity of huddling in fear, drenched in cold sweat and shaking, I wondered if the shooter had left since there had been no more sounds for so long. I pulled up the emergency number, but the speaker blared with a beeping noise followed by a loud automated message. It was so loud that I panicked and ended the call immediately. I thought, "They heard me calling the police!"As I silently buried my face in the pillow, sobbing, I heard a hoarse, sleepy voice at the door: "Kimi." It was Max! Max was alive! I forgot everything, sprang up, and opened the door."Who were you calling at this hour, you little rascal? Plotting another prank with those Bearman..." Max muttered, rubbing eyes. "I let it slide before... but you should know, swatting could make you arrested.”"I'm serious, Max, you have to believe me—I was really scared..." I said."Didn't the new nightlight work? Why call the police instead of me? I could've come to sleep with you. Well, here I am now," Max mumbled, shoving me aside and yanking half of my quilt and blankets over. "Make some space, I'm exhausted.""Wait, don't sleep yet, Max! I heard a gunshot earlier—" But Max was already fast asleep, breathing steadily, as if no one in the world could disturb those deep, sweet dreams.I thought to myself, at least Max was sleeping on the inside while I was near the door. If someone tried to break in, I'd fight them off. Max was warm and soft under the covers, radiating heat. I felt so warm, so safe, so secure. My heart stopped racing, my mind quieted, and my eyes grew heavy. Snuggling up to Max, I fell asleep.

It was 5:03 a.m. when Tony Stark woke up and immediately knew something was wrong He reached across the bed, searching for the familiar cold, pointy presence of one
 snarky Asgardian boyfriend. Instead, his hand landed on a pillow. A body-temperature pillow. Which meant Loki had been gone for a while.
Tony groaned, face smushing into the mattress like it personally offended him. “Unacceptable,” he muttered. “Relationship betrayal via pillow substitution.”
Still half-asleep, he rolled over, clutching the replacement pillow to his chest like a sad Victorian widow, contemplating his next move. Go back to sleep? Text Loki something passive-aggressive? Build a Loki-detection tracker?
Before he could settle on “all of the above,” he heard clanging from the kitchen. Clanging. As in, cooking. Tony blinked at the ceiling. “Oh no.”
Loki, literal god of mischief and chaos, standing in their sleek Stark Tower kitchen, wearing silk pajamas under a fluffy green apron that said ‘World’s Okayest Parental Figure’.
He was slicing apples with a dagger. Not a knife. A dagger.
"Is that... a thermos of goat’s milk?" Tony asked groggily from the doorway, rubbing his eyes.
Loki didn’t look up. “Peter requires nutrients to sustain mortal academic performance. Also, calcium.”
Tony squinted. “Did you label his sandwich?”
“I did,” Loki said proudly, holding up a sandwich with a glittery rune etched into the bread. “This will prevent hexes from pre-algebra witches.”
Tony stared.
Loki stared back.
Tony blinked. “You think there are witches in his math class.”
“I know there are,” Loki said, deadly serious.
Loki was still slicing strawberries like they had personally offended him in a past life—each one perfectly symmetrical, each cut somehow aggressive and elegant at the same time.
Tony leaned against the kitchen island, arms crossed, doing his best impression of “devastatingly charming billionaire who just woke up and wants attention.”
“Y’know,” he drawled, “there are much more fun ways to work with your hands this early in the morning.”
Loki didn’t even blink. “The last time I let you handle strawberries, they ended up in a martini. For Peter.”
Tony pointed dramatically. “Okay, first of all, that was an accident—”
“It was two ounces of vodka,” Loki interrupted flatly.
Tony shrugged, unbothered. “He looked thirsty.”
Loki continued ignoring him, now gently nestling the strawberries into a bento box so organized it could be used as a blueprint for small-scale architectural design. It even had compartments labeled in Old Norse.
Tony leaned closer. “You’re really not gonna bite? Not even a little flirty quip? A smirk? A raised eyebrow?”
Still nothing.
Finally, Loki glanced at him and said, completely serious, “We should drive Peter to school together.”
Tony blinked. “That’s... that’s not a no.”
“It’s his first day,” Loki said, as if that explained everything. “He will be nervous.”
Tony blinked again. “Right, okay, so you do love me, but only in a carpool-parent way right now.”
“Precisely.”
“Do I get a sticker?”
Loki shut the bento box with a magical click, turned to face him, and without missing a beat said, “You may have a gold star if you get dressed and brush your teeth.”
Tony threw his arms up. “Wow. Reduced to toddler status. This is my hell.”
Just then, Peter shuffled into the kitchen, hoodie half-on, looking like he hadn’t slept in six years.
“Please,” he mumbled, already regretting every choice that led to this household, “tell me you’re not fighting over who gets to drive me.”
Loki placed the bento box in front of him with a small, satisfied nod. “No, we’re both driving you.”
Peter squinted at it. “Did you... inscribe a protection rune on my grapes?”
Loki: “Yes.”
Peter: “...Cool.”
Tony: “I’m coming too because I am also a responsible adult.”

Emerald's not much of a people watcher. She finds it frustrating, usually; paranoia-inducing the rest of the time, always feeling like the random passersby will realize she's there.It wasn't always like this. She used to feel more confident in her ability to stay hidden. But here, in Vacuo, everything feels like it's been turned on its head.Emerald isn't grieving. She has no reason to. Nobody she was close to died.Maybe that's why she's out here, sitting on the sand, watching the former citizens of Atlas and Mantle try to survive.They look worn down, tired and angry and sad. The fine clothes of Atlas' elite are as faded and threadbare now as those of Mantle's poorest. The stress of the lack of food and near-daily Grimm attacks are taking their toll, too.Even so, there is hope. Hope that Emerald has had a part in, even if it feels wrong to say.Emerald closes her eyes and leans back onto the sand. Part of her wants to be out there, fighting Grimm. Rotating combat and rest duties made sense when it was suggested, but now the downtime feels more exhausting than the battles.Soft footsteps crunch in the sand nearby her, and Emerald cracks one eye open. The harsh sunlight silhouettes Ren, their body casting a shadow over her. Emerald can't see their face; she imagines a million expressions instead, ranging from calm to anger to joy.Ren sits smoothly next to her, cross-legged on the sand. Emerald blinks and Ren comes into focus, her hair still in the messy bun Nora made for her this morning. She doesn't look stressed or tired the way the people they're protecting do, but there are faint shadows under her eyes."You're going to get sand in your hair," Ren says.A tiny laugh escapes Emerald's lips. "At this point, I don't think I'll ever be able to get it out."Ren's lips turn upwards. Their smiles are always so soft."I thought you were on watch?" Emerald asks."Nora told me to go back." There's a carefully guarded edge to her tone.Emerald doesn't push. She should, probably, but it's gone wrong too many times for her to risk it now, even with Ren.Instead, she closes her eyes. If she tries hard enough, she can pretend she's on a beach somewhere. Mercury and Hazel are in the water, and Ren's next to her, taking her hand with their slender fingers.She could make it real, for a moment. The ocean waves, gently climbing up and down the sand. Hazel would like the beach, she thinks. She doesn't think Mercury's ever been. Maybe he would like it, or maybe he would fret about the risk of sand and saltwater getting into his legs.Emerald runs her thumb over the back of Ren's hand. "Do you like the beach?"Ren is quiet for a while. Then, "I don't know. I've never been.""We should go. After all of this is over."Ren hums. Emerald digs her boots into the sand. She should be out there, she thinks, making sure Nora was right in her decision to send Ren back. She should be fighting Grimm, earning her place. But she'd rather be here, Ren's hand in hers. For once, she's content with where she is.

The Feast of Redemption. The first week of Kingsway, or Parvulis, as the high-bloods called it, saw the Laetan putting on light shows with incredible illusions done in brilliant colors against the black of the night sky across Minrathous and in cities across the Empire. Rain, clouds, or a clear sky, it didn't matter, light filled the skies from sunset until often past midnight. If that was the extent of the festivities, Tarquin would have grumbled about the crowds and likely gone drinking with other Shadows or some of the more relaxed Templars, maybe even accepted an invitation to join in one of the dozens of feasts held publicly and privately in the city.But it never stopped with pretty lights.The first night was never the worst for the sound. The booming ignition of a fireball or the screeching sizzle of lightning was seen as necessary for some, but not desirable; on the first night the noise was all careful illusions of orchestra music or animal sounds, rarely, even speech. The displays on the first night were for the older, highly skilled Laetan, perhaps even a bored Altus or two, to show off. The lights were tasteful displays of art and the sounds were deliberately manipulated to enhance the visual effects. Tarquin always volunteered for extra duties that day. It was manageable and often requested off by his fellow Templars to enjoy the parties that were part of climbing the social ladder in Tevinter.Swapping shifts to cover someone's stint as evening temple decor early in the week was highly preferable to having to fight the urge to duck at his desk in the archives at each bone rattling crack of magical lightning or boom of Fade fire when the hands behind the magic became younger, less tactful, and more reckless later in the week. His flat was less insulated then the Templar archives, but being in Dock Town meant he was further from the big parties. Not that it helped when the drunken nobles from the wealthier districts came looking for rougher celebrations.The first thunder of the week caught him just at the door the first night after his extra shift. The boom was distant, had to be halfway across the city at least, but he'd still been going for the ground before he'd caught himself. The first bloody night. He growled and shouldered his door open, kicked it closed behind himself with a snap of his heel and tossed his helmet back into it's place onto the shelf. It was only needed when he signed up to cover a more public post and he didn't care for wearing it, but he did appreciate the level of anonymity it gave him.After his regular shift tomorrow, Tarquin had requested his annual leave, that way he didn't have to worry about not sleeping during the night. He'd told Dorian he wouldn't be in for the week… personal business to take care of. Mae had already known about his reaction to the light and the noise of the displays, just like she knew where to point him for a surgeon who wouldn't mind taking payments, or an alchemist specializing in reasonably priced personalized potions, among other things. When Clark was young, he often dreamt of drifting through space.
He’d be able to breathe up there; what kind of alien couldn’t survive without air?No -- the scary part was the solitude. How there would be no one else, for hundreds, thousands, millions of miles. There would be no astronaut to rescue him; no Han Solo in his Millennium Falcon, jumping through space-time; no Captain James T. Kirk telling Scotty, “we’ve got a live one. Beam him up, beam him up. Hey there. You’re safe with us. Could you tell us where you live? Where you call home?”And it was good that Captain Kirk never found him. Because in every one of those dreams, Clark would never have the heart to say,  no sir. I’m so sorry. You can just leave me here. I don’t have any place to call home. 
ii.
Clark became aware of his alien-ness through sound.Heartbeats. Breathing. Cars caught in ditches. Cows mooing at farmers. Sheep grazing in the fields. Dogs barking at the herds. Football games with bullhorns. Kids leaving for school. Kids leaving forever. News on the TV, on every TV set for thousands and thousands of miles, reporting on gun violence, murder, and those monstrous illegal immigrants who just kept sneaking through the border.“You’ve got to be careful, Clark,” Pa would mention. Sit himself in front of the TV, give Clark a concerned look. Clark would hear the plastic of the remote creak ever so gently under Pa’s grip.Pa would always tell him something like that. Pull up a channel with some politician yelling about some horrible undocumented alien and say,  you’ve got to be careful. Not everyone’s as accepting as me and your Ma. If they find out you’re an alien, they’ll take you away from us. And they’ll probably take a big ‘ol rocket ship and leave you in outer space.
 Now, outer space never seemed like a pleasant place to be deported to. So Clark tried his best to fit in.
He ignored all the noise no one else seemed to hear. Even when it made his jaw ache and his head buzz. And he tried to see things different –- paid more attention to the outside of people. The things they liked to talk about, like clothes, hair, skin color, accessories; things that seemed to set 'em apart. Not the bones and organs they all shared.And Clark started thinking different too. I’m not an alien, I’m not an alien, I’m not an alien.  He’d chant that internally when things got too loud -– too confusing –- too hard to bear. Standing up to say the pledge of allegiance. Finding a table at lunch. Chancing on a bully who took issue with Clark’s height.
   I’m just like you, I’m just like you, I’m just like you. 
   I belong, I belong, I belong...
Still, he dreamt of drifting through space.
iii.
“Why are you sitting like  that?” Clark gave Lois a look. The point of sitting like  that,  curled in, not super tall (not super… anything) was not to be asked questions like  that.  But Lois liked to question everything. At least, that’s what Clark was getting to understand.“Maybe that’s how they grow ‘em down on the farm!” somebody heckled a few desks over.Clark laughed along. It was better to be made fun of for being a hick than for being, well...And maybe Clark took advantage of it: the assumption that Clark Kent was big because he was homegrown on Kansas meals and spent his days, afternoons, and nights wrangling cows, hauling feed to pig troughs, or carrying bundles of apples, corn, and sunflowers to the Farmers’ Markets. Everyone in Metropolis seemed ready to accept this explanation.Everyone except Lois Lane.“If you’re a big guy, Smallville,” Lois said, arching an eyebrow, “you don’t have to be afraid to show it.”There was a wolf whistle. A barrage of comments -–  I didn’t take you for that kind of girl, Lane! What happened to our resident ice queen? And Lois was so distracted she didn't even notice how Clark ducked his head, flushing red to the roots of his hair.
He could feel his heart thud in his chest. It was louder than the sounds of the endless Metropolis traffic; the boisterous crowd filling the street; the plethora of underpaid cashiers ringing up coffees; the factories next to Suicide Slum exploding with metallic, automated symphonies.
   Ba-bump. Ba-bump. Ba-bump. 
And maybe Clark was still drifting. But maybe he'd stumbled on a sound that would lead him home.

The warm air inside the house enveloped him in a comforting way. Musty from being closed for so long, considering his parents weren't around, the smell of stored things hung heavy, circulating in the air.
 
Slowly, Rin stepped inside, walking through the place as if it were a strange yet familiar environment. Which, in fact, described the situation perfectly. It hadn't changed much since the last time—it never does.
 
He opened the windows, creating small gaps that invited the fresh air in. He turned on some lights and went up to his room, the whole way with a small warmth settled in his chest. Even if you're not particularly attached to your house, being back always brings a cozy nostalgia.
 He threw his heavy, cold jacket—a victim of the city's icy wind—onto the chair, which also held a forgotten school backpack. He changed his clothes for some light and warm ones. The beige sweater always suited him well.
 
He ran his hand over the neat bedspread, as if inspecting a pricey hotel room, testing how soft the mattress cover was. He thought about how much things had changed, though so much still seemed the same.
 
That's what nostalgia does to people.
 
The lady at the local convenience store, who used to sell him popsicles, looked older, with deeper lines and more prominent wrinkles. This time, instead of a popsicle, he bought a cigarette.
 
Not that he had never bought a pack there before. No, he'd done it a few times when he was younger, back when school classes weren't about English—which he was learning to eventually travel the world with his brother—or about art, which interested him. He'd ditch class whenever he could.
 
As he grew a grim expression and a reclusive demeanor over time, some troubled kids would occasionally treat him as an equal, inviting him to hang out, smoke a cigarette, drink some beer, and just wander around. It happened rarely, and Rin wasn't against it. He'd missed company ever since Sae left.
 
He learned to smoke with a cigarette borrowed from one of those kids. He didn't smoke it right away, so he wouldn't embarrass himself by coughing in front of them and ruining his tough guy image, so he waited until he got home and smoked alone in his room. The lighter he bought was black, and he carefully stuck an axe sticker on it with "I am here!" emblazoned in Comic Sans.
 
Smoking, actually, wasn't hard at all, and he didn't even cough much. It was a cold day, like this one when he came home, and the cigarette's warm air filled his lungs so comfortably it felt like a hug.
 
However, it was a careless and inexperienced act, which resulted in black ashes on the bedroom floor and a strong, unpleasant smell. He still remembers spraying deodorant all over the place after flinging the window open in desperate haste, hearing his mom yelling about dinner and coming up the stairs.
 
He didn't smoke much, nor often. He was an athlete and needed to stay healthy and fit, even more so if he wanted to keep up with his brother. He could count on the fingers of one hand the times he'd smoked after that, at least back then.
 
After that, his smoking only picked up when Sae came back and said all that bullshit to him like it was nothing. In retaliation, Rin trashed the whole room and smoked huddled on the balcony after spending some time curled up in bed, thinking about how useless he was, sure he'd been used and was disposable.
 
His heart filled with rage, and his lungs needed smoke to keep up.
 
Thinking about it still makes him click his tongue and roll his eyes. Remembering the pack that was shoved into his jacket pocket while the lady at the counter said something about wasted youth, Rin stood up and rummaged through his pocket to pull the pack out.
 
He unsealed the box and sniffed it. The smell of tobacco was pleasant, at least to him. He pulled out one of the small sticks and put it in his mouth, noticing the lack of a lighter. He grumbled discontentedly as he shuffled his feet across the cold floor to the kitchen.
 
Did his mom keep a lighter there? He had vague memories of it. Going out to buy another lighter would be a hassle.
 
He was rummaging through one of the bigger drawers, the kind where we usually keep junk and accessories that get forgotten for a long time until they're finally needed.
 
This was while the clinking of keys being handled and shoved into the doorknob irritated Sae's ears. Too loud for such a quiet street.
 
Rin didn't hear it; the metallic cutlery made too much noise for him to notice such small sounds. Not even when the door opened and muffled footsteps walked through the living room, followed by discreet green eyes staring with dull apathy at his back, still, Rin didn't notice any of it.
 
When, finally, a few seconds later, he found a matchbox and settled for it, lit the expected flame and carefully positioned it against the tip of the cigarette, which slowly turned black until small orange points surrounded by ashes ignited, Rin turned around while shoving the box

Sirius finds him boring, Peter doesn’t want to be involved with him for fear of also becoming a loser, and James doesn’t see him, too caught up with his own newly independent, eleven-year-old life.

The Pegasus Tribe.
They were a tribe that was sired by the God of the Seas.
Not born, not created by mortal means—but  sired , woven from salt, storm, and divinity. The sea had called to the sky, and the sky had answered. From that union came the Pegasi.
They were considered a myth, for it had been thousands of years since anyone had seen them—truly seen them.
Not just the faint silhouettes mistaken for clouds, nor the distant flashes of wingbeats across storm fronts. Real Pegasi, in their full form—hooves that never touched earth, eyes that shone like starlit depths, and wings that turned tides with a single beat—those had long vanished from mortal lands.
Said to dwell where sky kissed sea, the tribe vanished from the known continents long before the rise of the Roan Kingdom. Long before maps became borders. Long before humans forgot that power could be sacred without being corrupted.
Some claimed they had retreated into the Eastern Continent, beyond the broken cliffs of Akresia. Others whispered of a floating sanctuary, suspended above the Endless Sea, veiled in eternal mist and unreachable by any spell, artifact, or godless ambition. A place no mage nor sailor had ever returned from. A place where time may not even flow.
But all records—what little remained in forgotten corners of royal archives, buried beneath dust and imperial pride—agreed on one thing:
  The Pegasi were not mere beasts.
They were creatures of divine descent. Born with wings that shimmered like the ocean’s surface under moonlight—an iridescent sheen that shifted color with every breath. Their eyes were silvered mirrors, reflecting not just one’s appearance, but their fate, their truth.
And those who rode them?
Warriors chosen by the sea, bearing the Mark of Tides, a sigil etched in silver across their backs or chests, beating in sync with ocean currents. Not all who tried could bond with a Pegasus. It was not a matter of strength or title. It was a matter of soul.
The Riders of the Pegasus Tribe were said to command the rain, call lightning not from anger but from harmony, and cross continents as easily as birds crossed valleys. They whispered to the waves. They walked through storms as if through summer air. And in their silence, the gods once listened.
They were not just protectors.
They were enforcers of balance—between land and sea, sky and root, mortal and divine. A bridge between what was and what could be.
But power like that…It never goes unnoticed.
And it never goes unchallenged.
It was during the waning years of the Age of Myth—that last era when the gods still walked among mortals and magic still had memory—that the Pegasus Tribe disappeared.
Some claimed they had been hunted by Dragons. Not out of hatred, but out of fear. Dragons, proud and territorial, could not accept the idea of another race flying freely across the skies they had claimed as their own.
Others said it was the Demonic Race that brought them low—jealous of their purity, ravenous for their blood, which legend said could purge even the deepest corruption and restore mana roots long thought dead.
But no matter the cause, the end was the same.
Temples fell. Wings were broken. Skies mourned, and the sea grew quiet.
And so, with their disappearance, the world turned the page.
The great tribes became kingdoms. The kingdoms became empires. The gods fell silent.
And myths turned into bedtime stories.

Like a silent note slipping through thin walls, soft enough that I can’t recall when that melody wound itself into the background of every dream I ever had.

I gradually found myself drawing more often. I sat opposite, my hand busy, but my heart busier-memorizing your posture in that tranquil moment, so serene I dared not blink.
My pencil moved. My pages filled. I drew and drew. I couldn’t stop, for that beauty kept transforming. One stroke would appear, then fade to make way for a new, more dreamlike expression.
I was so absorbed that I hadn’t noticed you rise, step forward, and rest your hand on the arm of my chair.
“What are you drawing?”Your voice was like a pure raindrop in midsummer, cool, unhurried, intimate enough that I thought I could hear my heartbeat slip from my chest.
My hand jerked. I lowered my head. A single instant, but enough for me to compose a semblance of calm. I flipped the page, smiled, to maintain the usual.
“Just random sketches. I’m not satisfied with it yet.”
You didn’t press further or pry. You merely smiled, then turned back to your seat, humming an unrecognisable tune as you left.
I remained there. My hand rested on a blank page. My head tilted, still shadowed by your departing silhouette. Something sparkled inside me and drifted away, subtle, lingering.
One thing I understood with clarity: I had drawn you with all the tenderness I possessed. Every pencil line, every stroke of ink, held something I didn’t dare gaze at directly.
I called it: love.

For once in her life, Gotham sat frozen. It seemed even the most hardened of criminals didn’t have the energy to commit crimes on a tired Monday evening. A peaceful quiet had settled like a blanket over the city, nestling itself amongst the back alleys and streets.I sat alone on top of the building, eyeing pillows of steam as they burst forth from steel pillars, a stark contrast to the biting cold that nipped my cheeks. I tried to not let the bitterness of the Sunset bother me as I shoved my head further into my knees which pressed against my chest.As the painted streaks of pink and yellow faded into a smoky display of blue and black, I resigned myself to heading back inside. Taking one last glance at glittering fairy lights and admiring the screams of car engines as they rattled down pothole ridden streets, I turned to begin my descent downstairs.As I began my turn, a shadowed figure stood behind me, blackened in the night. A scream forced its way pass my pressed lips, a shrill cry in the night. The figure stood back in shock, the hood atop its head sliding down revealing panicked eyes of ocean blue.“Jason!” I gasped, pressing my hand against my racing heart. “You scared the shit outta me!”His eyes filled with guilt as he took a hesitant step forward, the hole ridden sleeve of his too big jumper sliding down his arms.“I’m sorry, I’m sorry! I didn’t mean to scare you, I swear!” He met my gaze, and I found myself unable to hold eye contact for more than a second before a strange heat coated my cheeks.“I was hoping you were up here,” He continued. “I came to give you this.”A sly grin spread its way across his face, cheeks dimpling in delight. He slipped a pale hand into his pocket and revealed a small plastic bag containing silver twisted chocolates.“Merry Christmas!” He cheered as his cold hands pressed against mine. I frowned as I took in thin bones that pressed against his skin, tracing up the dirty hoodie to his hollow cheeks still wearing that stupid smirk.“Jason…” I began, clutching his gift close. “I can’t accept this. How did you even manage to afford these? And I don’t have anything to give you!”“Hey, don’t worry about it! It’s a gift!” Again, those blue eyes stared at me with nothing but warmth.“Christmas isn’t for another two weeks…” Tears sprung to my eyes without warning, stinging. I blinked them back furiously, sniffling my nose.“Hey, are you crying?”“What? No! It’s the cold, it makes my nose run!”Jason laughed at my weak protests. I responded in turn by ripping open the weak plastic and pegging a chocolate at him in retaliation.“Asshole!” I cried as he laughed even harder.“I should’ve gotten you soap for that mouth of yours.” He giggled. Again, that strange heat crossed my face as I admired him and I found myself turning away glaring at the sparkling lights of Gotham city in protest.With a sigh, I turned back, grabbing his arm and bringing him back towards the frozen fire escape.“C’mon you brat. You’re sleeping at mine tonight; I don’t want you being alone.” I chastised.His eyes crinkled in joy once more, cheeks dimpling and smile creasing across his lips.“If you insist.”
