There was nothing but light and sand.Pale grains stretched out in every direction, glittering faintly under a skyless blue void. Levi stood in the middle of it—alone, broken, confused.His body didn’t hurt anymore.There was no wind, no heartbeat, no Rumbling. Just silence. Too still to be real.He blinked slowly, breathing shallow. His boots left shallow prints in the sand, the only proof he was really there.What is this?The quiet buzzed around him like it was waiting for something. He looked down at his hands, expecting them to tremble, but they didn’t. Everything felt strangely… light. Like he’d dropped something heavy without noticing.Then he heard it.Humming.Soft. Gentle. Like a thread pulled straight from memory. Like a hand brushing hair behind his ear when he was too tired to keep his eyes open.His feet moved on their own. Through the glittering white sand, toward the sound.And then he saw her.A woman standing with her back to him. Short, dark hair tied up messily. Worn clothes. Her arms were folded gently across her stomach, and her head tilted slightly as she hummed to no one in particular.Levi stopped.The air caught in his throat. His legs locked.No.It couldn’t be.She turned slowly, as if sensing him there—not startled, not confused. Just calm.Her eyes met his.And in that instant, everything inside him cracked.She hadn’t changed. Not really. She looked young, but tired. Soft, but worn. Her face was exactly how he remembered it—not from stories, but from the fragile images tucked away in the furthest corners of his mind. Faded, faint… but now standing in front of him.He didn’t say anything.He couldn’t.She smiled, small and sad.“…Levi?”His chest ached like something sharp had been lodged there for years. His hands clenched into fists.He didn’t understand what was happening.He didn’t care.“…Ma..?” he whispered.The moment the word left his mouth, his voice cracked—quiet and uneven. Like a child who hadn’t spoken aloud in days.Kuchel’s expression softened, and her lips parted like she might cry, but didn’t. “You remember me?”He nodded.His throat burned. His face didn’t change, but his eyes shimmered with something too raw to hide.“I remember your eyes.”He looked away suddenly, ashamed. “Why are you here? Why would he do this..?”“I don’t know,” she said gently, stepping closer. “But it’s enough.”He was frozen. He didn’t know how to breathe anymore.“I’ve… seen you,” she said quietly. “For a long time now. I’ve watched you grow. Watched you fight.”He looked at her again, uncertain.“You… watched me?”Kuchel nodded. “Since the moment I left. I stayed as close as I could. You were so small… and so angry. I wanted to hold you again every time you got hurt, and every time you had to stitch yourself back together.”He looked down, suddenly feeling very small in the vastness of the sand around them.“I haven’t done enough,” he muttered.“You did,” she said. “You have. And you carried so much more than a boy ever should’ve.”She reached her hand out, and though it didn’t quite touch him, Levi flinched at how familiar it felt.“I didn’t want you to grow up the way you did,” she whispered. “But even in that world… you still found ways to protect others. You still had a heart.”A pause.“I’m sorry I left you alone.”Levi’s eyes burned.“You didn’t want to,” he said, voice trembling. “You didn’t get the choice.”“No,” she agreed softly. “But I’m here now.”The silence between them was heavy—but not cold. Just full.He stepped forward.He didn’t speak.He didn’t ask her anything else.He just stood close, like the boy he used to be, staring at the woman who gave him life—and held none of the bitterness he thought would come.She smiled again, faint and warm. “You don’t have to keep carrying all of it.”Levi didn’t respond.But he looked up at her, eyes wide and quiet.And for a moment, she saw him the way he once was: barefoot in the dark, hungry and tired, clinging to a life that never gave him enough time to be a child.And now, he was just… her son.When the light began to shift and the vision started to dissolve, Kuchel reached out once more.“You’ve made me so proud, Levi,” she whispered. “I never stopped loving you. Not for a second.”She pressed her hand over his heart. “And when it’s over… I’ll be waiting.”The world faded.And Levi opened his eyes.The sound of colossal footsteps returned. The wind howled again. His body screamed with pain. But he stood still for a moment—longer than he should’ve—his hand slightly open at his side, like he was still trying to hold onto something that had slipped through his fingers.He didn’t say a word when he returned to the others.But something in him had changed.And for the first time in a long time…He didn’t feel so alone.

You only have a few minutes left on your phone plan. Were you really going to waste them to beg that sleazeball Ed Harnet for your job back?
Disgust ghosts itself down the small of your back, pressing itself like a firm hand.
Fucking prick.
You worked for the city’s prime time news network. That’s ‘worked’ as in past-tense.A budding journalist, fresh out of college. Naive.
You’d thought Ed had just taken a liking to you, had seen your potential.
Oh he’d seen  something , alright. Seen that you were wet behind the ears and possibly willing to go to lengths to prove yourself.

He hadn’t outright said it, hadn’t needed to -
 his hands implied it in the sickeningly slow way they moved down to the swell of your back.You’d been a deer in the headlights, and if that janitor hadn’t entered the room and flipped on the lights…
This kind of stuff just didn’t happen in real life. This was for TV and movies - not you.

Afterwards he’d stopped by your desk with a clandestine smile and his hand had reached out to caress your wrist nonchalantly.“If you’re planning on working late again tonight, maybe we can discuss your future here at the station in a bit more detail.”
 You reflexively slapped his hand away, and apparently, you’d also smacked your career into the damn garbage.
One of your stories detailing the rise in human on monster crime that was supposed to air later that week was pulled without explanation. Someone started a rumor that you’d plagiarized some of your more recent work, that you'd been deliberately misinterpreting numbers to make your segments more desirable. Over the course of two weeks your ego and reputation in the news industry was ruined.
You’d quit nearly a month and a half ago. Left before you got fired, sure that you could just rebuild at a different company. You had gumption and talent, how hard could it be to restart?Hard.
So unbelievably hard.
Jobs you should have been qualified for never called you back, and jobs you should have been overqualified for wouldn’t progress past an initial interview. You’d even applied at a local restaurant that you absolutely knew was desperate for workers, and they’d turned you down. You started taking the station off of your job history list, and still no luck anywhere.
After the first few you’d thought it must have been bad luck, but at this point, and god maybe you’re just paranoid, but you’d swear that you’d been blacklisted. Was that even a thing?

If you’d just stayed until they’d fired you maybe you could have at least applied for unemployment.

You haven't been responding to the group texts.""I've been working on some home maintenance, dad. What's up?"The voice on the other end shifted on the spot, seemingly looking for something. Tony and Abel were whisper yelling at Phonica (though it was clear that her father couldn't hear them at this point), trying to coax her to hang up."No I know, I know. The two of us are sitting on cracked vinyl, resting our glasses on a tacky tabletop, scoping out the butch scene in this new-to-us lesbian bar. The lighting is warm, muddled, and further stirred up by the haze of alcohol. A wall sconce glows behind you, and you are crowned holy by it. If I had to guess, I would bet that you’d be the patron saint of cycles, like the rotating of a ceramics wheel, or the cycle of bears and fish and water, or the way a lathe spins around and around. My dazzling, shimmering butch: the patron saint of all that moves.I am so pleasantly foggy, the joint we shared outside twisting with my drink to form a swirling, giggling mood. Everything is movement and light. Shoulder to shoulder, we are two orbiting planets, and your larger, stronger gravitational pull is inevitable. I set my hand on your leg, sliding upwards and squeezing. You turn from whichever new friend you were waving at to smile at me. I bring my hand up to the collar of your shirt, holding, tugging.“Kiss me, now.” I declare.You let yourself be pulled in. I intend the kiss to be sweet, brief, even. Just to feel that extra closeness for a second. I want more, of course I want more. But I’m not so far gone that my awareness has disappeared. Instead, I bite your lip for the satisfaction of your sharp inhale, then pull back. I take a sip of my drink, trying to appear cool and unaffected.You fluster in my periphery, while over the top of my glass, I catch someone looking at us. No, at you, at your mouth, still open and shining wet. She’s leaning against the end of the bar, all done up in leather and denim. Her dark hair is shaved close at the sides and back, but a little looser and longer on top, slicked back and feathery. The color of it melts into her leather jacket, which is clearly well-worn and well-kept. She leans, gleaming boots propped against the bar’s footboard. I see her jaw work as she drags her eyes across your body.She sees me watching her. We make electric eye contact. She tilts her head, an implicit questioning. I jerk my head upwards in a nod, lifting my glass towards her.She introduces herself in a sprawling mountain drawl. Her name is Lu. She’s handsome like the old protest photos we pore over together, strong bones and a wide jaw. She seems…metallic, sharp and rough, but her smile is like a storm breaking open. We speak with her at length about what she’s looking for tonight, what you and I are looking for. I watch you carefully the entire time. I make note of what we say that makes your ears twitch, what makes you squirm in your seat, what you do and don’t volunteer to the conversation. I feel at once your keeper and your ward.Eventually, an agreement is reached and we settle on going back to our house. The arrangement is such: Lu is going to tell you what to do, and you’re going to do it to me. It will be an overlapping act of submission and dominance. I’m wet at this novel and complex thought, can taste it on my tongue like sweet oil-spill iridescence.Eager to go, we call for a car. On the way home, Lu has you perform a demonstration on how to best rile me up. She directs you to tell me to sit stock-still in the back of the car, to earn your touch through good behavior. I am rigid as we speed down roads. I am silent, as you run your nails up the back of my neck. My eyes flutter, roll. Heat pools between my legs. Slick gathers in my boxers. You use your strength and that intimately detailed knowledge of me to impress Lu. You squeeze my wrists, just hard enough to make my chest heave. I look up to see her watching you as your eyes track the movements of my body. Your attention and exhaustivity have always been so captivating. We arrive and I am so pleasure-drunk that you have to help me out of the car.We press through the doorway in a flurry of material, our clothes and shoes discarded in a trail towards the bedroom. While you bring out our playthings, I entertain Lu. She stands, almost a whole head taller than me, taking in our space. Our photos, our art, the paint on the walls. I take a deliberate step towards her.When you emerge from your bedroom, we’re on the couch. I’m perched on the edge, the embodiment of posture, while she is relaxed, legs spread and feet planted. She orders you to sit between our feet. You do. She tells you to watch. You do. Lu tilts my chin up and kisses me. It’s exploratory, and I can understand the learning that she is doing, mimicking the movements you performed before. I hear you whimper when she pushes her tongue into my mouth. When I open my eyes, you’re up on your knees, hands on the edge of the couch. You are inches away from the two of us, your face hungry and wanting. I turn away from her to pull you in, hard and fast. You scramble up onto the couch, forgetting your instructions. On top of me, you bite and suck your way down my neck, thrusting against me. I can feel how wet you are through your jeans. I reach a hand underneath you, providing you with the heel of my palm

The world outside hummed with life—horns blaring, sirens in the distance, the bustle of a city that never knew peace for long. But in the quiet loft above it all, time had stilled.Steve sat at the edge of the bed,barefoot, his shirt half-buttoned, hair still damp from the shower. He wasn’t sure if the sun was rising or setting; all he knew was that Diana was standing by the window, bathed in gold.She was still in her armor, though her gauntlets lay on the table, and her lasso hung over the chair. Her back was to him, but he could see the way her shoulder rose and fell-slow, steady, like she was trying to hold the world together with each breath.“You’re quiet,” he said, voice soft.“I have to be,” she replied without turning. “If I speak, I’ll say things I can’t take back.”He stood, crossing the room without a sound, and placed a hand on her shoulder. Her skin was warm, her breath sharp for a moment at the touch, but she didn’t pull away.“What things?”he asked.She turned then, eyes bright- not with tears, with something heavier. “That I’m tired of fighting,”she said. “That the world is still cruel. That I brought you back only to feel like I’m losing you again. Every time you go on a mission, Steve…”His hand slid down his arm, fingers intertwining with hers. “I’m not going anywhere,” he said, and meant it. He always did. Even when it wasn’t true.Diana looked at him, really looked at him, the way she used to before the crash, before the decades of mourning. And now- now that he was here again, somehow, by fate or magic or maybe just stubborn love— she didn’t want to waste it.So she kissed him.Not out of longing, or fear. Not to stop time or escape it. But because it was the only truth she trusted.And Steve held her like a soldier afraid to break formation, but aching to surrender.When the kiss ended, she leaned her forehead against his. “Promise me,” she whispered.“I promise,” he said, not knowing exactly what he was promising—but knowing that for her, for them, he’d try.Even if the world never paused again.

SOMETIMES:
      I.
    
    ‘You wanted this, Elisabeth, remember?’
  Features carved from a smooth marble mask, Maximilian seethes like he never has since Franz was chosen as emperor.Gleaming with something greater than sadness, more potent than rage, his icy-blue eyes track the back of her flowing lace white veil, flowing from her dark, braided crown like a shroud of delicate gossamer.Her wedding dress train ripples like water over the cathedral aisle in swaths of fine chiffon.
The egg-sized jewel just above her forehead glitters in the light as she passes.Caressing her slender, creamy shoulders, she rolled back as if ready — but she is not.She did not desire this crown — she wanted the king whose head it adorns.She sees a bright future ahead of her, so she steps toward it eagerly, gracefully, oblivious to the cliff waiting where Franz is standing at the altar.This is not a wedding; it is a funeral, but Maximilian is the only one who hears the bells — sees her marching to a premature death, the only one mourning this imminent disaster.
    ‘But do you know what ‘this’ is?’
  Maximilian wishes he could have asked her, the night at the party, that even absinthe liquid courage could not force out through the cage of his teeth.
      II.
    Sometimes, he wonders what would’ve happened if he’d warned her— if he could’ve continued, said:
    ‘Your marriage to him will lead to a mediocre imitation of life.’
  Maximilian has lived his entire privileged yet lonely life in this lavish palace within this wretched family and thus has identified it for what it is while trapped in its walls.Doomed to return at his brother’s beck and call, like all other Austrians in this Empire.The curse of the imperial family disguised as a blessing.He wants to warn her again before the priest finishes the ceremony—one more time.
    'All your efforts will fail.'
  But life is a culmination of chances not taken, regrets piled up, and pain inflicted and given.He has enjoyed the comforts of a royal lifestyle and would not trade it for a commoner’s life, but it is a dark gift with a costly asking price.
    ‘Elisabeth, this is a gilded prison for a free bird like you. A woman I can only imagine in the sky.’
  
      III.
    Sometimes, Maximilian wonders how his brother is able to do it — seize every wild, impossible dream one can imagine.Claim a god-given power, inspire their mother’s devotion, and even obtain the love of a bride ill-suited for him, whom Franz will inevitably crush.As surely as a free butterfly tearing off her wings.So good, so wild, so infinitely beautiful.Yet, that is his right, as Emperor, to do as he wishes, have what he wishes, and toss aside even his own people with sanctioned executions if he so wishes.The moon, the sky, and the stars are all within his grasp.
    Is being the firstborn son enough to deserve all that?
  And now he is to sit idly, watching his brother slowly murder everything he adores about this unexpected woman he met too late.Franz snaked his way into her heart before he had a chance. What would have happened had his carriage been faster — had he arrived days before his older brother’s birthday? Would Franz have married Helene?“I would suit you better.”He remembers telling her at his party how his chest trembled; he forced his words to steady as if caging a beast wishing to claw its way out of his ribcage. But he also knew he couldn't and wouldn't force her.
      IV.
    
    However, sometimes, he wishes he hadn’t laughed, then maybe his life would not have become a joke.

[Rafael's mother is not dead, he simply hasn't seen her in over a decade--but she still manages to haunt him like a ghost. A nightmare.]
  Raf doesn't really get anxious before a show, and genuinely enjoys performing on stage--but the most difficult part of a performance for him are the hours right after a show has finished, starting from the moment he walks off the stage.Almost every single time, no matter how fun or well executed a performance was, there's a kind of quiet terror that follows him off the stage like a dark shadow and infects him once he's left the safety of the stage lights.He becomes uncharacteristically furtive, and while he will answer when spoken to, his responses are simple, short, with a kind of sharpness in tone that suggests a level of defensiveness. Like a child awaiting a harsh scolding. Because that's kinda...what he is, in that moment. He is waiting to be kept awake into the early hours of the morning by a lecture about what he did, what he didn't do, what he should have done differently, what needs to be improved upon before the next time. Or he's waiting to be told that he's gonna be on his own for a few days, because the people who are supposed to love and take care of him are "too disappointed to fairly manage him" right now. Or he's waiting to be dragged into a busy room populated by strangers he's supposed to impress while he's casually, conversationally picked apart in front of them by the person who brought him there in the first place; the person who wanted to show him off.It's a frustrating reaction to have...He's not a child, he's a grown ass man--and he owes venue staff, and his bandmates, and everyone else backstage a modicum of respect and kindness, and to thank them for their work, and to revel in the completion of a good show. But he's not really...he can't do that. He comes off as quietly despondent at best, or kind of a stuck up asshole at worst. When he did shows with Lacey, she called it his "post-performance tantrums" and exercised very little patience for his 'immature sulkiness' following concerts. And the low mood would persist for a solid week then after.Once he started doing shows and stuff with Margie, she'd initially wonder if his poor mood was because she had done something wrong, or didn't meet expectations, if it was a bad show.... It wouldn't be until the following day before Raf could find himself in a state of mind where he's able to explain what he's feeling, much less why. And...for whatever reason, he's reticent to offer the most simple explanation to her--because saying "it's a ptsd thing, just give me space and patience and don't take it personally because it's nothing to do with you" comes with the risk of being asked other questions about himself and his upbringing that he's not comfortable getting into and--it's a whole thing, in his mind. So the first few shows together are consistently...a bewilderingly negative experience for Margie, in that it's a very tense, quiet, insecure and shame-ridden 24-48 hours after the show--followed by delayed revelry days after the performance with Raf finally able to reflect positively upon the experience and assuring Margie that it actually was a great performance, and that he had a lot of fun--and they're able to recall their favorite moments together, etc.Unlike Lace, though, Margie never digs into him about his behavior. She just mirrors his silence, and then--very uncomfortably--gives him space because she doesn't really know what else she can do, and--assuming she's the problem--she doesn't want to risk messing things up even more, since she doesn't know what she did wrong in the first place. And, you know, there's only so many times Raf can reassure her, too late, that she was great, actually. And so he finally does relent to telling her that this is just...how he is after a show, that it's no one's fault, he's not mad at her or anyone--it's just ptsd. That's all he tells her, and, as per always with Margie--she doesn't try to pry out more information from him about it.Margie goes down her own little rabbit hole of research instead, and comes to Raf with the idea for a new post-performance routine (communicated with staff and such before hand to ensure accommodation) wherein they don't try to gladhand, or pack up, or do literally anything for the first half hour after they walk off stage. Instead, they find a quiet, dimly lit corner somewhere away from everything and just sit, and rest, no expectations, no obligations, nothing. Raf agrees to put this idea into practice, and it quickly evolves into, well idk... Being held and gently rocked like a child by someone who means something to him.

He has lost and lost and lost and now he is lost.He feels like he just thinks all the time, of everything that has gone wrong and what could go right.He is now Batman. But each time, he retreats the same way Taerae does, curling back in on himself, and waits. Sometimes he’ll bring him an offering—a treat to tempt him out. Sometimes Taerae accepts it, shedding his shell to carry Gunwook through a match instead, dragging him up the ranks in his wake. Sometimes he retreats further, slinking into the shadowy recesses as he declines. Gunwook tucks his tail between his legs then, slightly shy even as he dismisses his own invitation and runs off to paw at someone else.But he doesn’t push, even if it would be easy for him, even if all Taerae would do is squirm helplessly in his grasp.Gunwook tries again, spiraling back with a different approach each time, changing, adapting, molding himself to fit within the tight confines of Taerae’s walls, pulling back whenever he feels them start to crack.Taerae almost misses him when he stops, when the orbit breaks and Gunwook runs off to train his attention elsewhere, when Taerae finally earns the blessed solitude he’s yearned for.Almost.(Definitely.)But even when Taerae is sure that Gunwook’s moved on, he comes padding back to him, cautiously nudging against his shell and staring to see if Taerae will blink back at him.Gunwook tries again, so Taerae lets him.He could crush him still, one day, but he handles him with the utmost care, with the sort of gentle touch that lets Taerae believe that Gunwook would tiptoe on the eggshells he would feed him until his defenses had time to repair any damage he’s done.If Gunwook is willing to wait for Taerae to approach him at his snail’s pace, then maybe it’s worth it to stop the circling, the spiral closer and tighter until they finally meet at the center.

You’ve been so caught up in your head, opening and closing the door to your husband’s old room at his family’s house on autopilot, that Surya’s amused question snaps you out of it rather abruptly.
Originally, the two of you were only intending to come over for dinner – a weekly tradition of sorts, ever since Surya moved in with you on the farm. But “only dinner” turned into Archie showing you the newest additions to his rock collection, turned into board games, turned into watching TV, turned into… realising that the weather had taken a turn for the worse – much worse than the forecast would have ever had you expect. The occasional storm isn’t anything unusual this time of the year, but going out in one is still a different matter. Hence, it has collectively been decided best for Surya and you to wait it out here, staying the night to hopefully make it home dry come morning.
It's hardly a first either. You’ve stayed over many a time in the past, most notably on evenings spent looking after Archie, so his parents could have a night to themselves. Even between the two of you, the kid’s energy is a feat to match, leaving you passed out on the couch by the time Joko and Dinda returned more often than not. You’re so well-acquainted with the sofa by now, the bed is like a luxury upgrade.
That being said, with this situation being more planned than crashing on the couch – if only slightly – there’s the opportunity to get comfortable, properly settling down for the night. A spare toothbrush had easily been found somewhere hidden in the back of the bathroom cabinet, and you’re more than used (and happy) to share a blanket with Surya. Concerning sleepwear, though… Surya’s still got some clothes here that were packed in a box but never made the move. But beyond an old shirt for you to wear, it’s looking grim. In your own home, you’d be more than content to just forgo the pants entirely, but as comfortable and familiar as you are staying over… Yeah, you’d prefer wearing some.
Fortunately, Dinda had been quick to jump to your rescue, digging through the depths of her closet with the focus and determination of a hound. At first, you simply found her zeal endearing, if a bit odd, but the grin on her face as she triumphantly pushed the garment into your arms was a little too self-satisfied to only be caused by the accomplishment finding what she had been looking for – which at that moment you realised had been something quite specific instead of just any pair of pants. A fact she enthusiastically pointed out to you just a second later: “I wore these while I was pregnant with Archie! You can keep them.”
Subtle. Very subtle.
Which brought you to the situation you find yourself in now: Standing in the middle of the room, sweatpants in hand, feeling slightly flustered but mostly just amused. Propped up against the headboard of the bed, Surya’s still looking you over with one brow raised, evidently trying to place your behaviour.
“I think your aunt’s eager to be promoted to great-auntie.” Is the answer you ultimately settle on, holding up the maternity pants for a moment in explanation before getting changed. And while you manage to state so intentionally dryly, there’s a laugh just waiting to spill, the amusement tugging at the corners of your mouth.
As it often is, Surya does the laughing in your stead. “That so? Well, she’s never been exactly subtle about it…” You can feel his eyes on you as you give the wide waistband a scrutinising tug to gauge the chances of this actually staying on you once you move around. “They look good on you, though. Very cute.”
“Well, then you’ll be delighted to hear that I’ve been instructed to keep them. Since she ‘won’t be needing them anymore’.” By which Dinda clearly meant to imply that you will. Which you suppose could be true, but... Well, while discussed before, that’s always been something filed under “future plans” – albeit not so much a question of if rather than when.
“Oh, we’re really done being subtle then, are we?” Surya’s laughter dissolves into snickering as you climb into bed as well, settling down next to him. There’s a quiet, comfortable routine to slipping under the sheets, limbs tangling together with subconscious ease and certainty. And by the end of the procedure, you’re well content to never move again, feeling right at home, everything being where it should be.
“It would seem so…” The relaxation quickly setting into your bones, moulding your form into the cast of Surya’s arms around you, seeps into your voice and leaves it as little more than a mumble. It’s like the day’s endeavours catch up to you all at once after being blissfully ignorant of them while still engaged one way or another. But here, with a moment to breathe and the knowledge that this is it for the next couple hours, you finally unwind. Not to mention the rain pattering on the roof makes you feel even more cosy. And whatever’s gotten into Dinda is the last thing on your mind.

As Borna walked down the street, holding a handful of smooth, grey pebbles, his heart starting beating faster the closer he got to his destination.
He was going to his friend Luciana's house to confess his feelings in his own clumsy, pebble tossing way.
He'd had feelings for Luciana for a while now. They always had fun together, whether they were on the field or not. When she laughed, it sounded like wind chimes. She didn't show her eyes often, but when she did, they looked as beautiful as the summer sky.
Borna had been working up the courage to do this for weeks, and tonight, after combining the sugar rush provided by multiple cans of soda with teenage angst, he was finally going to make his move.
Finally arriving on her lawn, Borna took a deep breath, grabbed one of his tiny stones with his other hand, aimed carefully at her second story window, and tossed the first pebble.
Thunk.
Borna winced. Too hard.
He tried again, softening his throw.
Thwack.
Alright, that was a little better. Maybe. Borna wasn't sure, honestly. He actually couldn't see Luciana's window very clearly through the darkness. Still, he kept trying, each pebble desperately vying for Luciana's attention.
What Borna didn't know was that Luciana, in an attempt to battle the summer heat, had opened her window earlier in the evening. And, in a stroke of particularly bad luck, her parents had removed the window screen to clean it earlier in the week, leaving a gaping, unprotected hole into her bedroom.
So, instead of gently tapping against glass, Borna's pebbles were sailing right into Luciana's bedroom and landing somewhere inside.
Borna found out about this when one particular pebble landed with a thud, followed by a faint "Ouch!"
Borna froze, pebbles still clutched in his hand. He'd hit her. He'd actually hurt her. Panic surged through him.
"Luciana," he quietly called out, his voice trembling, "Are you ok? I'm so sorry."
A pause. Then, a shaky voice.
"Borna," Luciana called out, "Is that you? Are you throwing rocks at my head?"
"No," Borna responded, his face burning, "I mean, yes, but I thought your window was closed. I was trying to..."
He didn't know if he could finish that sentence. After what he'd done, he was completley mortified, hoping that the Earth would just swallow him whole before he had to face Luciana.
Sure enough, though, she did walk over to her window with messed up hair and an irritated expression that only later would he find out was masking slight amusement.
"Trying to what, Borna," Luciana questioned, rubbing the back of her head, "Give me a concussion?"
"I..." Borna stammered, "I just wanted to get your attention. I...I like you, Luciana. I have for a while."
This surprised Luciana a bit, but not for the reason you think. She'd suspected for a while that Borna had feelings for her, she just wasn't sure if he'd ever actually confess those feelings. She had to admit, she was always a little happier when hanging out with him. He was goofy and a bit dopey at times, but he also wore his heart on his sleeve and he always tried to make Luciana feel better about herself since they'd grown closer after giving each other pink eye.
So, the fact that Borna was actually telling Luciana how he felt made a genuine smile spread across her face. She leaned further out her window to make sure he could see it.
"Well, Borna," she responded, her voice soft, "I have to say, you went about it in the worst way possible, but you definitely got my attention."
Borna couldn't believe it. Even after hitting her with a pebble, his plan actually worked.
Luciana then parted her hair to make sure Borna could see into her eyes and see the sincerity behind her sentiment.
"But next time," Luciana teased, "Try flowers. And definitely check if the window is open first."
Borna managed a weak smile. He'd made a complete fool of himself, accidentally hurt the girl he was trying to impress, but somehow, despite all that, he'd wound up here, with Luciana accepting his feelings and leaving the door open for them to explore this more.
Maybe, just maybe, he really had a chance.

The skies over Miramar were clear, but Pete "Maverick" Mitchell didn’t notice. All he saw were clouds of memory, haunting the canopy glass like ghosts.It had been weeks since Goose’s death. The funeral. The report. The silence.Jester and Viper gave him some time, but not much. Too much idleness was dangerous for a pilot. They wanted him back in the cockpit—back in the rhythm, back in control.But every hop was the same.Maverick flew like a man inside a glass bottle. Sharp. Controlled. Distant. He followed all protocols. Ran through checklists. Lifted off perfectly. But once airborne, the fire was gone. He leveled off, maintained altitude, flew patterns like a machine.He didn’t engage.No banks. No barrel rolls. No G-pulling turns.He had a backseater with him every time—one of the instructors or other grads. Today it was Lt. Colin "Razor" Price, a by-the-book RIO with a sharp tongue and little patience.The moment they hit altitude, Razor was already pushing."Maverick, come on. Target acquisition in five. This isn’t sightseeing!"Maverick’s knuckles whitened on the stick."Jesus, man, you’ve been up here three times this week and you still won’t do jack. He couldn’t hear the engine—it was drowned out by the thump-thump-thump in his chest.Then—WHUMP.A sudden jolt. A spray of feathers across the left side of the canopy. The cockpit seemed to narrow, shrink, the sky pressing in from all sides.He heard Goose again. The rush of the spin. The ejection gone wrong.His chest tightened. Vision tunneled."Maverick! For the love of God, do something!"The voice was distant. Muffled. Like underwater.He couldn’t breathe.Everything was shaking. He didn’t know if it was the plane or his hands.Then the headset hissed.**"Maverick, talk to me. It’s Viper. You're not alone up there. We’ve got you. Just breathe.""Pete, this is Jester. Bring her in. Nice and slow. One engine’s still good. You can do this."The ground felt miles too close. The sky too far.His left hand trembled, barely able to hold the throttle steady. But somehow, guided by their voices, he started the descent.The runway came into view.Gear down. Flaps out. Stick shaking. Breath ragged.He touched down hard. The jet bounced once, then screamed as it finally skidded into a full stop.The canopy popped. With great force Mav pushed himself out of of seat, lightheaded. The moment the air hit his face, his knees buckled.He fell.

You’re awake."Jester was there. Arms crossed but face soft.Viper stood at the foot of the bed, nodding slightly."Where...""Infirmary," Jester said. "You collapsed on the tarmac. Took a full minute before anyone could get a pulse."Maverick blinked. The ceiling was spinning slowly."Panic attack," Viper said. "Severe one. Razor says you weren’t even hearing him."Maverick turned away. Shame burned under his skin."I couldn’t move. I froze.""And you still landed the jet," Jester replied. Not until your head and your heart are flying with you."Silence.Jester sat back down."We’re not grounding you. But we are pulling you for rest. Therapy. Time. "There is no escape." A faint voice spoke in the darkness, no emotions lacing its words. It was so quiet and yet felt like a thousand screams of agony directed at a startled man. At first, he didn't respond to the voice, tinkering with the door's lock in a desperate manner."Why don't you face me?" The same blank tone, but a smile was palpable when the voice talked. It was a child speaking, their little and innocent figure forming little by little in front of the man. They were transparent, ghostly pale, yet the man didn't seem bothered by that, no, something else was worrying him."Are you scared?" The kid tilted their head. Black tears rolled out of their lifeless eyes in copious amounts and fell on the floor tiles. They smiled nonetheless, enjoying every moment of the anxious scratching the man did at the door in a futile effort to open it. Anxiousness turned to frustration as he began banging on it, letting out cries that no one would respond to.The man let out a curse under his breath, realising that there was no escape from this room. He still refused to address the ghost's presence, his eyes scanned the four walls frantically for something, anything, that could help him out of his predicament. Arcade machines with chipped away paint and stickers, screens reflecting nothing but the void of the room. A withered rabbit suit, one of his own creation, that he had abandoned years ago along with this place. Rats squeaked as they crawled within the old walls.As water dripped from the ceiling, mixing with whatever grime covered the chequerboard tiles, the man felt a new presence behind him. Four other souls, eyes filled with pure and unfiltered agony, blocked the already locked door. The storm outside mimicked the children's rage; the man could perceive the flash of a lightning breaking in through the cracks in the roof.Cold, freezing hands tried to grab him, it was the first kid. He shook them off violently, eyes wide with increasing panic. The ghosts had taken a physical form and were going to take his life, just like he did with theirs. Symmetry.Where to hide? Where to run? What could save him? The only company he had was his victims' unyielding wrath, which equated to none. He yearned to find something familiar in this cage, something safe, something that could hide his monstrosity that he was forced to face."It's your time to be dead!" The first child said with a giggle, chasing the man across the room.No, he will not die. He will never. Not after he's come this far, not after everything he sacrificed.There, on the other side of the room, lied the limp body of that yellow rabbit suit. He remembers it. The children remember it. A comforting character that was there with him in his golden days, no matter what, through the most joyful of times and through the most heinous of crimes. It was a perfect facade, a shining halo a fallen angel would pick up and wear—masters of deceit.What is left of a man once he let his fears consume him?A beast fueled by instinct.So, he made a run for it, his newly polished leather shoes slipping over puddles in the process, but he would get to safety, he had to get to safety.The children watched in confusion and unease as the man put on the rabbit's head, halting their every movement. Swiftly and carelessly, he put on the rest of the suit. He could finally breathe. He was safe, and the monster was hidden behind a charade.He began laughing. A rich and thick laugh, resonating between walls.The five souls simply stared, even the one that tried to strangle him moments ago. Their sudden calmness made his confidence beam for just a split-second, his victorious roar transformed into a sinister chuckle. He won. They were scared, they were letting their fear take huge bites out of them, a growing parasite.However, this illusion shattered in the blink of an eye.The man in the suit screamed, shrieked, tried to articulate a final request for mercy, his lungs flooded with his own blood. He drowned in his own sins. Metal bolts forced themselves through his skin one by one, crushing his bones and organs in a distressing chorus of squelching, yelling, begging and wailing. The rabbit succumbed to the pain, muscles twitching involuntarily as it slowly made its way down to the floor. It took hurried gasping breaths, but they were all more useless than the last.The spirits started to fade as their job here was done. Their wounds were still burning, itching in the back of their brains, though staying here would be useless. Revenge could not heal them—their true freedom would come another day. The storm outside did not calm itself, but the bleeding man could hear himself more than any other noise.He was dying all alone, with the uncaring wind whistling through the cracks of the facility.He was dying all alone.He was dying.

Sometimes she almost forgot that the house used to be an actual pirate ship, since from the inside it tended to feel like a pretty normal, albeit very grand, home. She didn't really need the help, but the gesture did make Adaine's heart flutter. It wasn't anything new; for as long as they had known each other Fabian had always done these sorts of small things, and until recently Adaine had tried to ignore the way they made her feel. Also, recently, they had gotten more frequent and more explicitly romantic - as demonstrated in this moment where, once Adaine was securely stood inside the crow's nest, Fabian gently kissed her hand that he had been holding.Adaine felt a warm blush rising on her face. While they had both confessed their feelings to each other, this change in their relationship was still new, and she still sometimes felt a little embarrassed by how flustered he could make her.
"So," Adaine said as she cleared her throat, "what did you bring me up here for?""Well, I've always loved the view from up here," Fabian leant on the railing, "and I guess I wanted to share it with you."Adaine moved to lean on the railing next to him, and looked out over the scene before her. She was used to seeing Elmville from high up in her tower, but this really was something else. She could see the entire town, and far beyond. The sun was beginning to set, and hues of orange and pink painted the sky."So, what do you think?" Fabian asked from beside her.Adaine turned back towards Fabian to respond, and suddenly her breath caught in her throat. She had always found him quite beautiful, but up here, in this moment - with the wind billowing though his hair, the stretching landscape layed out behind him, and the bright colours of the evening sky contrasting perfectly with his dark skin and pale hair and eyes - he seemed almost ethereal.She moved without thinking, wrapping her arms around his neck and leaning in to plant a gentle kiss on his lips. She could feel Fabian smiling as he held her waist and returned the kiss. Slowly, Adaine pulled back just enough to look him in the eyes as she answered his question.
"It's beautiful."

It was a fresh spring morning when Yugyeom, the gentle florist of the tiny town of Everbloom, made a small mistake that would change two lives forever.Yugyeom loved flowers more than anything—he believed each bloom carried a secret wish. His flower shop, Petal & Bloom, was famous for bouquets that somehow seemed to find the hearts that needed them most.That morning, he arranged a bouquet of colorful tulips—pink for affection, yellow for cheerfulness, white for forgiveness, and red for deep love. He slipped a simple card inside: “May these brighten your day—Y.”He was supposed to deliver them to a loyal customer’s elderly mother, but in his distracted rush, he mixed up the address. Instead, the tulips ended up on your front porch—a place where lately, all the colors in life seemed to have washed away.When Yugyeom returned to the flower shop later, he realized the mistake. Feeling flustered yet hopeful, he found himself walking up the path to your little brick house, his heart hammering in his chest.You opened the door with the tulips in your arms, looking puzzled but strangely brighter than you had in weeks. “Hi… are you the one who sent these?” you asked softly, your eyes lingering on the vivid petals.Yugyeom scratched the back of his neck, a shy smile tugging at his lips. “Ah, yes—well, not exactly. They were meant for someone else, but… I think maybe they found the right home anyway.”You laughed—a sound like wind chimes stirring after a long, cold winter for him. “They’re beautiful. It’s been a long time since something this pretty showed up for me.”So began your gentle story. Yugyeom offered to bring you fresh tulips every week to make up for the mix-up, and you found yourself waiting for his knock on your door more eagerly each time.The two of you would sit on your porch steps, talking about everything—how Yugyeom fell in love with flowers when he was a boy helping his grandmother in her garden, and how you, despite your soft smile, had lately been lost in a swirl of misfortune: a job you hated, a dream that felt unreachable, friends who drifted away, and the quiet, creeping sadness that comes from being misunderstood.One warm afternoon, Yugyeom asked, “Want to get away for a bit?”You nodded without thinking, trusting him completely.You rode bikes down winding country lanes, petals from the blooming cherry trees brushing your hair. And Yugyeom… his soft smile hints at the heartfelt vow hidden in the flowers. His words feel like hope never fades; it’s perfect and magical, it brings eternal spring vibes. And his gentle touch is sweet and comforting, like a warm hug on a chilly spring morning—timeless and cozy, like a small-town flower shop that smells of fresh-cut stems and warm sun.Week by week, Yugyeom’s kindness helps you find color and warmth again—one tulip at a time—until love blooms where sorrow once lived.Slowly but sure, he brings you tulips and shy smiles, and you find yourself blooming again in ways you thought you’d forgotten. Together you pedal down flower-lined country roads, ride the sleepy town train under soft rain, and trade secrets and laughter like shared petals drifting on the breeze.On rainy days, you took the slow train that circled the town’s sleepy outskirts, the world outside turning into a watercolor blur as you talked for hours—about your wishes, fears, and silly secrets.Little by little, the colors returned. In Yugyeom’s gentle laughter and quiet charm, you found not just comfort but hope. When you doubted yourself, he’d place a fresh tulip in your hair and whisper, “You’re braver than you think. And even on your worst days, you’re blooming.”Spring stretched into early summer. As spring unfolds into early summer, so does a tender love story—proof that even in life’s harshest seasons, warmth always returns.
One evening, as fireflies blinked in the dusk, Yugyeom stood in front of your door again, holding a single tulip—this one, an orange one for happiness and new beginnings.He cleared his throat, cheeks pink. “You… you know what tulips mean in the language of flowers?”You smiled, brushing your fingers against his. “Tell me.”“They mean perfect love. Undying love. A promise that warmth always returns, even after the coldest winter.”Yugyeom took your hands in his. “I didn’t mean to send you those tulips that day. But now, I think… maybe I did.”With tears brimming but a heart fully blooming, you whispered back, “Thank you for bringing spring back to me.”You kissed under the blooming wisteria, the evening air full of soft promises. Under blossoming petals and flickering fireflies, you discover that sometimes the flowers that arrive by accident are the ones meant just for you all along.Love, in its gentlest form, has the power to root itself in life’s harshest soil, growing hope where there was none. Like tulips that burst through frost to greet the sun, sweet love reminds you that beauty and warmth can find you—even by accident—and change your world forever.

September 9, 2009Another year had begun—Junior year. Often said to be the most challenging and impactful year of High School. The year where everyone’s supposed to make the best decisions for their future.Thoughts raced rapidly through the mind of a crimson-striped hedgehog, Shadow. Besides his love for music and interest in skateboarding, he had no clue where he’d be years from now on. Lost in thought, he lost track of time.He gave one last glance at his full-length mirror, grabbed the final piece of his uniform, and slipped on his pin-covered backpack. With quick steps, he headed out of his apartment and skated off towards school. The past two years had been the same for Shadow—being an outcast.Many disliked him based on his appearance: red eyeliner, piercings, and the way he accessorized his uniform. Most never gave him a chance to be known. Over time, Shadow learned to live with it and even found it peaceful. Still, he had to admit—it got lonely sometimes.Arriving at school, he walked toward his usual rusty green locker. After unlocking it, his eyes paused on a photo taped inside—a picture of him and an old friend. Not a single day passed without Shadow missing him.The two had been inseparable—hanging out everyday, never skipping a moment, always goofing off and lighting up each other when things got rough. One was an optimistic blue blur, the other was a quiet and soft contrast. Best friends since the start of middle school.Until High School split the two into separate paths.A high-pitched voice cut through his thoughts. “Is he trying out for a band or funeral?”Shadow’s ears twitched at the comment. He didn’t bother turning around. Instead, he shoved his skateboard in the locker and walked away from the obnoxiously loud group giggling behind him.Upstairs in his new classroom, he noticed it was empty. Using the opportunity, he inhaled a deep breath.Picking a seat far from the front, he dropped his bag onto the floor and settled into the chair. A new year meant new faces to see, and Shadow couldn’t care less about meeting any of them. People just seemed to annoy the hell out of him.As introverted as he was, the odds of him  making new friends this year were just as low as they had been the previous two.Shadow reached into his bag for a pair of headphones and slipped them on. Minutes passed. Students trickled one after another. Eventually, the bell rang. Most students were already settled in their seats—or so Shadow thought.A high pitched voice broke through his music, followed by the fading sound of giggles.Footsteps grew louder.
Shadow knew what that meant.“Alright, I'll see you girls later at the cafeteria!”The obnoxious loud voice from earlier.Eyes shifted towards the pink-fur hedgehog now standing in the doorway.Amy Rose.“Pfft, what are you all staring at? Was it my clinking keychains?” Her lashes fluttered slightly—long and curled. She tilted her head, scanning the room with visible annoyance. Eyes darted from person to person. “Hmph..looks like you all left me the worst seat possible.”
Her gaze locked on the only open seat in the far back—next to a punk-looking hedgehog. Shadow.”Dammit,” Shadow muttered under his breath.The pink hedgehog smirked as she made her way across the room. “Who do we have here? The angsty-looking funeral reject from earlier? Ah, of course! My eyes never fail me.”She leaned in closer, poking at his shoulder.Her scent hit him—sweet, with a tropical touch.“Hey! Don’t ignore me. We’re going to be the best of friends! I'm Amy Rose, by the way.” As much as she tried to restrain herself from slipping a giggle, she failed.“Fuck off,” Shadow’s snapped.Just as the words left his mouth, the teacher walked into the classroom.For a split second, Amy didn’t laugh. Her eyes lingered onto the crimson-striped hedgehog like she was about to say something else. But she didn’t. Instead, leaned back onto her seat and reapplied lip gloss.Shadow glanced sideways. He was sure he’d seen that look before. Although, he wasn’t sure what it meant.This was going to be one long, irritating year with a popular kid by his side.

Spock had endured far more compromising situations with Nyota Uhura than he’d care to catalog—though his memory, regrettably, catalogued them with perfect clarity.She had kissed him senseless against a bulkhead. She had straddled him in her quarters, traced lazy circles on his bare back with those merciless nails, whispered entirely illogical things in his ear. He had survived all of it with a degree of composure that he privately considered impressive, even by Vulcan standards.But this—this was different. They were sitting in the mess hall. Fully clothed. Having tea. Talking about the day’s linguistic anomalies in the Saurian transmission logs. He was maintaining a reasonable heart rate. Until Nyota’s fingers found his under the table and laced them together. She didn’t even say anything. She just… held his hand. Spock felt a heat rise sharply up the back of his neck, flushing into his ears. His face, if he could self-diagnose, was burning.He turned to look at her in alarm. She was sipping her tea, completely at ease. She didn’t even glance at him—just rubbed her thumb along the back of his hand in slow, idle circles. The sensation sent a spike of something unbearable through him. He made a small, involuntary sound—somewhere between a breath and a hiccup and, Nyota would insist later, a giggle.He immediately cleared his throat. Twice.“I—” he started, voice cracked. “That is an unexpectedly intense… stimulus.”She looked at him over her mug, eyes quietly delighted. “Holding hands?”“It is… emotionally unshielded.” He swallowed. “There is no… contextual framework.”Nyota tilted her head. “You let me kiss you with tongue yesterday.”“That,” he said, somehow even more stiffly, “occurred in private. This is public. Casual. It implies… fondness.”Her thumb gave another slow pass over the inside of his wrist. His pupils dilated like she’d flipped a switch.“So,” she said, fighting back a grin, “kissing is fine. Scratching your back until you make that sound is fine. But hand-holding is… too much?”He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked down at their hands. Looked away.“Correct,” he said quietly. "The cultural implications—"Nyota leaned in, smiling softly now, all amusement fading into something gentler. “Spock,” she said, her voice warm, “you don’t have to pretend this stuff doesn’t affect you. I like that it does.”He looked at her then, slowly. “You are very… disarming.”She squeezed his hand once. “You giggled.”“I did not.”“You did.”“That was a respiratory adjustment.”“You giggled, Spock.”“Incorrect.”But he didn’t let go.

“Yo Suguru ,! Have you lost weight ?” Satoru questioned, looking his dark haired friend in the eyes, awaiting his response. Like he expected, it was something about the heat. Satoru didn’t let it get to him of course, knowing that he himself was the strongest, but also Suguru was too. It never bothered him, really. Despite what other people may say, Satoru held a lot of trust in his friends, since he didn’t grow up with many himself. But that was the first prick, the first nudge as it would all tumble down soon enough. “Its just the summer heat” Suguru said, smiling slightly at Satoru, as he shrugged it off. There was no need to worry about Suguru too much, since they are always together, the strongest. Nothing could get in the way of Satoru and Suguru. Like yin and yang, the puzzle and the final piece, like.. Dinner and a sweet treat after it all.
It had been a few weeks since the attack on Jujutsu Tech, and Satoru had really taken it quite well. Nothing seemed to get to the strongest after all! He had worked on perfecting his cursed technique, especially since he had just unlocked its full potential, hollow purple. Satoru’s fingers worked swiftly as he felt the energy float through his fingers as he chucked an eraser at the wall, waiting for it to stop just short so he wouldn’t collapse half the building. The familiarity of shoes made him turn his head towards the classroom door, entering a tired looking Suguru. Leaning back in his chair, Satoru looked at Suguru, his own head upside down as he rocked his chair back and forth, his glasses falling off of his head as he studied Suguru’s cold expression. But, Satoru knew his friend wasn’t always the most expression-filled unlike he was, so he clicked his teeth and turned his chair quickly to face his best friend. But as soon as Satoru was about to say something, Suguru opened his mouth.“Satoru, tell me. What would it be like to live in a world without weak people ?” the dark haired male questioned, a serious look on his pale face. His eyebags had gotten deeper, and his pupils were more dilated than usual. Satoru knew that Yaga had administered Suguru some new medicine to cope with his response to everything, but it felt off. LIke a strong flow of adrenaline had paralyzed his friend. Regardless, the white haired boy paused to think playfully, “Well, wouldn't that be a nice break for us, huh, Suguru.” He hummed playfully, letting the pads of his fingertips rest on Suguru’s cold knuckles, as the other slowly pulled away to stand back up. It’s been exactly 35 days, 4 hours and a little over 24 minutes since the ringing of gunshots has started to fade in Suguru’s ears.
Satoru never let anything get to him. Sure he got upset, but he never felt hopeless. He’s never felt truly scared, or that's what he told himself. Even though months had passed since he had to kill Suguru in that alleyway, putting on a strong face for his students, he still never let anything get to him! Within a swift movement, Satoru stood up proudly fixing his blindfold as he swayed through the hallways of his school, choosing to ignore the ringing that plagued his head. The ringing that he could do more, or the ringing that he could give it all up right now and single-handedly create a world where weak people don't exist. But of course,  nothing seems to bother the strongest like a world that is just between his fingers and righteousness.

The halls were full of students. With the arrival of new clones, or rather old clones, the student committee was planning a variety of activities that would help these not-so-young students reincorporate into society.In this committee was Herbie. Not even he knew how he had gotten there, he was an anxious guy of few, if not, no friends. He sometimes had the theory that he had only gotten there because he didn’t know how to say no, a favor leading to another and he was suddenly guiding tours around the school and its changes in the last twenty years to the old students.In one of these tours, a student in particular called his attention, and how not to? He was surrounded by clones that wanted to talk to him or take pictures with him. All eyes were on him and it was a nightmare to continue with the tour. At the end of he day, as he made arrangements to the end of the week, the same student got close to his seat. He was asking for information about a kitty that had been rescued and was in search of a home. That was nice, someone that cared about at animals. He found it adorable. The second time he met him was in the day of unity. During the chaos the whole thing was, he heard a comment about “today’s technology” and “clones in charge now were incompetent and stupid.". He laughed at the comment, agreeing with him and the boy apologized, “I’m not saying that you are” and all that. He spent his last few breaks like that, rehearsing a salute but never actually greeting him.One of these days, he saw a smaller student approaching this boy. You’re one of his fans.”“Fans?”“Come on, the band of our clone fathers hasn’t stopped being popular, we’re the closest thing to the original, I suppose.”“Ah, of course… no, it isn’t like that.”“If you say so… hey, your face is familiar. New moon, so there’s no bright orb, and honestly, he can’t see much of the stars given the sheer amount of light pollution in L.A., but he knows they’re still there, twinkling down.He breathes in deep, holds the air in his lungs, and then exhales, measured. “I wish you were still around,” he says. “I mean, but not really, because then I’d have to send you on, and, like, honestly, that would probably break me, but you know what I mean. I could really use some advice right now.”He shifts, one ankle propped up on the other.“Did you know? When I was born?” As always, no answer. Jack is, after all, talking only to himself. “I assume there’s no sign or anything when someone is born that, hey, guess what’s gonna happen later: this crazy manifestation of abilities. Can’t turn ‘em down, can’t give ‘em back. Just one of those things you got chosen for and saddled with no matter if you can handle it or not.”He scoffs. “And I’m not saying I can’t handle it. He kind of wishes he could see the stars. He’d have to get out of the city for that, and driving through traffic would take hours, but out in the desert, it’s worth it to see how the cosmos go pink and blotchy around the smattering of lights. He’s never quite figured out if the realm he sends things to is there or nowhere. Maybe it doesn’t matter, in the end.“I feel like it’s maybe becoming more than I can handle,” Jack admits aloud. “Which I really don’t like. I’m not the sort of person who just gives up, you know? You’d never let me, not with something that really mattered. And yeah, this does matter, it’s also just… hard. It’s fucking hard.”He tilts his head to the side to look at the vague outline of the headstone he can pick out in the darkness. “So there’s this song, you probably knew it, by Kate Bush, from the 80s. And it got really popular because it was used in this show, the recent season of… anyway, not the point.” He sighs. “I really feel like that song recently. For me, there’s a guy. And I know what you’d say, you’d… actually, you know what, I don’t know what you’d say. I don’t know if you’d like him. He’s so obnoxious, and he’s constantly challenging me, and he’s absolutely the absurd side of punk trying too hard, and he…”Fuck. That catches in Jack’s throat. It’s been a long time since he’s gotten emotional here, amongst the graves, so maybe he’s due, but still. He blinks up at the sky as the corners of his eyes blur, stinging hot. “He makes me feel alive,” Jack whispers. “When almost everything in my life anymore is steeped with death, he makes me feel alive.”He probably ought to go soon; he’s got an early morning plane to catch, and he already exists on so little sleep he’s amazed he’s still upright.“I don’t want you to worry,” Jack says to the stillness of the night. “I’ve got people around me, people who care about me. People who… really matter to me. I’m gonna keep them safe if its the last thing I ever do.”He sits up. He’s probably got dirt clinging to his curls, so he runs a hand through the bun to shake the strands a bit, dislodging any clumps. And then he sighs again, dragging his fingers down his face. He can’t really put this off any longer.

He missed all the laughs, the nights eating ice cream together when they were still kids, young and happy with no worries and no regrets. Lewis knew he would’ve never gotten Nico back, not after all that shit he had put him through.  He was the reason Nico destroyed himself race after race, only to defeat him. Lewis found himself thinking about how things could’ve gone differently if only he wouldn’t had been such a selfish asshole, too hungry for glory to care about that boy that used to be his whole world.  Nico and him had rapidly grew apart, year after year. There was nothing they desired more than being teammates in Formula One. They had talked about that for hours that night in Greece under the stars.  But now things were different.  There would’ve never been another night under the stars—no more unicycling together, no more ping-pong matches, no more shared happiness over each other’s successes. There would never be “Nico and Lewis” again, just Nico and just Lewis.
Nico was now married and had two beautiful little girls with his wife Vivian, and Lewis felt like an idiot for not being able to start a family and move on just like Nico did.
Remorse continued to eat him alive, despite all the years that had passed.  He couldn’t even look Nico in the eyes without feeling tears ready to flow from his brown eyes that day in Barcelona when he found the blonde he had tried to avoid for years in front of him ready to interview him.  He had run away like a rabbit the moment Nico finished with the questions of the post-race interview.  The memories of that day in Barcelona six years before were too many and so strong that Lewis couldn’t even think anymore.
He had run in his driver’s room and locked the door ignoring Toto’s worried voice coming from outside asking him if everything was okay. Of course nothing was okay. Lewis had cried for half an hour that day. He thought he would’ve never cried for Nico ever again but that day he cried all the tears he had kept inside for six long years,  and now, sat in the balcony of his apartment in Monaco he caught himself crying once again at the thought of what he had lost. He could hear Nico’s voice and the laughters, his and of his daughters, while he played with them just a few floors above.  It was a starry night. It was July. but he wasn’t in Greece with the man he had loved for years. He was alone, mourning something that would’ve never come back.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

Vi noticed the sad look first, “What’s wrong, Lavie?”
Lavender, without a word, hopped up to their bed and dramatically fell on her back. “I’m sick,” She replied.
“What hurts?” Caitlyn asked, putting her hand on Lavender’s forehead to check for a fever.
Lavender wasn’t prepared for that question, so she had to think a little. “Boogies.”

“It’s in here somewhere,” Caitlyn muttered to herself, “Stay here, darling, I’ll get the thermometer.”
Lavender wasn’t bothered by the fuss she had created, not feeling bad one bit, mostly not realizing the worried looks on her mothers faces. The only thing she didn’t like was when Vi made her blow into the napkin, squeezing it around her nose and that she couldn’t speak when the thermometer was in her mouth.

Caitlyn and Vi looked at her confused, then it clicked.
“So, you thought that you’d get a puppy, because when mom Cait was sick she got her puppies?” Vi asked, grinning.

First, came the awareness of breath. Without the aid of machines, breathing became heavier, more pronounced. Every inhale brought something cool and fresh racing through his nose, down his throat, and finally to his lungs. Slowly, his consciousness returned to him, trickling in like flickering lights, until he became aware of the work his body was putting in to prepare him for awakening.
Next, came the perception of sound. His ears trembled slightly with what they heard: the sharp ticking of the clock, the sound of his own breathing. The soft hum of machines he somehow knew were still attached to him. And then – the song of other people’s voices. Like gears neatly clicking back into place, like a soft motor whirring back to life, his hearing returned to him and he reveled in how the sensation made him feel.
Finally, this was what prompted him to open his eyes. The voices fell away in an instant.
It was blurry at first, and the lights that greeted him were so bright that he became afraid. But after testing his eyes, opening and closing them rapidly – one, two, one, two, blinking the building liquid away – his vision cleared and the boy was afraid no longer.
The face of his old guardian came into view, the back of his head surrounded by light, as if enveloped by a warm halo.

  She has always known that something was awaiting her - not on the other side of the horizon, but somewhere behind herself. Something whispering. Something calling her name.

    her.
  
  I woke with a snap—lungs gasping, body slick with cold sweat. My heartbeat slammed against my ribs like it was trying to get out. Darkness pressed in on all sides. I blinked, slow and thick, vision swimming until the familiar outline of my bedroom came into focus. Stone walls, always damp. A single wooden frame beneath me—the same bed I’d shared with my mother since I was born. And the linen cloth twisted around my legs, soaked from the same nightmare that haunted me every time the moon rose too full. Always the same cursed dream.
  
  Me, running. Through the sparse trees of Thirevin, branches whipping at my face, lungs tearing open. The snow crunches under my boots, but it feels like I’m moving through water—too slow. Too heavy. And behind me—it hunts. A shadow, tall as the pines. Buzzing. Humming. The kind of sound you hear in your teeth. I never see its face. Just feel it. A cold weight pressing against my spine. Skin prickling.
  
  
    “Neira…”
  
   it whispers, 
  
    “You cannot outrun me.”
  
  
    
  
  I run harder. My chest burns. My legs ache. But it doesn’t matter—it’s always faster. And just as the cold closes in, as those fingers reach for me—I wake. Sweat trickled down my back. My lungs still begged for air.
  
  I threw my legs over the side of the bed and placed my feet against the cold stone floor. The chilly winter air crawls inside my thin nightgown, sending chills down my spine. I wrapped my arms tight around my waist and tiptoed into the kitchen, the hem of my nightgown dragging behind me like fog. I spot her instantly—cross-legged in front of the hearth, flames crackling in perfect silence.
  
  As a child, I never understood how she made fire without kindling. No fuel. No sound. Just presence.
  
  I let my gaze settle on the blaze, its heat brushing over skin still damp from the nightmare. She turns, slow and deliberate, ice-blue eyes locking with mine like she’d sensed me long before I stepped into the room. She probably had.
  
  I don’t know much about my mother. I know she was born in Vel Orynth—the ruined city southwest of Thirevin. I know she carries Virethi blood, ancient and cursed, older than the Embervein itself. She’s shown me the legend of their fall more times than I can count.
  
  Once, the Virethi sat beside thrones, whispering counsel to kings, warlords, healers, even death-judges. Keepers of knowledge. Bearers of truth. Until one of them said something forbidden. No one remembers the words—only what came after. The Embervein erupted. The world cracked open. Since that day, every Virethi child is born with their tongue sealed—a glowing scar across the neck known as the mark of silence. A vow to keep all knowledge in silence.
  
  My mother has never spoken a word to me. So what I know of her is fragmented. Shadowed. Half-inherited, half-imagined. I know all Virethi are born with a fire-language—they call it firetongue. My mother’s is Firesight.
  
  She can shape memory and prophecy in flame—letting the hearth become her mouth, her mind. Visions curl from the fire like smoke, formed by thought alone.
  
  The first time she showed me her ability to project, my heart stopped. Her eyes had glossed over with a mix of pride and knowledge as she manipulated the flames to take the shape of her memory of me being born. And still, every time she projects her Firesight, she gets the same sparkle in her ice-blue eyes, and it always fascinates me.
  
  I tear my eyes away from my mother’s cautious gaze and stare into the fire she has started, hoping that she will show me something. The flames start rising, licking the wood in the hearth and curling into the shape of a broad-shouldered man carrying a sword by his side. The man mounts a large horse and rides straight into the middle of the fire, the flames swallowing him whole before lowering down into quiet embers.
  
  “My father?” I ask my mother, and she nods in agreement. I smile at her, knowing exactly what she’s asking me.
  
  “No, not him tonight. The nightmare was about that shadow creature hunting me again.”
  
  I get chills at the recollection of the horrible nightmare. I’m so exhausted by having the same damn dream terrorizing me—some variation for once would actually be a relief. I watch as her eyes gloss over with the same familiar sparkle she always gets

The one who broke this fragile bit of elusion Bink had allowed himself for just a moment. His side ached when he thought about that.Now, sitting in a dingy bar somewhere north of Saveen, he didn’t feel like a person anymore. Betrayed by the one person he thought he could trust, stabbed in the back and thrown away like garbage. He frowned. How could he have been so stupid? He should have known better. He stood up and pushed away from the table to head out of the bar.It was snowing up here, but Bink barely felt the stab of frostbite on his paws. Or the cold on his entire body as snowflakes hit him. He hasn’t bothered putting on more clothes than he usually wore, and he wouldn’t do it now either. He stomped through the white mountain top, passing aarakogra as he went. They stared, but he barely gave them more than a grunt.He kept walking, even when he felt like his feet would give out. Soon enough he stood in front of the grand fall that this place was named after. The giant cliff where the aarakogra nested and lived. His heart was beating in his throat as he watched the waves break on the jagged stones at the bottom.He shuffled closer to the edge. He could feel the updraft of the air against his face and grinned. The aarakogra were smart. Nest where there's an updraft, so you can take off better. But Bink didn’t have wings. He had nothing left to lose, and no one left to disappoint. Like dying in battle, dying with a sword through his throat, struck down by the gods themselves for his bloodshed. Something different than the quiet breeze he felt now.

Great heroes dying of old age, something that history books will mention in passing. But now he stood at this ledge, the way to release down down down. Another step. His toes were dangling off the edge now. One more small shuffle, a slight push, anything and he would be gone for good.
A sharp inhale and he slowly lifted his paw off the ground. He closed his eyes and concentrated on the breeze in his fur. A soft smile tugged at his lips even as he felt his own death around him. Just one more step and–“Bink?” He was ripped out of his thoughts almost immediately, stumbling back and tripping over a stone in the process. He landed hard in the snow with a grunt, definitely opening up the wound on his stomach again. He looked up towards the voice he heard, but didn’t recognize the face.“Oh my gods, it's really you! Between the Evanuris, Aelia, and the ten other handfuls of enemies she and her companions dealt with as of late, the moments of genuine calm were becoming farther and fewer by the second. At her desk with an old case note to occupy her she took time to do more of what she did best, work. Despite the lack of sleep and the others urging her to take a break, it was as if every bone in her body forbade it from happening. She sipped on her tea that was the only thing keeping her up at this point as she searched for leads. Much to her dismay (and pleasure if she were honest) however, she found herself occupied with more ardent thoughts instead of work. What was once a list of potential suspects was now a tiny doodle of Rook surrounded in hearts.
  
    He is such trouble.
  
  It wasn’t her fault that his charm had finally managed to rub off on her, well, maybe a little. But she couldn’t deny the man’s persistence and natural allure found a way for her to open up to him in a way she never considered in a long time. Their talks along the piers of Dock Town, his insistence on helping with her cases, even learning how to fry fish just the way she liked it. It was a level of reliance she hadn't known in a long while, a level that had her smiling softly at the doodle of him that now took up more than half the page. She couldn’t help but chuckle, even after making things official she still felt like such a giddy schoolgirl.
  “Why?” She sighed, “why does he make me like this?”
  It didn’t help that he was quite the looker despite being someone who spent most of his time covered in darkspawn guts. Her smile grew wider as she continued on with her drawing, sketching from his jawline down to his neck and chest; a vivid image planted in her mind from all the times she saw him training shirtless. Continuing on down to his torso and stopping right at his hips, tapping the tip of her pen rapidly with anticipation.
  
    Careful Neve
  
  , she told herself trying to stop a new wave of thoughts that threatened to flood her mind. Her pen seemed to have a mind of its own however, 
  
    just a little lower-
  
  “My forehead is not that big.” Startled quite literally out of her mind, Neve yelped in surprise when she looked up to see her subject matter in the flesh. “You did good on my nose though and a…few other things.”
  “Oh uhm-” She scrambled to cover the doodle though she knew it was already too late. “Rook. You’re back!” That wide grin she liked oh so much just beaming with amusement. 
  
    How long has he been standing there?!
  
  “Just got in a little while ago, I woulda came to see you sooner but darkspawn blood doesn’t wash out easily.” He wore his usual black button up with long sleeves and a pair of grey breeches, standing proudly as always with his hands resting behind his back. She always did appreciate his tendency to freshen up after a day (or two most likely) in the field, especially before seeing her. “I 
  
    was
  
   gonna ask if you were busy but you have more important work to deal with.”
  She rolled her eyes at his teasing words, “Come on Trouble, what’s brought you by?” 
  
    And not just to see me of course.
  
   Though she wouldn’t have minded that as well.
  “Well, let's just say darkspawn weren’t the only thing we found in Hossberg today.” From behind his back Rook revealed a tiny bundle of blue flowers in a glass vase. “Brona’s Bloom, at least that’s what Antoine said. I just thought you might like them.”
  Neve could do nothing else but simply smile, “Rook- I- of course I do.” She stood to take a whiff of them, shocked at the sweet aroma that contrasted their environment. “I wasn’t sure much of anything survived out in the Wetlands honestly.”
  If it wasn’t the darkspawn or the Grey Wardens protecting what remained of Lavendel, it was most likely dead. The last bits of plant life Neve could even remotely recall were the trees now twisted beyond all corruption.
  “Turns out kicking the Blight’s ass as of late cleared up a few patches of these. Popular with the spirits too apparently.” Rook chuckled and Neve wasn’t sure if it was either a joke or not. “I figured I’d give a few of them a rest from that place.”

  “Yea they are.” She peered up to see him looking at not the flowers but her, enough to reignite the heat in her face.
  “Really, thank you Rook.”

    Quinton
