In truth, Malleus had no destination in mind when he teletransported away from Diasomnia.He just wanted some peace and a quiet place he could slowly unwind the tension filling his body. They are both things he cannot have in his dorm. The students are a bit too loud as they go on with their days, so different from the servants back at home. That place is lively, free of the punishments that scared so many of the people Malleus grew up around. It’s not a bad change. Malleus can appreciate that, even if he wishes they’d get closer to him more often.But Malleus is a man who flourishes in silence. It’s in the quiet moments that the weight of time truly catches up to him, only for him to lose grasp of it again as he starts processing. It’s a strange thing, although not entirely unpleasant. It’s just how he is.Still, the bright tapestries and sand-colored walls were... Unexpected, to say the least.It is quiet here, just as he wished, although for a completely different reason than he expected. The lights are turned off while the windows are open wide. Outside, Malleus can see people sitting around a bonfire. They are staring at the sky, silent and solemn. Even from the distance and the darkness, Malleus can tell they are all beastmen.He heard stories about it before. Beastmen hold the stars in high regards, believing them to be the souls of the deceased. Malleus doesn’t know if it is true. The stars he knew decades before are the same ones he sees today. But, he supposes, it would be nice if true. There is a solace in knowing your loved ones are still watching over you—that, just maybe, his parents are also there, looking after him in the only way they can.He closes his eyes. The sound of light breathing and snores reaches his ears. Malleus can feel its scent, flowers and tea and sunlight, the scent of life, so at odds with the power it possesses... Malleus glances at the bed. He knows exactly who lies under the pile of blankets.He didn’t have any destination in mind when he left Diasomnia... But he’d lie if he said he isn’t shocked to have ended in Leona Kingscholar’s room of all places. Even more shocking, that Leona remains sound asleep despite his sudden invasion. This never happened before, with the lion man always startling awake as soon as Malleus approached. It made it impossible to even see what Leona looks like when asleep.Did the tension disappear from its shoulders? Did the furrow of its brows smooth out? Did its lips part, the barest hint of fangs to be seen? If Malleus got a proper look at its face... Would he be able to see a Leona that wasn’t weighed down by pain and sorrow?He wants to know. He doesn’t dare to get closer to the bed, however. Malleus has no wish to disturb Leona’s sleep, especially now that it’s still recovering from his overblot. It needs all the rest it can get. It’s the least Malleus, as one of the reasons behind Leona’s despair, can do for it.Huh. Now that he thinks about it, he hasn’t seen Leona since the tournament. Could it be that his mind subconsciously wanted to see Leona, and his seemingly aimless magic made it happen? Malleus isn’t sure, but he doesn’t think it unlikely, either.“Heh.” He smiles. Hope isn’t typically a nostalgic man; sentimentality better suited his teammates. He’s not Flandre who went back to some noodle shop just to reminisce. He’s not Shanks with his heartfelt messages. He’s not Tarzan, he can never be the leader the way the jungler was. And he’s not Kael, quiet but mischievous and sweet only to his brothers. He was just a quiet man.However, every once in a while, he gets enough time and silence for himself that he can reminisce even only for a second. Like now, he’s sitting on the floor, luggage open, holding onto the newest jersey to join his collection and legacy.
This time, the fabric was black, the familiar red noticeably missing except for the small splotch in the team’s logo. It’s not the first time he had a black jersey, EDG and JDG both come to mind. The light hasn’t died down, the fire still burning when he sees his midlaner.
Looking to the other side of the room, Shanks’ luggage was already packed nice and tidy. The man himself was noticeably missing, probably playing with Bali and the cat one last time. Even those fruit fly glasses were on his nightstand, waiting to be worn and shown off.“Hey, Wang Jie! I look so cool, right?” He asked like he ever cared about other people’s opinions, he wasn’t even expecting a reply. But the fact he asked Hope, cared about Hope’s opinions enough to ask, it made his heart flutter. So Hope chuckled, because otherwise, he might’ve said something unbefitting of the situation. 
He shook his head as Shanks went back to doing poses in front of their mirror.The first time Hope and Shanks met, properly met, was in 2022. Him, fresh out of a defeat at Worlds semifinals, and Shanks, fresh out of a 0-16 summer split. But there they stood, equal footing with no pretentions as future teammates. And Hope couldn’t help but think about how loud the midlaner was. Hope was a quiet man but the smile on Shanks’ face rendered him speechless in a way that he hadn’t learned was possible.

Is that what it entailed? No, no, this was much worse than anything a release could entail. It was like his body was being pulled one way and then yanked another. It was tug-o-war with his limbs for rope and his mind the end goal. Carelessly children pulled the rope back and forth, not knowing it could simply snap in a matter of seconds. They say Hell is other people—but what would that make the plane of reality that exists only between the living and the dead? Would it truly be a hell without suffering? Without your body feeling like it was being ripped to shreds? How can Hell possibly be other people if loneliness will eat away at you like a ravenous beast? Their next hangout comes sooner than they had expected.
The adults in their lives still hadn't fully come around. Their friends were but very slowly.
Not that it was a date or anything. They hadn't called it a date anyway. But it's not like they're feelings for each other were a secret. At least not to each other. The people around them might not be as aware.
The lack of clarification didn’t exactly stop any nervousness the two might be feeling. Not in the slightest. When Victor had floated up to her bedroom window to steal her away for a while her dad and his aunt were at a conference, Nova didn't just have butterflies in her stomach. She had bats. With teeth.
It was the first chance they’d gotten to really be alone since everything.
“Do you trust me?”
Yes, she almost says with a little too much fervor. She trusts him more than she should trust someone she's known for this short of an amount of time. But that might be a bit too forward this early.
“Yes.” She says softly. “Why?”
“Because we're going flying.”
She'd admittedly really liked flying with the first time around. It was exhilarating. She definitely doesn't mind doing it again. So she climbs out of her bedroom window and lets him take her into the air.
With their fingers interlaced and the wind in her hair as they fly over Sunnyside, she's never felt better. Especially with the way he's looking at her.
“I know that we’ve established that you trust me. But how much do you trust me?” He grins at her, a mischievous glint in his eyes. Suddenly, they're not just soaring. They're twirling and twisting in the air using some admittedly impressive maneuvers.
She laughs loud enough that she's sure that the people on the ground can hear her.
“Trying to impress me?”
“That depends. Is it working?” She can't see his face with the position they're currently in but she can hear the smile in his voice.
“Maybe a little?”
“Only a little?” He pulls her to her, holding her against his chest. They're practically dancing now even with no ground beneath their feet. “I might've been practicing. But you make a much better partner than Vargas.”
“Well, it's paying off.” She laughs. She barely even notices how they're being slowly lowered down to the ground with how much she's having. “That was so fun. Why'd you stop?”
“Because that's not all I have planned. We’ve got at least a couple of hours until my dad and your aunt gets back. We might as well make the most of it.”
They’d landed in a patch of woodland that didn't look like it was anywhere near either of their villages.
“Where are we?”
“I'm not entirely sure. I found this place a couple years ago. I’d gotten into a fight with my aunt, took off flying, and this was before I fully mastered flying so I might have free fell and crash landed here.”
“Might have?” She raises an eyebrow at him, crossing her arms over her chest.
“Yes. Might have. Anyway, I quickly learned that this place is a pretty good place to get away if you need some time away. Sometimes I come out here to work on my art or when training to be the next leader of the vampires gets to be too much. So I figured it was probably a pretty good place for a date. I mean, a hangout. Unless this is a date to you. Because I-”
She grabs him by his jacket, pulling him to her and pressing her lips to his. It takes about three seconds for him to respond, grabbing her waist and kissing her back.
“You were babbling.” She whispers once they've broken the kiss. Her cheeks are burning hotter than usual. And if not for him smiling at her she might’ve thought she overstepped.
“I really need to do that more often.”

The world has slipped its shape, gone slack and cold around her. The air tastes of nothing, feels of nothing, slides through her like frigid wind knifing through an empty canyon. There is no light—no darkness either. Only a gnawing lack. She is nowhere. Nothing. Blown apart like a flock of startled birds. A murmuration of memories. A suggestion of a self.Tavania.The word splits the empty like a stone bouncing off the sides of a bottomless well. Something to catch, something to reach for. Is it hers? Does it matter? She has no hands to hold it.Tavania, again.She tries to answer, but has no mouth, nor any voice that will fit inside what she is now. Too tight. Too hollow. Too nothing. Too everything.
  I’m here.
Gale—She doesn’t know if she says it or thinks it. But she knows him, dimly; knows him but cannot feel him. Cannot see him. Cannot find him. Cannot lose him.Breathe, he says.Hands. Hands on hands—her hands—folded over a fragile cage of bone where lies a lone little starling, too battered to fly.
  Breathe with me.
Air pushes past lips—her lips. She tastes him in it. The burn of wanting. To see him, to see anything. A shape. A shadow. Even the dark would be kinder than this devouring void.In. Out.The cage cracks and stutters open. Rises. Falls. Almost too shallow to mean anything.Again.Deeper, this time, because he is there. A solid thing to lend her lungs—her lungs—weight and form. He breathes with her, slow and sure, like teaching a child the trick of it.“That's my girl,” he murmurs, closer now. Gale, who will not let her drift too far. Gale, who gathers the shattered pieces when she is in danger of being lost. “Come back to me.”She tries. Tries to remember the shape of herself. He leads her, helps her to demarcate the edges, where he ends and she begins—his forehead pressed against hers; his hand, solid at the nape of her neck. The other gently tap-tap-tapping against her sternum, to remind that little starling she has some fight in her yet.Feeling creeps back like first light through dawn fog, starting as a tingle in her fingers—her fingers. Colour comes after in trembling threads. A strand of silver; his hair. A sliver of blue; his robe.Her name again, low against her ear, as he weaves the torn world back together around her. Tavania. Still here. Still whole.A sob cracks her open; Gale cups her cheek, thumbs away what comes spilling out.“There you are,” he whispers. He is smiling, and she can see it. “Well done, love.”When she leans into him, safe and real, it does not feel like returning.It feels like remembering she was never truly lost.

Every breath seemed to take him back in time: the clang of metal, the acrid smell of gunpowder, the taste of blood in his mouth. It was like an acrylic stain on a white canvas. Finally. Maybe, for the first time, he could stop fighting.He remembered the exact moment he had thrown the Z-Drive at Viktor. The roar of the explosion, the blinding light, the heat burning his skin, the deafening boom that filled every corner of the field. His body hung in the air like a ragdoll, then was thrown far away, bouncing on the ground until it stopped among dust and debris. A sky that, strangely, seemed almost calm again.With superhuman effort, he got his body moving again. His hands trembled. His legs wobbled. Brothers. Firelights. People who had believed in him, who had followed his voice until the very last moment. Crushed by the weight of a war no one truly wanted to fight. He felt himself collapse inside. As if every breath suddenly became a crime. But he forced himself to move forward.
  The living. Look for the living, Ekko. Not the dead.

Through the smoke haze and the dense dust hanging in the air like a shroud, Ekko finally managed to make out faces.Living faces.Some staggered, hands clenched over deep wounds. A constant, private dialogue between body and beat, defying stillness even in solitude.**Separate melodies. Distinct rhythms.** Five currents flowing in parallel streams through the shared space. It could have felt fractured, disjointed. Lonely, even, in the dorm's sudden spaciousness.But then, hunger struck. Or habit. Or simply the invisible pull.They gravitated towards the kitchen. Minho, buzzing from his win, practically bounced off the doorframe. Kibum, pausing his fashion tribunal, drifted in, eyes still critically scanning the real-world tableau. Jonghyun emerged, blinking away the intensity of his piano world, a glass of water in hand. Jinki’s humming stopped as he followed the scent of reheated leftovers. Taemin slipped in silently, drawn by the gathering energy, his body still holding the ghost of the practice room rhythm.Suddenly, the kitchen was alive. Elbows bumped at the fridge. A hand darted out to **steal a piece of kimchi** from someone else’s plate, met with a half-hearted swat and a grin. Minho animatedly recounted his digital conquest, arms flying. Kibum countered with a biting observation about Minho’s mismatched socks, sparking a mock debate. Jonghyun offered a quiet, witty interjection that made Jinki chuckle, the sound warm and deep. Taemin leaned against the counter, a small smile playing on his lips as he watched the familiar chaos unfold, his fingers tapping an absent rhythm on the laminate.The separate melodies didn't clash; they **seamlessly wove together**. Minho's exuberance became the percussion under Kibum's sharp staccato commentary. Jonghyun's quieter interjections were the harmonic counterpoint to Jinki's grounding bass-line presence. Taemin's silent observation and subtle movements were the grace notes. The cacophony of stealing food, bumping shoulders, debating nonsense – it wasn't noise. It was their **familiar, comforting symphony**.**"Yah! Pass the rice,"** Minho called, reaching over Taemin, who effortlessly slid the bowl towards him without breaking his silent observation of Kibum's latest dramatic gesture.The request wasn't an interruption; it was the next bar in the score. Five notes. One chord. Home.

Feyd-Rautha pressed his mouth to the scar beneath Sade's ribs, here was a wound that had not killed its bearer. Here was a map of survival written in raised flesh. He traced its length with his teeth, measuring its worth against the countless marks he'd left on lesser men, and found it superior. The body beneath him answered as Feyd’s hands in his hair were precise, surgical in their intent, as if cataloging each strand like entries in a ledger. Feyd had been worshipped before, by screaming crowds in the gladiator pits, by trembling servants, by those who mistook brutality for divinity, but Sade touched him like a man assessing a weapon's balance, like a scholar verifying an ancient text. His fingers mapped the ridges of Feyd's spine as though reading Braille, as though the Harkonnen sigil burned between his shoulder blades might whisper secrets if pressed hard enough.
  The first time Feyd saw Sade bare, he understood why the man always wore black. His skin was the color of Giedi Prime's midnight, not the oil-slick dark of the industrial sectors, but the deep, starless void between the outer moons. Feyd had seen slaves flayed for lesser beauties. He pressed his palm to the dip of Sade's collarbone and marveled at how the bone refused to yield. Even unarmed, even supine, the man carried himself like a blade sheathed in shadow. Feyd's mouth followed the branching tributaries of veins along Sade's inner arm, tasting salt and the faint metallic tang of whatever poison Ploutons kept circulating in their blood. He bit down, not hard enough to break skin, but enough to feel the pulse jump against his teeth. Sade exhaled through his nose, a sound that might have been annoyance or approval, with him, the difference was academic. Feyd-Rautha had spent his life collecting reactions— the gasp of a dying man, the whimper of a bedmate, the roar of a crowd—but these breaths and tremors of pure pleasure, they were a language he'd never been taught. He licked a stripe up the column of Sade's throat and felt the vibration of a swallowed curse.
  Feyd took communion at the altar of Sade's hips. The Plouton heir lay sprawled across the black silk sheets like a sacrifice left out for darker gods, his thighs parted just enough to suggest invitation for Feyd to drag his nails down the pale insides, watching the skin bloom red in their wake. He had never been one for patience, had always preferred the immediacy of knives, but this was a different kind of cutting. When he finally bent to his task, it was with the same focused brutality he brought to the arena. Sade's fingers twisted in the sheets, then in Feyd's back, not guiding, not restraining, simply anchoring, as if to remind them both that this was happening, that they were here, that for all their carefully cultivated poisons, they could still be reduced to this: a mouth, a gasp, the wet, obscene sound of flesh yielding to hunger. Feyd, who had once made a priest recant his faith with a hot iron and a slow hand, found himself praying to nothing and everything when Sade came apart before him.
  When the sweat had cooled and the bite marks had begun to purple, Feyd pressed his forehead to the space between Sade's shoulder blades and breathed. He smelled like the sandalwood soap his house imported from Caladan, like the faint ozone tang of a hidden shock-blade, like the inevitable. Feyd had not known that another’s body could ever fit against him like this, as though their skeletons had been designed to interlock. Sade shifted, just slightly, and Feyd felt the movement travel through his own ribs like a seismic event. He did not speak. Neither did Sade. The silence between them was honest, a rare thing in the Imperium, rarer still between men like them.
  "You would bind yourself to me?" Sade wasn’t sure whether it was a question or a demand.
  "I would bind myself to a blade," Feyd said, "if it cut my enemies."
  There was a pause that stretched between them.
  “You are a fool.”
  “I am yours.”
  He would have carved out his own heart and laid it at Sade’s feet if asked. He would have burned Giedi Prime to ash. He would have drowned in the blood of every Atreides, every Harkonnen, every last soul in the Imperium if it meant Sade’s fingers stayed tangled with his, if it meant Sade’s voice still whispered his name like a repeated prayer.
  
    Sade,
  
  
    It is a strange thing to write to a man who will not write back. Strange, but not unfamiliar. You have always been a creature of silence. I do not expect an answer. I would not trust one if it came.
  
  
    It stings like salt on an open wound, this place. The sun is a cruel god here, it does not shine so much as sear, peeling the flesh from your bones if you stand too long in its gaze. The Fremen worship it, the mad bastards. They worship the sand too, and the worms that churn beneath it. I suppose when your world is nothing but death, you learn to pray to whatever might spare you for another hour.
  
  
    You would

“They called me Number Nineteen.”'
I knelt on the down comforter, fingers brushing the matted fur behind his ear.When the morning light spilled in, he finally unclenched his trembling fist. It was another normal day. The sun was beaming. Your tea was hot. The graves in your yard were cleaned. You sat in your armchair like usual, looking over your graveyard as if they were your prized possessions (which they were). Ophelia was supposed to come back from school in a few hours, so you thought it was time to kill some time.Just as you got up, you felt a strange force in the air. You didn't know what it was. You figured it was a ghost trying to get back at you, but you remembered they only spawn at night. You looked up.You saw a mysterious pointer in the air. It clicked around for a few minutes until it went away. Huh.Normal day in strangetown.You started walking again but bumped into something. It was long. And heavy.You looked down and… there was a man.Not just any man. You remembered that bright blue outfit. Those matching dark blue eyes.This was the deliveryman who you invited over a couple months ago, only for him to meet the same fate that you had for your other victims! He was one of your first kills, so you kept him in the freezer so as to not look suspicious– was Grim playing a sick joke on you?The employee looked up at you. He didn't mutter a single word. Instead, he babbled.What.The hell.You kneeled down– your knees cracked and your hip almost dislocated as you looked closer to your name tag.“Knut Futa”. What an unfortunate name.He kept staring at you. What was this grown man–phantom- or whatever the hell he was– doing here? Did the pointer in the sky have something to do with this?You waited for him to get up. He didn't budge. Instead he stared at you. Maybe he was paralyzed?Maybe not. He moved his arms and legs around. He rolled side to side. Maybe he just couldn't stand.So you did what any normal person would do, and picked him up. As you did you swore your back snapped straight in half. You really had to stop bending over.The man looked at you. He looked… innocent. Pure.It was the same feeling you got when you held your niece for the first time. Cute aggression. He was almost… babylike.He gurgled. So maybe he was actually a baby.You decided to take him back into your house. The very same house you had stuffed him in the freezer all those years ago. You placed him down on the floor like you went into autopilot.Now you had to decide what to do with him.Should you kill him again? No. That'd be the equivalent of killing an actual child. Keep him around? Ophelia would suspect something if a grown ass man was lying on the floor and drinking from a baby bottle.Hmm.You sat next to him, watching as he babbled. Maybe there was a secret third option.

No one remembers where they came from—only that their songs tamed demons and their swords destroyed them. Their legacy continued across generations. Soon, the people began to worship them.The descendants of these hunters built castles and raised walls around their lands to protect their subjects. Over time, they became more than guardians—they became rulers. Queens, governors, generals. And gradually, grew further and further away from their noble purpose, until it twisted into politics, greed, and power.The demons, once hunted and slain for the good of all, became means to an end. Every governor who wished to join the kingdom protected by the Reigning Hunters had to be willing to pledge themselves under their yoke. once they actually started talking outside of soccer practice.

Do you believe in 11:11 wishes? They say that if you make a wish at exactly 11:11, the universe might listen.
Seungmin never believed in things like that. He’s always been practical, grounded in logic, in science. To him, everything had an explanation, and miracles were nothing but comforting illusions. “Miracle” wasn’t even in his vocabulary.

Today marked six years since their death. Six years since he’d been left alone in this world. And yet, the guilt hadn’t loosened its grip on him. It clung tighter with every passing year, whispering all the things he should have said, all the things he should have done.
It happened at night, the last fight with his parents. Fights weren’t new in their home, they had fought many times before. Most of them started because of Seungmin. And most of the time, it was his parents who swallowed their pride first and asked for forgiveness.
“Seungmin-ah, we’re only afraid that if we let you chase this music dream of yours... your life might amount to nothing. Medicine is more practical. It’s certain.”
His mother’s voice is calm, measured like she’s trying so hard not to upset him. But to Seungmin, every word feels like a slap.
What do they know? What do they ever know? They can’t even spare a few hours to watch his school performances. They never see how much he’s poured into this.
“Mom, I’m not a child anymore! Let me decide for myself! This is my life!” he shouts, his voice cracking under the weight of his anger.

  Bullshit. This life is bullshit.
All his life, he’s gotten what he wanted. Maybe because he’s their only child, spoiled, yes, but wasn’t that their choice? They loved him the only way they knew how: by giving in. But why now, when it matters most, do they suddenly decide to stand their ground?

    "Love your parents while you still can."
  
A bitter laugh claws its way out of his throat. Love them? They can’t even love me enough to let me be who I am.

Morning comes too fast. Too loud. His parents knock on his door, voices soft, pleading. They try again to explain. That they’re just worried. That they want what’s best.
But Seungmin doesn’t want to hear it. Not today. Not ever.

The body in front of him has been dead for a while, long enough that maggots have taken up residence in a few places, and it means nothing to him.
 The nanites coalesce into shiny black claws and insert themselves into his jaws and over his teeth, extending his muscles and joints until his mouth opens further than any human’s should and his teeth become perfect knife-edged daggers.
  Miles sinks his new claws into the meat, uncaring of the discoloration and creeping rot, and slices downward.
 His claws cut through flesh, fat, skin, and groove the bones below.
 Deeper within, the rot hasn’t reached as far, and the organs are mostly still their expected color.
 It wouldn’t matter if they weren’t.
  The nanites in his claws confirm that the body has the nutrients and minerals they and their host need.
 Miles digs his claws back into the body and hoists it up to his mouth.
 He’s drooling a black, sticky liquid that’s more nanite than saliva; dead and dying machines reprogrammed for one last job.
  He sinks his teeth into the lacerated flesh.
 The nanites prevent him from tasting anything but pleasant, intoxicating flavors, even when he knows that he’s eating rotting meat.
 The Swarm will handle any unruly microbes, and is far too eager for more materials to let something as stupid as taste stop it from acquiring more.
  Old blood drips down his chin, mixing with the nanite fluid.
 It would be easier to lay the body down and eat it off the floor, but Miles is clinging to whatever humanity he has left and he will not tear into the corpse like a starving coyote.
 Instead, he hoists the limp, ungainly body to his face and lets the shark-like build of his mouth rip chunks from it.
  He’s disgusted, on an emotional level, but the nanites are everywhere within him and won’t let him feel nausea, or taste anything but good, mouthwatering flavors even when he feels some unfortunate maggots crush between broad, flattened molars.
 Maggots eat rotting flesh, and Miles eats rotting flesh and anything else the Swarm deems useful.
  He catches a rib and snaps it easily; the calcium isn’t of particular use to the Swarm but the marrow is rich in iron and the trace minerals and metals are always of interest.
 Miles groans when he hits the liver, the flavor so good he worries that the Swarm is trying to activate arousal to encourage him to eat more of it faster.
 He uses his claws to slice it free and feels the uncomfortable prickling sensation of nanites expanding his throat so he can simply swallow it down, get it into their system faster.
  He does so, less out of desire and more out of a dull curiosity to see how the Swarm will handle it; Miles has only gotten sick once or twice, and only after eating something with some damn powerful toxins.
 He feels the organ glide down his throat, compressing further and further until it sits in his stomach more like a milkshake than a solid object, and he wonders if he’s been given teeth in his throat.
  It doesn’t really matter.
 The Swarm wants more, so he takes another mouthful of rotting meat and chews it spitefully.
 He will eat his way or not at all, he tells himself, and swallows only to fill his mouth again.
  The Swarm purrs and encourages him, because for all its incredible power it still needs a host body to produce its nanites, still needs Miles Upshur alive in some capacity and that means fueling his body along with its own.
 It can reshape his body, alter his cells, but it cannot create them and cannot survive without them.
  Miles rips more flesh from the corpse and swallows it, then snaps another rib.
 The shards of bone he swallows should perforate his digestive system, but the Swarm will dissolve them easily and has reinforced the walls of his organs long before now.
  He makes the mistake of looking before he takes another bite and a faint shudder runs through him; the skin is black and bulging with larvae, and it doesn’t stop him.
 More material for him and the Swarm, and it does not care that all of Miles’ quietly suppressed instincts are screaming in horror.
  He’s going to eat most, if not all, of this body, and there’s nothing he can do to stop himself.

It is a universally-acknowledged truth at Chastillon that His Majesty King Laurent possesses many rare and exquisite qualities: an intellect sharper than a freshly whetted dagger, a tongue that could eviscerate a council chamber with a single phrase, and—apparently—a secret fondness for holding hands. It’s the sort of thing no one dares mention, not if they value their dignity or their life, but Émile, who has spent a decade learning when to keep his mouth shut, has become an expert observer of the quiet, dangerous art of happiness.
  He catches the kings at it on a morning so crisp it could snap—one of those days when your breath hovers pale in the air, when the frost on the rose beds glitters, and the garden smells faintly of earth and violets waking up for spring. The world is hushed except for the birds and a distant bell in the city below. Émile trails at a polite distance, boots shining, blue cloak weighted by dew and duty. There are no barracks now, only the soft hush of peacetime and the peculiar weight of new responsibilities—both of which seem lighter, somehow, when seen from the garden path.
  Ahead, Damen—sun-blessed, impossibly broad, still more hero than king in the way he moves—ambles beside Laurent, who is all winter poise and spring promise. Their hands are laced together, Laurent’s thumb tracing slow, idle circles over Damen’s knuckles.
  It shouldn’t be remarkable, except that it is. Two kings, whose every gesture is fodder for gossip and history, looking so quietly, stupidly happy. Damen glances down at their joined hands, a smile blooming on his face so soft and golden that Émile half-expects the rose bushes to burst into flower just to keep pace.
  There’s a peculiar energy in the air—awkwardly intimate, as if the world itself has agreed to look away for this moment. Émile ought to avert his gaze, but after all these years, he’s earned the right to be a little nosy. Besides, it’s the only thing happening this morning that isn’t a security briefing or a tedious inspection of the gates, entrances, and walkways.
  Laurent’s posture softens—shoulders loosening, the hard, wintry lines of his profile easing into something almost gentle. The only sounds are the rhythmic scuff of boots on gravel, the faint shush of hands brushing against velvet cloaks, and Damen’s voice—a low, private rumble for Laurent alone.
  Laurent’s cheeks go faintly pink, but he doesn’t let go.
  Émile, meant to be on alert for assassins, finds himself grinning behind his hand. He almost feels… happy for them. Ridiculous. Disgusting. He blames the weather—and, if anyone asks, he’ll claim the dew in his eyes is just an occupational hazard.
  And if his chest aches, just a little, he blames that on the cold as well.
  Spring has ambushed Lys with its usual lack of decorum. The riverbanks are a riot of green—wild poppies and buttercups so thick they threaten to trip even the most seasoned foot soldier. The city’s famed stone bridges arch gracefully overhead, their reflections shimmering beside laundry strung between willows and the little boats drifting by. Beyond the rooftops and spires, the mountains rise in the distance, their snowy caps catching the sunlight, blue and white against the horizon—a reminder of wildness just beyond the city’s reach. The air is syrupy with the scent of water mint, mud, and honey, all tangled together with the incessant drone of bees and the wild shrieks of children racing between groves.
  Émile, these days, is responsible not only for national security but also, somehow, for ensuring that neither king nor small dog is swept away by the current. He stands beneath the dappled shade of a willow—boots damp, cloak a patchwork of grass stains, starburst badge catching the gold of late sun—close enough to intervene if any overenthusiastic citizen or particularly aggressive duck fancies its chances, far enough to pretend that the royal pair sprawled by the river are simply ordinary men.
  Which, Émile reflects, they most certainly are not.
  Laurent is—miraculously—at his most relaxed: sleeves rolled, boots muddy, a streak of grass on his jaw and a blue-eyed glint of mischief that puts Émile instantly on high alert. Damen, having abandoned his official dignity for the afternoon, lounges in the buttercups, biceps pillowed behind his head, looking so at home Émile half-expects him to sprout roots.
  He watches as Laurent, with the careful calculation of a man planning a coup, selects a daisy and weaves it through Damen’s hair. Damen, distracted by a riverside game with two local children, doesn’t notice at first. But as the garland grows—violets, primroses, the odd bluebell snuck in with a flourish—Damen’s ears turn a deep, traitorous red.

Snow softly crunching underfoot was the only sound Law had heard for miles. It was early, or late, depending on how you saw things; so dark and frigid that no one was out. Law felt like the only man on the island.He was grateful for that. The last thing he wanted was an audience.He hadn't even let his crew come with him. He'd left them on the Tang a few hours ago, bobbing in the icy shallows off the coast. Right about then, the cook was probably just starting to stir and think about brewing coffee. Everyone else would still be fast asleep.Law didn’t envy them. He didn’t want a soft bed, warm blankets, or breakfast. He wanted this, or at least would settle for it. His actual desire would go unmet, like almost all of them. It seemed like all he ever did was want what he couldn’t have.Unachievable things, nebulous feelings, people who were long dead: Law counted them like sheep as he made his way across Minion Island. Navigating by memory, he trudged through deep snowdrifts, following a ridge of hills backed by skinny pine trees.It was just like he remembered. A few centuries—nevermind thirteen years—wouldn’t have made a difference here.❅Even before he made out the silhouette of the old building, Law felt it getting close. There was something in the air. Too much time had passed, but he still followed it along the hills as they slumped into loose embankments. Eventually, over the top of them, he saw a dilapidated roof and the broken brick exterior of an abandoned facility's upper floors.He summited the nearest embankment, all compacted and iced over. He had to smash the toes of his boots in with every step to get a grip. By the time he made it to the top, he was sweating under his coat, and he stood for a while, staring down from the vantage point, letting the wind cool him off.He’d come up off to one side of the back of the building. Moonlight streamed through the largest breaks in its shell, showing slivers of an interior gone to hell: rotten floorboards, inner walls buckling, everything dusted with snow. Around the corner, he could see the courtyard. The ground was mostly flat there, with only a few small snowdrifts, and dotted with the charcoal remains of a few squatter’s fires.He hopped down from the embankment when the cold started to nip, landing with a crack on frozen ground. He strode into the courtyard, where wind swept loose snow as it skated over it. Law’s coat flapped and his hat nearly blew off as it tore past him and slammed into the building, reverbing through the guts of the first floor.He shivered as he turned on his heels, looking around the yard. He wondered which innocuous few feet of ground was where it’d happened. Hard to say; there was no evidence and his own memories of that night were unreliable. He’d been so sick that what he remembered most clearly were sensory details.The hardness of the trunk. How tired the cold made him. The crackle of pistol shots. The hot stink of blood… Useless. He picked a spot at random, dropping to his knees where he stood just as the wind started to ease off.Law padded the ice down, his breaths puffing out in front of him like smoke. At the thought, he caught a whiff of that smell again: plant ash and menthol coated roll paper, as clear as the night was cold.Impossible. Of course it was.He cleared his throat.Like he had so many times since his benefactor’s death, he said, “Uh, hey, Cora-san. It’s me.” He spoke softly, but his voice still echoed through the empty grounds. “Sorry; I know it’s been a while, but can we talk?”Law imagined the pine tree swaying at the far edge of the yard was Cora-san nodding.“Thanks,” he sighed, a little relief creeping in. He’d been holding his breath for weeks. Avoiding Cora-san, avoiding this. Not that avoiding it made any difference. September came and went like it always did, and so did October. Whether Law dragged his own feet or not, time kept marching.“You know what day it is?” he asked. “Probably not. Guess you wouldn’t need to.”He shifted his weight again and the snow under him packed further down. Cold seeped through his pants, numbing his shins. His toes were tingling. So were his fingers. The tip of his nose hurt. He’d have to head back soon.“It was my birthday, not too long ago.” Law swallowed, his throat feeling tight. “The guys made this huge pudding. It was alright. They’d be badly chapped later, and it’d hurt like hell. He welcomed the pain. It’d be his souvenir, the only real thing he could take away.“Twenty-six this year,” he said hollowly. “Same as when you…”His hand curled up, making a snowball, and his eyes started to sting. Knock Out hates medicine.While he understands the usefulness of this field, this  understanding does not make his hatred any more bearable. Every time he enters the med. bay, it was as if invisible walls are closing in on him, and their pressure makes him feel claustrophobic. Every time he has to touch medical instruments that feel heavy, disgusting, and cursed. Every time from him expected to do his job brilliantly, that the mech in front of him will soon stand up, even if it is almost reduced to gray scrap metal. And if he fails, then death will lie on his servos. Death doesn't bother him as much as it had to. But this feeling was almost unbearable. After most of operations, Knock Out was dirty and tired. Too much work, too much dirt, too much pressure, too much responsibility. Even if their leader doesn't care about the health of his soldiers. He didn't choose to be a medic, and this fact only makes it worse. Sometimes, on particularly bad days, he remembers how the thin and seemingly fragile servos burrow into his cabels and deeper, alarmingly close to his restlessly flickering spark, how roughly they dig into his plates and tear them away without turning off the pain receptors and he writhes, writhes, trying to reach for that place but he can't. It hurts, Primus, it hurts, just stop...!— ...oc? Knock Out? Knocks? Amberlight? — Knock Out can't help but flinch slightly as a vaguely familiar voice breaks through the abyss of dark memories.He yanks one of the servos off the table to swing, but the larger servo intercepts it almost immediately, squeezing too gently for such a firm grip. Before he can try to break free, familiar voice reaches him again:— Are you with me now, Amberlight? — It takes Knockout a humiliatingly long time to realize that his optics were offline, and when he finally turns it on and focuses, a familiar orange faceplates framed in gray and blue metal appears right in front of him.— Welcome back, Doc, — mech (Breakdown, Knock Out reminding to himself, his Conjux, Breakdown) says softly, smiling, causing the corners of his optics to wrinkle slightly. Now then Knock Out is no longer struggling, Breakdown lets go of his servo and moves to his back under the wheels, soothingly massaging the plates while grabing and pushing the medic’s other servo away from the table. — You blacked out for a while. Are you having another attack? Want to rest?— Uh… — he forces out a glitchy answer, but almost immediately reboots his vocalizer, looking back at the table where his claw marks remain. — I'm fine, Br-rakedown. Just some bad thoughts. Nothing special. I need to get back to finish work.— Work can wait. You're clearly in no condition to work right now. — The former wrecker remarks, wrapping his field around medic, and it feels like a blanket, making Knock Out lose what little bravado he'd managed to muster. — I may not be an expert, but I understand that you're exhausted and need a rest. You've done a lot of work today and you deserve it. I can handle the details. After all it's not for nothing that I'm your assistant.He chuckles, causing Knock Out to smile weakly.— Seriously, take a rest, maybe even go on a recharge. I'll finish everything for you, it's not a problem for me. — His voice softens even more as he leans down to press his helmet to Knock Out's, and servo that wasn't on medic back touches his chest, right where the spark was. — And I'm pretty sure carriers don't need extra stress.Knock Out snorts quietly, pressing his helmet lightly in response. He closes his optics, allowing himself to enjoy this cozy moment with mech that has caught his spark for a moment.— You do realize that I won't rest properly until you come, right? — medic says half-jokingly.— I'll finish everything in no time, you won't even have time to notice, — Breakdown answers him with such a confident grin that Knockout doesn't have the strength to argue further.— Well, then I'll be waiting for you, my spark. — pressing his helmet against the other's one last time, Knock Out pulls away and heads for the exit of the med bay.Before leaving, he stops and turns around, watching bulky figure of his Conjux painstakingly assemble the jumbled instruments, and his spark sings with love for this mech.Knock Out may hate medicine, but thanks to it and his servos, Breakdown is still alive. And no matter how strong this hatred is, Breakdown is much more important than his feelings to medicine. Those sweet smiles, that sometimes almost naive behavior and such gentle treatment are worth it to once again go into med bay and take the instruments into the manipulators. His knowledge and position as a medic provide them with some measure of safetyKnockout may hate medicine, but he loves Breakdown. And his gratitude and recognition of the efforts invested, despite the disgust, is enough to enter the med bay. Cut off every damn time. With these thoughts, Knockout leaves the room to wait Breakdown in their cabin.

Keith stared at the grave in front of him as Adam brushed his hair. “I miss him.” Adam only hummed at his words as his hands paused. “Do…do you think-” Keith pushed his sleeve up a bit, revealing dark purple marks that used to look like scars.
“Don't.” Adam put his sleeve back in place. “You know those have to stay hidden until they're gone.” Keith let his hand fall to his lap.
His eyes focused on the photo in front of the grave as Adam's hands started to move again. “But-” Keith wanted to tell James and Lance, they'd understand and he wanted to know if Shiro knew. “I said don't.” Keith looked down at his lap as Adam shut the conversation down like always.
Every time Keith even thought of mentioning his marks to anyone, Adam shut it down immediately. “Why?” Keith wanted to know, he needed to know. “Because I'm not entertaining your fantasies, they'll only leave you upset.” Keith turned to look at Adam when he felt a gentle tap to his shoulder, signaling Adam was done with his hair.
“But what if it's not just a fantasy? What if-” Adam pressed a finger to Keith's lips, silencing him. “And if it is?” Adam raised a brow.
“It's better to play it safe.” Adam's hand moved to cradle his face. Keith immediately melted into the touch as his eyes fell shut, this was one of the only times Adam actually saw him. “I can't risk losing you.” Keith opened his eyes and saw Adam's fear leaking into his features.
“It's just a little longer, I promise.” Adam gave a small smile but to Keith, it felt like it was meant for someone else. “I know.” Keith gave a weak smile in return.
Adam pulled his hand away and wiped both hands against his loose pants. Keith had a feeling it was due to him. “You better go find James and Lance, I'm sure they're looking for you.” Adam turned his attention to the grave. Keith nodded and stood as he moved out of the way.
Keith stared at Adam, his eyes locked onto the loose braid Adam always styled his hair into. It was the only thing they had in common besides the grief they had over Shiro. “I…I love you.” The words were quiet as a whisper and Keith didn't even know if Adam heard him or not. He didn't even know if Adam actually loved him.
But he does know that as long as he hides his marks, he can keep the last remaining family he has. And luckily for him, he won't have to worry about them for long and neither will Adam.
Adam will finally see him.

The cicadas screamed in the summer air.The blue shade of the shop was a short respite from the sun. From next to Damon, Kai pulled at his collar, trying to cool down.“Excuse me, ma’am. Can we grab some ice cream?”The cooler was a slice of heaven, “Ahh, nice and cool… wait– there’s barely any left!” Just a bag of ice, some drinks, and a singular papico left, right at the bottom.“Dang. All they got is papico.” The cicadas were a constant noise.As if it was mocking them, the sign outside the shop still read– “‘Frusty-cold ice cream available!’-- My ass! What the hell’s ‘Frusty-cold’, anyway?” The sign fluttered in the wind as if to reply, dancing in a dizzy dose of summer heat.Under the shade of the corner store featured a vending machine, old newspapers, half-dead potted plants, and Damon and Kai sitting on a bench. Even the toys inside the gachapon machines on their other side appeared to be dying of thirst.
Damon sucked on the frosty milkshake inside the papico bottle, eyes somewhere in the middle distance, “I can’t believe we were forced to run long-distance in this weather…”Kai laughed, “Right? It’s straight-up torchure!”“...Kai. You said “torture” all weird.”“Oh, did I?”
Damon took the papico out of his mouth, “Torture’s pronounced like ‘scorcher’, not ‘for sure’.”Kai looked at him, then looked back into the distance, “Gotcha,” He bit the papico he bought, “Torture… it’s torture. I’ll remember that next time.”The mountains in the distance were framed by summer.“...So…” Damon frowned, “…You really don’t remember going missing in the mountains for over a week?”“Nope, not at all.”“...It’s been six months since you did. I guess you’re not gonna remember anything more than what you can already.”“Isn’t it fine? How long are you gonna keep asking me about it anyway– hey!” Damon shoved down Kai’s head.“Of course it’s not. Everyone was worried about you.”“Quit it!” Damon let go.Kai fixed his hair with a hand, chuckling softly, “So you missed me while I was gone?”“Nope,” Damon looked away, “Not really...”“Liar. You totally cried for days, I can tell– ah!!” Damon was shoving his head down, “Again?!”“Don’t get carried away.”“Why do you always do that…” Damon’s hand twitched in Kai’s hair.“Hey,” Like Kai, his head was facing down, “I’m gonna ask you a weird question,” He let go.
“What is it?” Kai grinned, hand automatically coming up to fix his hair, “Let me guess... you like me?”“No,” Damon wasn’t meeting his eyes again, just staring at the trees against the summer sun, and how they glimmered and swayed,
“...Listen. This isn’t something I’ve just thought of right now. It’s been on my mind ever since you went missing and came back. So I’ve been wondering about it for a while….”The cicadas were deafening.He seemed lost in his mind.Damon's tone was conversational.“You aren’t the real Kai, are you?”...Kai froze from where he stared at him.“Huh?” For some reason, he couldn’t tear his eyes away from Damon, “......Why…?”Damon looked up.Kai’s hair dripped down his skin, melted through his eye into rivets of pink, white and black. It tore through the skin of his cheek, off his skin like it’d been shredded. It broke his smile of disbelief into something monstrous, “ I’m supposed to be a perfect copy of him… ”The formless patterns merged, growing over Kai’s face like the arms of a deep-sea creature, wavering, reaching towards Damon, splattering shadows over his skin.
Damon couldn’t breathe, “...Ah…”
The snailed mess of squelch became spindles of wire and tongue, licking over wide eyes before they could touch him.And then Kai was hugging him– the sudden weight almost an attack.“Please…” His voice was desperate, holding him closer then he’d ever had before, “...Don’t tell anyone…”Damon couldn’t move. He couldn’t erase what he’d just seen from his mind. His skin shook from where Kai gripped it.Kai was crying, voice breaking, “This is the first time I’ve lived as a human. School, friends, ice cream– I’m having so much fun for the first time…” A sniff. Damon could feel the rivets over his shoulder– that creature that crawled out of Kai’s face, “I may be borrowing this body, and this personality… but my feelings for you are real…”His breath stuttered, “So please… I don’t want to kill you…”
Tears splotched into his shoulder. Damon could feel the same ones rolling down his face. All at once he could breathe, but he struggled to get a breath in. His hands shook, as if surprised to be touching Kai at all.He felt himself go lightheaded. Lost in his mind.
   Kai’s… Kai’s not around anymore… 
   And if that’s how it is, then I want him to be by my side… even if he’s fake…
 
He closed his eyes, and felt the tear fall over his cheek. His words felt hollow.“Okay… nice to meet you... ‘Kai’."

Yudai never meant to open a shelter.Not officially, anyway.He was twenty-six when the last line snapped, when the tenth kid in four years slipped through the cracks of the system and disappeared, and all Yudai could do was sit at his desk with a cold cup of vending machine coffee and pretend the silence in the office didn’t feel like a scream.No one else seemed to care. Or maybe they did, but only within the limits of a clipboard, a phone call, a deadline. “We did everything we could,” They would say. But Yudai knew that wasn’t true.
No one had stayed.Except him.So when the landlord offered a run-down house on the edge of the city for dirt cheap, with creaky stairs, a rotting porch, and a roof that threatened mutiny every time it rained, Yudai signed the lease. It was a four-bedroom, two-bath wreck with cigarette burns in the carpet and peeling walls that smelled like old smoke and mildew. He moved in with a space heater, a secondhand futon, and an aching sense of failure that wrapped around his ribs like wire.The house was never supposed to be anything more than a hiding place for Yudai himself.But then came Euijoo, fifteen, bruised knuckles, and a stare too old for his face. Yudai found him outside the convenience store, shivering in the rain with a busted lip and no shoes. Yudai gave him a blanket and some rice balls. Euijoo showed up the next night with a trash bag full of clothes and asked, “Can I crash for a while?”And then came Maki and Taki, the half-brothers who spoke more with glances than words. They didn’t say what they were running from, but the shadows under their eyes said enough. Jo arrived after getting kicked out of his fifth foster placement, angry at the world and carrying a duffel bag full of broken electronics he refused to throw away. Harua, found in the back of a laundromat, hadn’t spoken in weeks. He didn’t have to, the bruises on his arms told the story.Yuma came last. He didn’t bring much, just silence, and a habit of looking over his shoulder too much, like the past might be catching up with him at any second.And then there was Nicholas.Nicholas didn’t knock. He didn’t ask. He showed up during a storm, soaking wet, furious and shaking, with red around his eyes and blood on his shirt. He stood in the doorway, stared Yudai down, and said, “I don’t need your pity. I just need somewhere to sleep.”Yudai opened the door wider.Now, the house breathes with mismatched life. The kitchen table is scratched and cluttered. The living room smells like instant noodles and teenagers. Someone is always yelling. Someone is always laughing. Someone is always crying in the bathroom, trying to be quiet about it.It’s chaos.But it’s also home.Not a perfect one. Not a clean one. But a real one.Yudai never meant to open a shelter.He just didn’t know how to keep watching kids fall through the cracks.So he made a place where the broken ones could land.And maybe, just maybe, begin to heal.But the kids aren’t the only ones who need to heal. She’d nestled her head against her left arm, the right still outstretched, since Quynh had yet to let go of her hand.The way Quynh kept hold of her, Andromache had no chance but to cradle her fingers against the side of Quynh’s face.And maybe, feeling her gentle touch like this, was the reason why Quynh hadn’t released her hand yet. Regulus climbed the spiral staircase quietly, his footsteps muffled against ancient stone. The castle was still, save for the soft creak of shifting beams and the occasional hoot of an owl drifting in from the open sky. He held a book under his arm, more for the excuse than anything else. Reading was easier than sleeping these days.The Astronomy Tower had become his refuge over the past few months. A quiet space above it all, where no one expected him to be anything.So of course, tonight—James Potter was already there.Leaning against the stone railing, his curls tousled by the wind, arms crossed lazily over his chest, James was looking up at the stars like they were old friends. The moonlight spilled over his face, turning his gold into silver.Regulus froze for a second too long.James looked over, grinning as if he’d been expecting him. “Hey.”Regulus cleared his throat and stepped forward, a little too stiffly. “Didn’t think anyone would be here.”James shrugged. “Didn’t think I counted?”Regulus narrowed his eyes slightly, but said nothing. He crossed the tower floor and took his usual bench—furthest from the ledge, where the wind wasn’t as sharp. He pulled out his book and opened it halfway, pretending to read.He could feel James watching him, but not in a hostile way. Not even teasing. Just... aware. Curious. Like he always was.It had been almost a year since he left Grimmauld Place. Since Sirius had flung open his bedroom door at three in the morning and said, "You coming or not?"And Regulus had gone.No plan. No wand packed. Just… gone.He’d spent that summer learning what silence sounded like without judgment. What it meant to live in a house where people laughed loudly and never apologized for it. The Potters had given him a room. Mrs. Potter had given him second helpings and space to breathe. And James—James had given him everything he didn’t know how to name.“You’ve been quiet lately,” James said softly, breaking the silence.Regulus turned a page he hadn’t read. “I’m always quiet.”James gave a huff of laughter, but didn’t argue. “Right. You’ve been quieter.”There it was. That warmth. That awful, infuriating warmth in his voice that made Regulus feel both held and exposed.“Nothing’s wrong,” Regulus said, a little too quickly.James didn’t press. He never did. Just leaned back on the railing again and tilted his head toward the stars.Regulus followed his gaze before he could stop himself.James Potter was not beautiful in the usual way. His jaw was too sharp, his smile too wide, his nose slightly crooked from a broom accident in Third Year. But under moonlight, with that ridiculous kindness glowing from him like a second sun, he was—Devastating.Regulus looked away sharply, heat prickling at the back of his neck.This wasn’t new. He’d been dodging it for months now—this thing that bloomed slowly every time James touched his arm without thinking, or remembered how he liked his tea, or sat next to him even when Regulus was being insufferable.He had explained it away, over and over again.James was just friendly. Just too Gryffindor for his own good.Regulus was just lonely. Just confused. Just grateful.But now, sitting in the quiet with nothing between them but stars and unspoken things, Regulus felt it settle into his chest with terrifying clarity.He was in love.Somehow, impossibly, he had fallen for James Potter. Slowly, stupidly, deeply. And now he couldn’t breathe around it.His fingers tightened around the book in his lap.James turned toward him again, brows lifted slightly. “You okay?”Regulus nodded, too fast. “Yes. Fine.”A beat of silence. Then James, casually:“You know, you don’t have to lie to me all the time.”Regulus looked up sharply. “I’m not—”James just smiled. Not smug, not triumphant. Soft.“You do, though. And it’s okay.” He turned back to the stars. “I just thought you should know that you don’t have to.”Regulus stared at him. At the slope of his shoulders, the mess of his hair, the ease of him.Something inside Regulus cracked, quietly.He swallowed. “You make it difficult.”James looked back at him, puzzled. “What?”“Being around you,” Regulus said, voice flat but trembling slightly. “It’s… difficult.”James blinked, processing. “Oh.”Another pause.Regulus stood abruptly. “I should go.”“Reg—” James started, but Regulus was already heading for the stairs.He didn’t look back. He couldn’t.Not tonight.

Commodus sneered as he entered the shrine of Apollo.Well, not shrine. More like a room that just so happened to have paintings and statues of him.And these depictions of Apollo might be a teeny bit destroyed.It was the perfect room. Where he could vent, take out his anger, and plot his revenge, for Apollo would arrive soon, and he needed the perfect performance.   To achieve control o’er the city you crave,
  Place your past love in your games.
  Send him to an early grave,
  Destroy the house that underhand your aims.
  
  Be careful of the Sun’s wrath,
  Lest sight decide to abandon your path.
  Ally yourself with creatures polite,
  And let your feelings of betrayal reach the light.
Smiling even more, he grabbed the hatchet left at the side of the door, freshly sharpened for a new round of beheading.Stalking closer to the freshly replaced wooden statue, he struck at the head. You gave me your blessings, and then you kill me.”He soundproofed this room for a reason.His heart pounded. Not of exertion, though. Of something else. Something Commodus didn’t want to name.And he won’t.
  He still loves Apollo.
He bit down at his lip, not even wincing when ichor leaked out. It would be a nuisance to heal, but he would rather do that than admit that one secret.The feelings? They never faded.Unbidden, his mind danced to Apollo. Golden hair, bright smile, looks that possibly rivalled Venus. Not that Venus would be pleased if she heard that.Oh, he can’t wait until Apollo came. When he would be finally dead, then Commodus would finally be at peace.Hopefully.“Princeps?” a servant called from the intercom.Commodus quickly wiped the ichor away, “Yes?” he asked, irritated.“Apollo is here.”“I’ll be there.”The Apollo that arrived did not match with his memory, to Commodus’ plummeting disappointment.Oh well, it would be easier to kill him anyways if he didn’t remind Commodus of past romance.He put Apollo into his elaborately planned dress rehearsal, and much to his glee, Livia finally started to be violent.And then, the Hunters of Diana decided to barge in and ruin everything.Apollo escaped successfully on a dragon built by the son of Vulcan.Thankfully, this was just the dress rehearsal.He needed to punish Lityerses, though.The Blemmyae were ordered to set a bomb, and that sly snake somehow managed to kill them. His best Blemmyae.How dare he.He would make the pain hurt.He was glad that Lityerses summoned the brains to put a tracker on the griffins, because that lead him to that wretched Waystation, which would lead to him at least accomplishing one of these goals.Or not.That damn Apollo, who he still hasn’t moved on from, decided to face him like a fool, and Lityerses betrayed him! Wilson is smiling until he enters his office. It’s his doctor smile, not the big, golden retriever one he saves for (now ex) girlfriends. When the door shuts, the smile goes with it. Wilson sighs, exhaling all the breath in his lungs, before he takes a seat at his desk. It’s nothing new for him, he thinks as he rests his head in his hands. Another patient dead, he’s an oncologist, it’s standard fare. Loud clinic shift, it’s always busy. Blinding lights, it’s a hospital for fuck’s sake. It’s nothing new. So he sits in the dark office and tries to steady his breathing. It would work too, if the door didn’t open, that is.“Ugh…” he groans, looking up as the lights flick on. The taptaptap of a cane, followed by an agitating, grating voice.“What causes tachycardia, vomiting blood, and partial paralysis?”“Not now, House,” Wilson sighs. “And turn the lights back off.”House continues his diagnostic monologue, ignoring Wilson’s disinterest. 	“What’s got your panties in a twist?” he finishes. Wilson looks up again, not bothering to hide his discomfort.“Nothing. Why would anything be wrong?” Wilson says, the sarcasm not lost on House. House, in turn, flops onto the couch in the office and puts his feet up on the armrest.“It’s no fun if you don’t play along,” House says with a mock pout. “Now what is it? Mommy and daddy fighting again?”“Can you shut up for two seconds?” Wilson shouts, his voice shaking. “And turn off the damn lights,” he adds as he takes a breath. House doesn’t respond, but Wilson hears shuffling and a moment later the room is plunged into darkness again. The couch squeaks as House returns to his seat. The room is silent for a moment.“Are you breathing?”The question is so absurd it makes Wilson look up in the dark room. “What? Of course I- What does that mean?”“Not like that,” House groans. “I mean, you’re not gonna start hyperventilating or something. Right?” If Wilson didn’t know better, he’d say House was concerned. It takes Wilson a moment to respond as he manages a shaky breath.“No,” he says. “I’m fine.” The couch squeaks again as House shifts.“Good.”Neither one breaks the silence.

"Did you have fun today?" Felix asks, putting his phone aside as Hyunjin comes out of the bathroom, having washed off the day's filming fatigue.
  They hadn't exchanged a word since they returned, both tired and not needing to for their usual routine. Now, however, Hyunjin squints happily at the welcome question. He climbs onto the bed where Felix is propped against the pillows, sitting on the duvet, and settles beside him, burying his nose in Felix's neck and inhaling the familiar scent. Felix, of course, isn't referring to lunch at restaurants or bowling.
  "Yeah, the food was good, and the game was great. And Innie's surprise worked out. It'll make excellent code."
  Felix hums, running a hand through Hyunjin's short, light hair, gently massaging his scalp. Under Felix's hand, Hyunjin melts like ice cream in the summer sun.
  "What was the most fun?"
  Felix traces his fingertips along Hyunjin's temples, caressing the cartilage of his ears, and Hyunjin presses himself even closer. If he could, he'd crawl under Felix's skin, dissolve into him like an effervescent vitamin in a mug, like drops of watercolor paint in a glass – he'd color him so everyone would know the best person in the world was taken. That he was only for Hyunjin. Hyunjin doesn't believe in God all that much, but sometimes he feels the urge to pray that Yongbok would stay with him forever. That they would stay together forever.
  "Mm, Jinnie? Teasing me was the most fun, right?"
  "Yes," Hyunjin breathes out. Because it was.
  Teasing Felix is always fun, but teasing him the way he did today – purposefully – was thrilling, a sweet languor in his lower belly. To the curling of his toes. Fun in the best sense of the word.
  He started even before filming began: in the car, he sat next to him, discreetly stroking Felix's palm and occasionally his thigh, snorting into Felix's sensitive neck, laughing at someone's joke. Felix froze like a stone statue at one point, and Chan shot them a strange look – they usually didn't allow themselves such behavior in front of others. Hyunjin wasn't particularly worried: the driver probably hadn't noticed, and even if they had, nothing criminal was done. He continued while they were getting their makeup done, mostly throwing playful comments. He briefly touched him during the break, only calming down during the lunch filming and bowling, though if they had been sitting closer, he wouldn't have resisted stroking Felix's leg. And in the evening, he didn't resist, in fact. He finished with some comment about gaming skills – he couldn't remember which one – but from the look he received in return, he knew he'd achieved the desired result and that everything would be brought up tonight.
  "Don't you think you overdid it?"

The sunlight spilled into the captain’s cabin in delicate streaks, warming the wooden floorboards and tracing gentle lines over the blanket-strewn bed. Beyond the walls of the quiet cabin, the Polar Tang hummed with the soft rhythms of morning – quiet footsteps on the various decks, the clink of breakfast pans in the galley, and the muffled voices of crewmates exchanging sleepy greetings.
The sea was calm today. Cora could feel it in the sway of the ship, that slow, contented rock that had always made his muscles feel a little looser, a little more lax.
He stretched, limbs sprawling messily across the bed, and yawned with all the freedom of someone who had slept deeply and well. The kind of sleep he hadn't known in years – too long on the run, too long in hiding, too long worrying about a boy who was now a man with sun-forged eyes and a jaw always set too tight.
But here, in this small, shared space, in this slice of peace they'd finally carved out together, he could sleep again – in a way he hadn’t since he was a small boy, protected by his mother and father. This companionship he now had with Law was still fresh, still new, and the both of them were nevertheless unaccustomed to the physical intimacy that came with sharing space with another person, and yet…
He rolled over with a groggy smile, hoping to find a still-sleeping Law curled under the sheets, tangled up and for once unguarded in slumber.
Instead, he was met with empty linen. Not wholly uncommon, in all honesty, although the quiet scratch of a pen nearby told him he was not alone.
"Good morning, sweetheart," Cora murmured softly, propping himself up on his elbows. His voice, still husky with sleep, rang into the room with the cheer of someone who had absolutely no idea what time it was. "Huh. You’re usually in the med bay or bridge by the time I wake up. We must have woken up at the same time!"
A glance over and, there, at the small desk by the window, sat his handsome Law – shirt rumpled, sleeves pushed to the elbows, dark hair a wild mess of flattened flicks from where fingers had worried through it all night. His back was hunched, shoulders stiff, and the bluish shadows under his eyes told Cora everything. Law paused mid-sentence, pen hovering just above the page, and turned slowly. His eyes met Cora’s for a long, silent beat.
Then he nodded. Just once. A subtle, almost imperceptible gesture. One Cora had come to recognise as Law’s version of a white flag. Not agreement, not denial – just quiet acceptance. A tacit let it go.
Cora’s smile faltered.
He sat up fully, brushing a hand through his hair as he studied the younger man more closely. The desk was littered with notes – patient logs, inventory sheets, medical diagrams – and at the edge of the desk, the mug Cora had left for him the night before sat cold and untouched. A second, empty mug rested beside it, its rim stained with fresh coffee. The clock on the wall ticked toward seven o’clock.
“You didn’t sleep at all, did you,” Cora stated softly. It wasn’t a question.
Law didn’t answer. He never did, not when the truth was obvious and the lie too pointless to offer.
Cora swung his legs over the side of the bed and stood, bare feet padding across the floor. He reached out and touched Law’s shoulder gently. Tense. Coiled like wire. Not a flinch, but close.
“How long has it been like this?” he asked.
Still no reply.
Cora’s fingers slipped down Law’s arm, a quiet brush meant more for comfort than contact, and he sighed. “Okay. Alright. You’re not ready to talk about it.”
He turned away, rubbing at his eyes as he moved toward the door, snagging a hoodie from the arm of the sofa. It was his favourite, now; Law had it made especially for him – maroon and black, similar to his yellow sweater, with the Heart Pirate emblem front and centre. He pulled it on, knowing that the crew couldn’t care less if anyone wandered around in pyjama bottoms only, but he had been dragged up a little better than that.
Just as his head popped out the neckline of the sweater, he called over his shoulder with a lightness he didn’t feel, “Well, if you’re going to be stubborn about it, at least let me get you breakfast.” He paused to flash a broad smile. “And then I’m locking you in this room and swaddling you like a baby until you pass out from second-hand embarrassment.”
Rolling his eyes, Law made a tired noise – half-scoff, half-laugh. Small. But there.
It was a start.

By the time he lay his head down on his pillow each night, he could barely feel his own face.
  His smile sickened him. Seeing that passive and demeaning expression stare back at him from his room’s small bronze mirror made him want to tear his skin off. Given his own way, Jin Guangyao would never let that accursed expression grace his face again.
  But as soon as Lan Xichen looked his way with his own lopsided grin, Jin Guangyao found smiling to be the most natural thing in the world.

I hate when Ellie comes home from college.
The week before she arrives my parents are already nagging at me.
“Why could you have ended up like her.” “You had so much potential.” “You were just as smart, if not smarter. You just didn’t have the work ethic.” It pissed me the fuck off.
It’s not like I’m not doing anything with my life. I have a decent enough remote programming job that gave me enough money for disposable shit. Or, at least, enough money if I didn’t have to pay rent. Which is the only reason why I’m still living with them. If everything wasn’t so goddamn expensive I’d be nowhere near my hometown.
And when she got home, oh, it was so fucking annoying. They treated her like a goddamn princess, worshipped the fucking ground she stood on. Every couple of days, they’d whisk her away for celebratory dinners at her favourite restaurants, and buy her all sorts of snacks, and would bring her to the mall where she’d buy all sorts of her stupid cheesy young adult romance novels. Queer stupid cheesy young adult romance novels. When I came home with a copy of Sayuri-san no Imouto wa Tenshi they yelled at me all night and locked me in my room for the weekend. What fucking double standard did she chance onto? It wasn’t fair.
At least they’ve resigned themselves to leaving me alone. They ignore me in the hallways and my mom avoids eye contact while she brings food to my room even though I buy my own snacks and groceries, even though I cook for myself mostly these days. They don’t barge into my room like when I was younger. They let me smoke up as much as I want and just ignore the smell. They ignore the needles and estradiol vials. It’s probably better than I could have hoped for. Doesn’t mean it still kind of bothers me when they shower Ellie in attention. Speaking of.
For some reason Ellie is crowding my mind today. Usually whatever management gives me is simple enough that I can bang it out in a couple hours and move on to sleeping or gaming for the rest of the day, since management is made up of two dozen business school dipshits who panic at the sight of any discrepancy. But today I’m off. I kept having to read and reread emails and the words on my screen kept blurring together. It had to be because of what happened earlier.
  “Your den smells like shit,” my mother scolded, as I brushed down the pile of plates that I brought from my dorm when I dropped out. Tomato sauce clung to the surface. I elected to stay silent.
  “What happened? You used to be so fastidious.” She dropped the plates into the sink, letting them clatter together. I can’t help but flinch.
  “Mom!” Ellie said.
  Both of our eyes whipped towards her, standing in the doorway between the kitchen and the dining room.
  “Stop yelling at her,” she said. “She hasn’t done anything wrong.”
  “What hasn’t she done wrong? She used to be such a decent boy, now-”
  “Mom! Stop!” She sighed. “Let me take over the dishes for now, okay?”
  My mother huffed, and shuffled away. My eyes are pinned to the dirty sink water.
  I felt Ellie’s hand squeeze lightly on my arm. I had expected her to step up to the sink next to me. But instead, her arms wrapped around my waist, her head resting between my shoulder blades. Strands of her soft black hair tickled the back on my neck, and I could feel her breath through my shirt.
  I froze. My face flushed. Something… was happening.
  “I’m sorry, Casey…” she murmured, her cheek nuzzling into me. “I know it’s been hard for you… I wish I could make it up to you, I’d do anything…”
  I flipped around, suddenly face to face, inches away. I stared into her stupid big, dark brown eyes, and my mouth gaped as she smiled at me.
  “Uh…”
  I twisted, freeing myself from her loose grip. I made a rush to my room and closed the door behind me, all while Ellie called after me.

I slam my laptop shut and lean over to haphazardly place it on my cluttered working desk from my bed. I groan as I bring myself back to standing. I peek outside my window, and have a sudden realization: I had apparently worked into the darkness. More horribly, I did not notice that a thunderstorm had apparently blown in and now my blinds were damp. Fuck. Well, no use worrying about that now.
One heavy duty piss later, and I’m back in bed, packing a bowl into a new bong I had picked up from my latest snacks and weed stockpile run, The Internet’s Hive Mind blasting through my vinyl system. Thank the lord that when my parents came here they joined corporate America, because the both of them had to last-minute join an important business thing two states away. I’m so glad I could smoke in peace. Except.
I hear a knock on my bedroom door, and I jump, bong still in hand, lighter in position. I carefully place it back on my nightstand before pulling myself up with a groan. Parents are gone, so that means Ellie’s back from what
