Reggie is running for his life.It's a feeling he hasn't known in a long time. It's not like fear isn't his constant companion these days, but he mostly trusts himself. There's some of that old confidence still there, the arrogance that once nearly cost him his life and is now carrying him forward every step of the way in hiding. But now? With the wind whipping past him and his heart that isn't his pumping overtime and knowing he can't keep this up for another hundred miles? Right now he's all of three years old again, running from a bullet on legs that feel clumsy and stumpy with leftover baby fat. Just that this time, the bullet's winning. And gaining on him.How the fuck did he find us?! is his last thought before the whistling-arrow sound that's been following him for the past three state lines is finally closing in, and Reggie closes his eyes and lets himself get tackled to the ground, knowing, at least, that she is still safe. He kept far away from their home. Homelander's never gonna find her. Never gonna find Nate and the boys, either. He did good, he thinks, in his last years. He doesn't know if it made up for it all, but he did what he could.He can die happy."I told you to stop running!" says a voice that doesn't really fit the hands that are holding him down with an iron grip. Naked hands, no pleather. "You probably didn't hear me over the wind, but I've been telling you since Connecticut. Sorry, man." The iron grip loosens almost immediately, and the first thing Reggie sees when he finally dares to open an eye is a hand extended towards him, trying to help him up.There's destruction around them. A long groove in the earth where they slid along the ground, physics finally catching up with them both.He looks up. The hand doesn't belong to Homelander. It belongs to a young man with a distantly familiar face and shaggy dark-blonde hair. Reggie can barely catch his breath, heart still beating a mile a minute, muscles in his legs twinging with what he hopes aren't the first signs of aging. The young man who's been following him for so long is barely breaking a sweat, seemingly unaware that he just beat the fastest man in the world in a race that once would have garnered the attention of millions of viewers. "Who the fuck are you?" Reggie asks, and that's a stupid question, he knows, but it's the first thing he can think of. He's definitely seen this face before, somewhere. No wonder. That's a supe, alright."Seriously?" The young man's face scrunches up in disapproval, and it's that angry twitch around the nose that clues Reggie in more than anything, even before the other supe gives up his name. "We lived on the same floor for, like, two years! I'm-""Ryan," Reggie breathes and finally takes the offered hand because he's starting to feel like an asshole for leaving the boy hanging for this long, now that he's over his panic. "I honestly didn't even know you were still alive." Okay, maybe that was a more asshole thing to say. But it is true. These days, it's become difficult to keep tabs on who's still here and who isn't. And of the supes that remain, who's still decent and who's turned into a fascist pig. He still doesn't know for sure which side Ryan's coin has landed on, but the boy is wearing normal clothes, so that's a good sign."I could say the same about you." Ryan pulls him to his feet with a kind of strength that reminds Reggie of other times. Being pushed down over a fucking milkshake, for one. "I wasn't trying to hunt you down or anything. I saw you running, and I just wanted to see a familiar face, I guess. I didn't really think that maybe you were actually running from me instead of just ignoring me."Reggie dusts his clothes off and looks around. He is vaguely aware of where they are, but he isn't looking forward to having to run all the way back home from here. "You're fucking fast, man," he says. "You scared me so bad. I thought you were-""Yeah, that's what I figured. I just had to get your attention. Sorry again for, you know, scaring you. Didn't mean to."They're standing around awkwardly for way too long. It feels anticlimactic. If this was a shitty Vought movie, then Reggie would be getting bored in the cinema about now. This is the kind of terrible drawn-out tension that would have Adam Bourke yell 'Cut!' in his insufferable tone. Bourke's dead. Pissed off one supe too many, apparently, now that murder of humans isn't exactly a crime anymore under the right circumstances. Seeing Ryan honestly feels like a throwback to a different time. The boy disappeared before it all went wrong, and despite having grown about five inches and his face having lost most of its childish softness, he's a reminder of a time before things went to shit so spectacularly. This is a symbol of hope if Reggie's ever seen one, and he really did think he lost all hope. But if a supe kid can still make it on these streets, then there's hope for the rest of them. Especially a supe kid that may just be leagues stronger

The day was like any other. Wake up exhausted, pack my briefcase with my uniform and badge, and head to the station. The train ride was uneventful as it had been for quite some time. Civilians were either on their phones, reading books or newspapers, or sleeping. Some even just stood there, staring out into the vast expanse of the city that flew by while holding onto the hanging straps above their heads. I recognized most of them from their unique sounds as my eyes were closed, knowing their tells from many years of taking this train to and from work: students, librarians, chefs, you name it. I’d looked into their lives without them having a clue. Though not through conventional methods. No… this was a world of quirks after all. And some were gifted, others cursed, still others with not one to their name. Those were the ones who tended to commit crime in the areas I investigated. They were desperate to be someone, to be noticed in a society where having a quirk meant being important. And if you didn’t have one then… well, you were no one.
 
I sighed in irritation as someone’s phone received a text next to me, the sound jarring in the otherwise quiet train car. The person was younger, likely in their late teens. Why were they sitting when someone older than them was standing directly across from them? I felt myself wince at the sound of the person typing, their phone clearly not set to silent. My eyes shifted to their phone screen, my quirk automatically coming to life without my say. I’d been right: nineteen, two parents, one in a tax inspector, the other a doctor. Three siblings who’d made careers in civil service - two specialists and one in the comprehensive services.
 
I tore my eyes from the screen and scowled, adjusting my briefcase so it was closer to me. That kid wasn’t going to live up to the expectations of their family. With yet another quiet sigh, I nudged their arm to get their attention. When they looked up at me, I motioned my head to the person across from them who clearly needed to sit at this point. To my hidden satisfaction, they got up immediately and bowed quickly in apology. At least there were still young people who were polite.
 
The train had a few more stops before my destination. At that point, I was struggling to stay awake despite my copious amount of coffee. With a stretch of my sore back and neck, I got off the train car with the rest of the passengers with briefcase in hand and towards the stairs. With a swipe of my train card, I went up and out, breathing in the fresh air of Musutafu City. Not that it was that fresh however.
 
Countless civilians made their way about their lives, not reacting much to my presence as I made my way to the police station. I kept my head down, not interested in seeing anything but the ground beneath my feet. I didn’t want to see anything or anyone. How long had my hands been shaking?
 
The moment I entered, I heard someone approach me. Closing my eyes with a deep breath, I raised my head and nodded in greeting. This was a regular occurrence for me. Everyone in the station knew what I was capable of, so it had been a majority vote for me to do so for their sakes. Their argument? Keep their private lives private. It made sense. I had nothing against them.
 
“Detective Uchida.” I would recognize that voice anywhere. The faintest of smiles graced my lips for my long-time colleague, Detective Tsukauchi. “I hope your travels weren’t too bad on those old bones.” A soft chuckle left me as I followed him through the building to his office.
 
Only once we were inside with the curtains closed did I dare open my eyes. It was about time too, otherwise I could’ve fallen asleep. I set my briefcase down next to me and sat down, the cork board on the wall filled with sticky notes and different thread. My eyes traced each one to their corresponding picture or note, taking in the information like a sponge in water. All I heard was our breathing and the ticking of the clock on the wall, the occasional sound of the other officers going about their business. My gaze shifted to his after quite some time had passed, my brow furrowed in irritation.
 
“That criminal struck again, huh?” I said dryly as I leaned back in my chair. It didn’t make sense in the slightest.
 
“From the evidence we’ve gathered so far, the victims were unconnected.” Tsukauchi began, his arms crossed in contemplation. “No family ties, no work connections, nothing.” I felt my scowl deepen, my exhaustion from earlier creeping in again. “As far as the public is concerned, this is an unfortunate accident that our force is investigating.” I found myself tapping the armrest repeatedly as I thought about the scene. It was brutally horrific, just like this criminal had always done. It was their special mark in the end.
 
This was going to be a long day.

PROLOGUE: SEBASTIAN
The world was dark, and it was cold, and it was wet. That was all Sebastian's world had been lately. Dark, cold, wet. Sometimes, in intervals, the dark gave way to light- but it was a strange, unnatural light tinged with wrongness; the color of the paper reams they pinned to the walls of every room, or the color of his body as he saw it in glimpses of reinforced glass and hammered metal.And sometimes, the cold and wet would be replaced by just cold. Cold tables beneath his bare skin, until his skin wasn't really skin anymore, and he couldn't feel the burn, anyway. Cold instruments prodding him. Cold voices mumbling things in a diction so far from the warm, accented tongues he knew that he could hardly understand them. It didn't matter, though. Even if he could understand them, it still wouldn't make sense. None of it would. This place that kept him was so entrenched in nothingness- so far away from all semblance of normalcy that logic fell flat to the seafloor.Cold.Wet.Dark.Hungry.Hurt.Sharp.Numb.He couldn't feel his fingers. They didn't feel like fingers now. Had his nails always been so long? He couldn't remember. Remembering took so much- It took resources they wouldn't give him-They needed him empty for surgery, they'd said, but why was he having surgery? Was something wrong with him? People had surgery when things were wrong with them. When he was 9, he had his tonsils removed. They were wrong. Mamá had worried because he had bled into his mouth. Sometimes he tasted blood here, too; Maybe they were taking out his tonsils again. Sebastian needed to tell them that his tonsils were already gone....Wet.His hair was dripping. Black strands that had perhaps been curly a long time ago. Now they were just wet. He was always wet, but he was never bathing. This water was salty. He couldn't drink it. It tasted like chlorine, and they kept him in it for a long time. He thought he might drown, but he never did. When they forced his head under, he just choked and thrashed, but he never drowned. That made them happy....Hungry.There was no food for him here. Sometimes, they stuck him with sharp things that kept him awake. The sharp things had no flavor, and they never touched his mouth. There was no spice, nor savor, nor salt. But he did not die. So he supposed, he must have been eating something, though it never reached his stomach. There was nothing to be regurgitated on an empty stomach. Nothing to asphyxiate on while prone along an operating table. It was convenient....Hurt.Everything hurt. When the bright lights came on, he wanted to hide. They didn't want him to hide. They strapped his legs to a table and chained his arms with plastic things. There was a new limb where one wasn't supposed to be. They chained that one, too. He was lucky on the days they stabbed him. It hurt less, then, but he wondered if they only did it to stop his screaming. They did nothing to stop it when he was alone, though, and that was when the dark came back. Sebastian wondered if he could hide in the dark from them, the way he used to hide with his mother. She liked to find him. It made her laugh, and he liked to hear her laugh, so he kept hiding.
He couldn't hide here.Nobody laughed when he did.

Maomao wasn’t stupid. She knew exactly where her husband was, even as she ate dinner alone. Even as she bathed, before getting ready for bed. She knew exactly what he was doing, and why.
Because he loved her, he had said. So they could spend more time together.
Well, Maomao was currently down a husband, and right now, they were spending zero time together.
“Bastard,” she muttered as she clambered into bed alone. “He’s probably the only one with his candles still lit in the entire complex other than the patrol. Stupid, stupid man. And mean.” Maomao settled, tucking herself in under the blankets. The cool autumn air seeped through the windows. “I want my heater back.”
She sighed softly, rolling onto her side. Her eyes caught on the empty space next to her. And she sighed again.
Who would’ve guessed that she would grow so attached to that stupid, shiny-haired, sparkly-eyed man after all? To the point where she wouldn’t be able to sleep well without him next to her? It was laughable, really. Past Maomao would’ve been horrified at what she’d become.
After a good ten minutes of rolling around with no hope of sleep coming to her anytime soon, Maomao heaved another sigh— she sighed a lot these days— and got up. Toeing her shoes on, she padded over to the wardrobe to pull on one of the longer, darker outer coats. One of Jinshi’s, really. It was, of course, a little long on her, but Maomao didn’t care. She liked it better than her own robe.
Sneaking out of the house compound was easy. Making her way to the outer court offices was also surprisingly easy. Was security just really bad tonight? Or did the palace have actual issues that she should be concern about?
Maomao shook her head and kept going. She’d think about that later.
When she approached his office, her heart sank as she spotted the lit candles glowing from inside. She knocked softly before stepping inside.
Jinshi’s tensed shoulders relaxed when he realized that it was her, his pinched expression melting into something sweeter as she walked to him.
“What are you doing here, wife?” he asked her, gently squeezing her hands. “I thought you would’ve gone to sleep already. It’s late.”
“You’re not there,” Maomao retorted irritably. “It’s cold, and you aren’t there, and you said you’d be doing work so we could spend more time together. Well, I, for one, haven’t seen you all day. Gaoshun tells me that you didn’t even take a break for dinner. You’ve been here since your rounds this morning, and Basen had to practically shove lunch down your throat.” She noticed the white-knuckled grip she had on his fingers and released them. “You’re not resting enough, husband. You’re not taking care of yourself. You’re not eating, you’re not coming back to sleep, you’re not seeing sunlight for hours. And—” she exhaled— “That’s not good for your health.”
Her husband’s placid smile did nothing to appease her, not even as he kissed the back of her hand. “I’m sorry, my love,” Jinshi said earnestly. “I just wanted to get this paperwork out of the way so we could spend a few days together without the distractions they bring.”
“That’s fine and all, but you still need to take care of yourself.” Maomao grabbed his chin, careful to not hurt him too much. “You are just a man. You need rest. You need food. What you’re doing will only hurt you in the long run.”
Jinshi leaned into her touch. “I know,” he said. “I’m sorry.” And he kissed her fingers before he turned back to the papers in front of him. Maomao wanted to throw something.
“‘I’m sorry’ doesn’t cut it,” she snapped, grabbing at his wrist only to let go like he was fire. Her brain still screamed ‘danger’ every time, even though she knew in her heart that he wouldn’t hurt her. It’s fine, she said to herself. Calm down. He knows what he’s doing to himself. You don’t need to guard and hound his every move. You’re only his wife. And yet, she couldn’t help but keep speaking. As if she was in a trance, words spilled out of her mouth without her being able to stop them. “You apologize and you go straight back to work like it doesn’t matter. Like your own health doesn’t matter. You are just a man, Jinshi. You need food. You need rest. You need water, or tea, or something to hydrate yourself with. You need sleep. You can’t keep… overworking yourself like that’s all you were meant to do.”
“But it’s…” Jinshi faltered. “It’s for you.”
Maomao inhaled sharply. Exhale. Do it. Don’t show that you’re angry. That won’t help your argument.
She let out her breath. A frustrated one. She didn’t know if Jinshi knew it for what it was.

We’ve got to be in good shape to take down those daybies.”

He wanted to smile but he chickened out and awkwardly ducked his head.He swear he heard her laugh through the window and he smiled a little. Gathering his courage he left the cabin and walked outside. He was going to talk to her.

The sun was so bright it made the gallows look clean.
  Ava stood at the back of the crowd, her shawl pulled tight around her shoulders, though the heat pressed like a hand against her chest. The dirt beneath her boots had been swept clear for the execution. A courtesy, they said. The people of Dustmere liked their deaths to be orderly.
  JC stood on the platform, wrists bound, lip split. His shirt was torn at the collar. Someone had tried to clean him up, maybe out of guilt, perhaps pity. It hadn’t helped much. His eyes scanned the crowd like he was looking for a familiar star in a sky gone strange.
  He found her.
  Ava didn’t move. She held his gaze like it was a thread she could climb if she pulled hard enough. He smiled, broken, wide, and beautiful. The kind of smile meant to say: 
  
    You’ll live. You’ll forget me.
  
  A lie.
  Spurs clicked on wood. The crowd parted like a curtain drawn back.
  Beatrice Young walked up the steps, slow as a sermon. She wore a long black duster that moved like smoke, and her silver hair was braided down her back, tied at the end with a piece of red twine. Her hat cast a shadow that swallowed her eyes, but Ava could see the line of her jaw, calm, sure, and practiced.
  She wasn’t a lawman. Wasn’t a marshal. The badge she wore at her belt was carved from bone, not metal. No one questioned it.
  Beatrice stepped behind JC and reached for the rope. She didn’t hand it to a deputy. She didn’t ask for a last word. She looped it around his neck with hands that had done it too many times to fumble.
  JC flinched when the knot tightened.
  She leaned in, just for a breath, and said something in his ear. Ava couldn’t hear it, but she saw the way his face changed. He didn’t look scared after that. He just looked tired.
  Someone in the crowd started to pray. Another shushed them.
  JC looked at Ava again. “Ava,” he said. His voice carried clearly across the dust. No tremble in it. “I meant it. I meant all of it.”
  Ava’s throat tightened. She didn’t blink.
  Beatrice stepped to the lever. The world paused, then it didn’t. The wood cracked. The trapdoor dropped.
  JC fell.
  The rope caught. His boots jerked once. Then twice. Then still. Ava watched until his shadow stopped swaying.
  She didn’t cry.
  
    
  
  _____
  
    
  
  
    
  
  The door to her room shut with a wooden gasp, then silence.
  Ava stood in the center, fingers twitching at her sides, still wearing the dust of the gallows. The shutters rattled softly in the breeze, one hinge coming loose with every gust, but the room didn’t move. It hadn’t changed. Not since this morning. Not since last week. The same cracked basin. Same stained lace curtain. Same dent in the floor where JC had dropped his satchel and kicked off his boots, laughing about something no one else would ever remember now.
  She unpinned her shawl and tossed it over the chair. Her fingers found the tin without looking. Tucked behind the loose board in the bottom drawer, same as always. She placed it on the table like it was something sacred.
  Inside the tin were the last pieces of him she hadn’t already buried.
  Six letters, each folded into quarters, the paper softened from being opened too many times. The ink in some places was smudged, either from rain or from the nights she hadn’t been able to hold back tears. She didn’t remember which.
  A single daisy, pressed flat between the third and fourth letter. Its petals had browned, edges curled like it had tried to hold on. JC had picked it from a field outside Dustmere and tucked it behind her ear, grinning like he’d invented the gesture.
  A pocket watch with a broken hinge. It ticked once every seven seconds. She’d timed it once on a sleepless night, thinking maybe the rhythm might comfort her. It didn’t. It was like a dying heartbeat, slow, steady, and wrong.
  And the last thing: a torn playing card. The Queen of Hearts. He’d inked over her face in red, heavy strokes that stained the border and bled into her crown. He said it looked more like Ava that way. Said she was the kind of queen who didn’t wait to be dealt, just took the deck and set it on fire.
  Ava ran her thumb along the card’s edge. It had been a joke. He’d called her that once, 
  
    his queen
  
  , in a voice that made the word sound like a promise. It had embarrassed her. She’d thrown the card at his chest. He caught it, kissed it, and slipped it into her coat.
  She placed it in the basin.
  The first letter followed. Then the flower. Then the second letter.
  One by one.
  She lit a match from the tin near the stove. It took the first time. The flame flickered blue, then orange, then steady.
  She didn’t hurry.
  Each letter curled like a leaf. The words vanished line by line. One said 
  
    your hands smell like cedar
  
  . Another said 
  
    I have a bad feeling, stay in tomorrow
  
  . The last one didn’t say anything. Just her name, over and over, written until the ink bled through. Ava dropped it in last.

This week has been stressful. Beyond stressful, if you ask Keigo-- but Hawks would be quick to brush off any negativity and call it light work.
The workload has been anything but light.
Two villain attacks, major ones that involved civilian casualties, had proven to be connected to the same ungrounded drug ring that the Hawks agency has been chasing for a month now. Simultaneous to leading that investigation, he’s also been charged with assisting the third-year UA students in preparing for this year’s sports festival, a tradition Aizawa (of all people) had reinstated after the war. Something about “keeping traditions alive” or some bullshit. Everyone knew it was to get UA’s attendance numbers back up from the dismal levels they reached post-war.
Along with training the students, Hawks has also found himself responsible for keeping tabs on a loose branch of the Miruko Agency that was struggling to keep with with a sudden crime spike in their district, doubling his sidekicks up with them on patrols while Miruko was out of town attending a “Female Heroes” confrence that she sponsered.
All of this culminated in Hawks overworking to compensate for his overstretched and under-resourced staff. He’d been too distracted to see the connection between the villain attacks before it was too late, and now people are dead. That was the final straw that caused a sleepless night to bleed over into a 10-hour workday that came with a migrain from hell and horrible back pain.
Keigo brushed it off as overtiredness mixing with stress. That proved to be a horrible mistake, and maybe if he was paying better attention he could’ve noticed the signs quicker.
It was the end of patrol when he finally felt the first wave of gut-twisting cramps. Almost doubling over in shock, he drops a few feet in altitude before he can straighten out. Thankfully his sidekicks don’t notice, nor do they question when he swoops down to collect them for an early end to patrol, claiming the quiet afternoon as a weak excuse for why they were returning early.
The whole flight back Hawks desperately hopes he’s wrong, that maybe it was just something bad he ate that’s leaving him bloated and cramping, but he knows the familiar feeling far too well to mistake it for anything else.
A quick trip to the bathroom confirms his worst fear.
Somehow, Keigo must have done something to piss off the most vengeful god in existence or he somehow obtained the worst bad karma he’s ever had. Because theres no other way that, after three fucking years of not having a period, he starts in the middle of his workday during the worst week ever. No. Fucking. Way.
Patrol may have ended, but the day is far from over. He still has four hours of scheduled in-office time (with three meetings, two virtual conferences, and a stack of paperwork taller than he is) before his next patrol where he’s helping Team Bunny pick up some of the slack. Then it’s off the Hero clock, on the Mentor clock because he’s gonna spend the next three hours at UA helping his little protégé and his classmates.
Tokoyami is a great kid, and so are his classmates, Hawks can’t ditch. And Miruko’s sidekicks really need the help. And he absolutely can’t miss these meetings with sponsors and charities.
So he pushes through.

The rest of the day is a blur.
The pain meds thankfully do their job long enough for him to sit through all his meetings, and he slams the five-hour energy to fight off brain fog long enough to actually make notes about all the people he talked to. With his signature speed and precision, he manages to read and approve of about half before he has to go back out on the streets again.

Or was, before she was born – long whorled horns hang around the house, with points sharp enough to pierce skin, strange pearlescent white and nearly as long as her arm. As soon as she was old enough to ask, he told her the stories of each. All unicorns bloodthirsty enough to kill any young girl or boy that crossed their path, ducking their horns and charging, and him, the heroic hunter, spilling their silver blood with his crossbow. She had been forbidden from going anywhere in the woods more than a shout’s length away. Since her birth, he had hunted only the less dangerous animals, deer and rabbits and whatever else he could find, and sold the spoils in town, all to keep her away from the dangers of the unicorns.
Today this is set to change.
Today she is to be the bait.
The other story she was told about unicorns, once she was older –  they like what is untouched, Cara. You must remain pure, for I will have an important job for you soon. And so she did as her father asked, and did not go with any of the village boys, and did not let her hands wander any further at night than was absolutely necessary, and did not mind, for she was going to help her father. And she could tell the necessity of her work, for he brought back less and less from his hunts, and their supplies dwindled, and a unicorn would need to be killed soon for their luck to change.
Her father came while she was dressing, in the icy dark of that morning, to hand her a bundle of fabric. A white dress. Loose, shapeless, nothing she had seen before. He had given her the strangest instruction:  wear nothing underneath. When he had prepared her for this before, he had described, in that short way which was so characteristic of him, that she would wait in the clearing. That the unicorn, scenting a virgin, would be lured to where she was. That he, waiting in the woods with his crossbow, would watch, and at the moment that the unicorn was to pierce her chest with its horn – as that was all unicorns truly wanted to do, kill – he would leap out and slay it, her safe and their financial future secured. He did not explain the strange instruction of his, and she had not had time to think of it as her nerves overtook her on their walk into the woods.
She did think of it now, on her stump, the friction of the bark uncomfortable, her father watching from some unseen place. But the sun was rising and the clearing warming and the unicorn and its threat of death could not be far away.
She had sat for long enough for her lower body to be tingling with static and sleep when finally there was movement. A flash in the trees. Her heart seized and her breath held. She closed her eyes. She must be brave for her father– must trust in his marksmanship– must think of having enough to eat–
The creature that steps into the clearing is … beautiful, is her first thought. Like a horse but more lithe, with silvery-white fur and a mane that seems to shine and its – his, she corrects quickly, having looked over his body – horn nearly a foot long. A younger unicorn, then. Strangely, that even now Nienor might still remember how their fresh, white petals had felt beneath her fingers - smooth, brittle, delicate, yet ever taut, like the drawn strings of a bow. 
  "Hello, little lady," came a voice, soft as a whispering breeze through the trees.

Beautiful she was, as all Elves were, and the cool, post-winter sun cast its pale beams upon the dark braid that lay over her shoulder. Above the Elf-maid's head, birds flitted and chirruped, as though they sought to weave her a crown from the motion of their wings - though there was nought of queenliness in her bearing. Her movements were honest, unadorned, uncertain.

  "I knew your brother once," she said. 
  "What is he like?" Nienor asked at once, her eyes wide with eager curiosity.

  Afterwards she knelt amidst the flowers and traced her fingers across the petals, one by one, as Nienor herself had done but moments before. Yet the Elf-maid was quick in that beyond reckoning, and light - so light that it seemed she scarcely moved at all, as though it were the wind alone that stirred the nodding white heads of the blossoms. And whenas at last she lifted her gaze to Nienor, her grey eyes were alight with mirth. 
  "They are wise flowers," she said. "And from them flows a lesson greater than aught that might fall from the lips of our wisest loremasters, little lady." 
  "What lesson, lady?" Nienor asked anon, wide-eyed again, with all the frankness of still childhood curiosity. 
  "I am no lady, but Nellas," the Elven maid replied, turning her gaze once more to the field of flowers, as if lost in thought. "And the lesson is simple, and such: the sun and light rise even after the blackest of times." 
She is no sun and snowdrops are all fools, Nienor now knows, and she leaps.

Jezzi had wondered, ever since getting the message, how she would feel about this reunion. It had only been a year - no; almost two now. So much had happened it was hard to keep track. Sometimes in life you say goodbye thinking it’s probably forever, and then you get the double pleasant surprises of survival and reunion.
“If we were going to meet again”, she said to Sammo as she put on her coat, “I would have expected it to be in Ferrix. Or whatever’s left of it. I guess we’ll only know about that when this is all over.” She headed for the door, called “See you later,” and headed for the elevator and the start of the short walk from the apartment to the turbolift up to the station.
On the train, she relaxed in her usual seat by the door and watched the cityscape flash by. Coruscant: unending, grey, magnificent and brutal, side by side and sometimes all at once.
She hated it. She missed Ferrix, of course, but she even missed Mina-Rau, although she hadn’t stayed there long. The rumour had reached them that Cassian’s boss, as they universally thought of the unknown figure, had received confirmation that another ship had made it off Ferrix, shortly after their own. Jezzi had guessed, at the time, that this was Pegla’s plan - stay behind to get a second ship ready. There was a rumour that Sammo had been on that ship, along with a few others who she could later confirm: Femmi, Granik, Jayni. Those were the ones she knew about, at least. The others.. who knows. Scattered across the galaxy, their fates uncertain but at least that meant she didn’t have to mourn them for sure. She supposed that was a good thing, anyway.
When she reached her stop she took another turbolift down to sublevel 35.
 She was a little early so she bought herself a caf from a kiosk and took her time on the short walk to the Amedda Multi-World Community Centre and the scheduled rendezvous.
They arrived a little early.
The embraces came freely. Jezzi had been vaguely wondering if it would be awkward, but they had all known each other too long for that. Bix was thinner than before, pale and her eyes a little sunken, but her hug was strong and her smile broad. Cassian looked tired too - again, paler than Jezzi remembered - but still had that air of determination that she had always sensed about him, even when he was at his lowest ebb and most apathetic in the days after his return from Mimban. At its strongest when he had told them that day, after the Funeral: “I’ll find you.” And he had.
Cassian had lacked direction all those years. Now, he had committed. Had set a course forward into whatever the future might bring. Today was all about commitment of another kind.
Jezzi brought them in to the atrium area where there were a few seats. It was a relatively spacious waiting room. “Would you like a caf?” Jezzi asked, indicating the little cafe bar, with the bored proprietor, an old Tarlafar named Lorf, staring over at them with brazen curiousity.
“No, but I’d love some water. My mouth is so dry.” Bix offered another smile as she said this but Jezzi could see that she was nervous. Cassian was too, although he hid it better. The only clue was in his slightly over enthusiastic ironic chuckle as Jezzi joked about how so few things could make someone like Bix truly nervous these days. There was something else too, though. When Jezzi added how happy she was to see Bix healthy and smiling, even using the word “recovered”, Cassian’s mouth closed a little too quickly and there was a slight darkening in his eyes before he glanced away. Just for a second. Meanwhile, Bix smiled even more broadly and Jezzi knew then that this was not a subject she should linger on for long. She had the good excuse, anyway, of getting them some water from the cafe.When she returned to the table with the cups the couple were silent, the mood not so much awkward as contemplative. But they soon fell back into small talk: the frustrations of the journey, that yes, they were working hard, frequently off-planet. In terms of actual news.. there wasn’t so much to share as she had already spoken with them both at length via comms. Careful to use a public booth. In terms of their personal lives, she knew the headlines, as they did hers. There was no need to talk about any of that.
Jezzi had known Bix from birth and Cassian since his arrival at age 9 but they had changed so much since… the Funeral. Despite the violence and destruction that had followed, the panic and the despair, it was still the face of Maarva that Jezzi thought of as her last true memory of Ferrix. “Now I’m dead. And I yearn to lift you”.
The words had haunted her along with the ghosts of those lost.
The appointed time was nearing and Jezzi focused now on outlining what was going to happen. They all knew, of course. Jezzi in person but Cassian and Bix through observation in the way of all Ferrixians, valuing as they did the public marking of life’s journey points.
Jezzi concluded with more words they all knew already to be

When he sees a vacant bench outside at the picnic table, he likes to imagine Neil, reading his script to a starry-eyed audience, with his eyebrows furrowing at every sentence or facial expression, sometimes in confusion as he pens the definition of words in the margin.He confesses that in his imagination, Neil had always existed in the wind, the stars, and the ripples of the unbounding lake beside Welton. When they had their walks on the dock admiring the ducks and ripples made from the rocks they’d skipped against the water's surface.When Autumn erupts he feels it in the breeze, when Mother Nature shares her beauty again, he finds himself deep in thought, Neil loved Autumn, the weather was just right, the leaves decorated the Earth, and they’d hear that crunch beneath their shoes.When Summer arrives, Todd visits Iceland with his family, to be acquainted with the cousins he’d barely kept in touch with. His cousins had told him the Aurora Borealis was perfect for reconnecting and rekindling their friendship. Yet, when Todd sees it, his mind un-voluntarily wanders to Neil. When they speak about their school life, Todd puts on his rehearsed smile, telling them ‘all’s well,’ then discussing some of his classes.He never tells them about the part where he writes poetry. They needn’t know.They needn't know about his poetic grief, he wouldn’t want to sour the mood, he's here to reconnect and distract his mind.To look at the Aurora Borealis, was to look into the eyes of Neil, the eyes of someone who just found out they’ve got something worthwhile, some passion to pursue far into adulthood.
When Summer ends he’s back at Hellton for the winter’s harshness. It felt as though the universe had mistaken him for a fool, as the snow fell rapidly, encasing everything. When he daydreams he dreams of a reality where Neil still exists, cheerful, and ever sweet. Doing everything acting related, his smile achingly wide and unwavering. Sometimes he wishes to see that smile again, to go back in time and fix it all.Then, he sees Neil sweater, it’s the color of the freshly fallen maple leaves. He holds it delicately, heaven knows he could never wash it. It’ll lose everything that made it Neil. Everything that made it special, yet if ghosts were real he wonders how Neil would feel about him and his sweater. Maybe he’d want it back. Perhaps he'd use it as a lucky sweater now that Todd's snuggled in it.When he sleeps, one dream plagues his mind like a disease. The saddest he'd ever seen Neil, had been after his father's conversation about being a doctor.Sometimes Todd was angry, more so over his inability to notice and over Tom Perry's own negligence of Neil's needs and wants, his fury was bitter and unkind, yet he couldn't pull himself to speak up against Tom. He'd caused Neil's death, that had been clear as day.
The final reminder of Neil had been his letter, one Neil would never receive;I'm aware this letter will never see you, but I suppose maybe that's a good thing,If you were here i'd sit and talk to you about the Aurora Borealis for hours, to the point you'd get sick of it maybe.You made me swoon like a maiden, and for that I'm forever grateful, but i must admit,I have anger brewing within me.
Please, do not think any less of me,
my actions are not of envy or jealousy, they are of rage and mourning, I speak as if you are still alive.Perhaps, you'd have loved the tale of Icarus. Or any Greek tragedy, now I see why you did what you did,it doesn't hurt any less though.With all my heart,
Todd.

It's a busy day at The Lucky Rabbit Casino. And for Chance, its owner, it was a special day as well. After the ordeal of being trapped in a death game where you'd die and respawn for entertainment, it kinda makes you think about what decisions could've gotten you there. So, when everyone got out of that situation, Chance decided that he would make amends to the people he had wronged. And the main person on that list? Don Sonnellino, better known as simply Mafioso.He was another casino owner, but the mafia also ran his place, so it was a bit less friendly to newcomers. But Chance had heard about a massive prize being offered if you could win a simple card game. The prize? A beautiful, black continental giant rabbit. Apparently, Mafioso wanted to have an event in his community. Whoever won the game got the bunny. But the game was rigged from the start. Mafioso had a deal that if no one won the rabbit by the end of the night, he could take them home. As they say, the house always wins. Even iTrapped, his once-best friend, now ex-friend, had told him he would lose his money.But Chance was no quitter. He was stubborn and would never back down from a challenge. He knew rigged games inside and out, being in the business. He knew he could win. But how? The odds were all stacked against him. Well, he had his ways. So, with a confident smirk, he played the game... And won. And his winning card? A King of Spades. So, he got the bunny and named him Spade.Mafioso was pissed. He loved rabbits, had one of his own named Angel, and wanted her to have a friend. So, Chance was put on his target list.But after being forsakened, after leaving the death games behind, he made amends with the Don. So now, once a week, Mafioso comes to The Lucky Rabbit for a little bunny playdate.
Chance sits in his office, soothing music and a calm, gentle atmosphere around him as he waits for his guest to arrive. Spade already knows what day it is, and is running around, having zoomies and doing binkies. "You excited to see your girlfriend, Spade?" He asks a bit jokingly, to which Spade makes a small honk of approval. "Well, Maf just texted me that he's here, so you stay right there." He gets up, smiling a bit as Spade continues to run around and be silly before he heads out the door. The sounds of machines fill his ears as he walks toward the front door, where Mafioso is standing, Angel sitting politely at his feet."Hello, Chance," Mafioso says, his voice stern and almost cold, if it wasn't for the tiniest smile on his face. "I'm assuming someone is excited to see Angel.""Oh yeah. He's been zooming for the past 30 minutes in there."At that statement, a sound that rarely comes out of Mafioso's lips escapes. A small chuckle. "Well, let's not keep him waiting." He then starts walking with Chance towards his office, Angel hopping alongside them with excitement.As soon as the door opens, Angel and Spade run at each other, hopping around each other in circles, sniffing and licking each other.Chance offers his guest a chair and opens up a small mini fridge by his desk as he sits down. "Damn, I need to buy more drinks for this. You want some baby carrots or something? That's all I got right now.""How do you, an owner of a casino, not have anything in your fridge?""I kept putting it off, I guess."Mafioso sighs a bit. "Why don't you call that pizza boy? He knows how to make good food.""That's the thing." Chance retorts, looking at him. "Elliot's the manager of the place now. I don't wanna bother him. He's got, like, important business stuff to do.""Ah, yes, super important business stuff... at a pizza place."Chance sighs a bit. "Fine, but if he says he can't do anything for us, you owe me... a Bloxy Cola.""Deal. And if he's able to come, you pay for the pizza."So, Chance finds the number for Builder Brothers' Pizza and gives it a dial. And after a few rings, Elliot picks up, using his customer service voice. "Thank you for calling Builder Brothers' Pizza. My name's Elliot. How can I help you?""Hey, Elliot."And just by hearing Chance's voice, the customer service act drops. "Oh, hey, Chance. Why are you calling the pizza place's phone? You have my phone number."He lets out a small sigh before speaking again. "Because Mafioso and I wanna order some pizza."Elliot is quiet for a moment before his voice chuckles out, "I keep forgetting you two are friends now." Chance can hear Elliot get out his order pad before continuing. "What would you guys like?"After discussing for a moment, they settle on some sausage pizza and some Fizzly soda. But before Elliot hangs up, Mafioso says something that makes Chance and Elliot blush a bit. "Don't keep us waiting, Elliot. There's some things that Chance and I have to talk with you about." And with that, he hangs up Chance's phone and hands it back to him.Chance is completely red in the face. Mafioso and he have discussed their shared... appreciation for Elliot. But to hear him actually hint at it out loud made his blood run

"I expected things like this to happen every time it rains, though."She could hear a soft mumbling from people beside her. That short conversation makes her panicked even more. She raised her backpack above her head as she winced at the thought of her notebooks drenched.Just as she stepped forward, a soft tap on her shoulder made her stop in her tracks. Startled, she turned and met a pair of warm, hesitant doe-like eyes. A boy about her age stood there, shifting his weight nervously as he held out a bright yellow umbrella covered in printed cartoon characters. The girl caught a sight of a violin case on the other hand of his.She brought her eyes back to the boy, eyebrows slightly arched, waiting for the boy to say something. She slowly removing her headphones so she could hear him clearly. She blinked, caught between gratitude and shyness."Thank you." Failed again.Junebug blinked slowly, chewing on a mouthful of air and radiating disinterest.Hangman whistled low.“I mean, you are athletic, right?”“Say one more word and I’m calling Will to come get me,” Swerve snapped, gritting his teeth. “He has a car with air-conditioning.”“Will also has the core strength of a feral spider monkey and no fear of dying. Holmes had been unusually quiet all evening, and not in the way that I was most accustomed to. After all of our decades together, I had often seen him silent while thinking, or absolutely refusing to speak while suffering from one of his bouts of melancholy. I had little reason to think that such tendencies would change even now that we had retired to a charming farmhouse in Sussex.This, however, seemed different from his customary silences. Indeed, although I could not be certain, it seemed to me as if he was nearly on the verge of tears at times. We ate our dinner more or less in total quiet, only occasionally interrupted by my comments on the excellent meal that our old housekeeper had prepared. She was still more silent than Holmes, vastly uninterested in conversation, and only materialized when needed before retreating to her own small cottage on the property.“I hope she does not think that we are unappreciative of her work,” I said, setting down my fork at last. “Although in truth she seems perfectly content never to exchange two words with us. Did you go out of your way to find the least sociable housekeeper in all Sussex?”Holmes did not at first answer me, idly dipping his spoon in his soup without actually eating much of it. Then he stirred slightly, giving me a faint smile, although he did not meet my gaze. “I admit that I may have sought someone who was not particularly chatty. I have little wish to be the center of village gossip.”“I think that is unlikely, since the village is some little distance away.”“I did contemplate changing my name when we moved here,” he said, in a tone that suggested he was completely serious. “However, you are an exceptionally horrible liar, and I thought it unlikely that you could sustain any such deception. It is a pity that all of your inaccurate, dramatic stories have made me such a household name, Watson.”He sounded almost bitter, and I found myself taken aback. “I had thought you no longer objected to my stories. You said last year that it was all right if I published—”“I am aware of what I said,” Holmes snapped, then winced. “Forgive me. I do not mean to be horrible to you, I am simply somewhat… I feel odd.”“I have noticed,” I said softly, extending my hand over the table. “Pray tell me what is wrong.”Letting out a soft sigh, Holmes rested his long, thin hand lightly in my grasp. He still would not look at me, but that was not uncommon, for he found such contact difficult when his emotions were roused. “Well, well, I am a little confused as to my own difficulty, in truth. I had a faint jolt earlier, you see, and I am somewhat agitated.”That told me very little, for while Holmes is the strongest and more enduring of men, certain things can cause him immense difficulty.   He was a charming man — one who knew exactly what he was doing to you. Each step perfectly calculated, each hair meticulously placed.

Holding your hand when he spoke to you, rubbing his thumb into your palm, coaxing you into agreeing with anything and everything he had to say. His voice was like velvet, and he used it to his advantage. He played you like he’d done this before, carefully, casually, and he would likely do it again once your worth had dried up.
  You knew this, of course.

    many.

His leg would bounce idly against the creaky floorboards, testing the worn, frayed wood below his boot. His fingertips would drum against his thigh in sets of four, matching the beat of the whining wood and contributing to a larger symphony within his own mind. Occasionally, he would hum to himself, but it would only last for seconds at a time before falling into silence again, met only with the cicadas hissing in the brush beyond the sliding door.
  These behaviors were subtle at first, but as the two of you reached the climax of your time together, his patience was waning. Gradually, you bore witness to the Jhin that existed under the mask.
  It was hot. Overwhelmingly humid this late into the summer, and Jhin had chosen one of the worst spaces to play his part with you. Sweat clung to your neck as the light hit your sandaled feet, and your finger pulled idly at the collar to your robes, letting out a tense breath. Your head was starting to feel light, fuzzy. Just beyond the door, open and inviting and 
  
    mocking
  
   you, natural springs were lined in rocks damp with shallow pools, but just as your eyes landed on the water —
  
    “Patience,
  
   my darling,” his voice cut in, and the wet hairs on the back of your neck stood on end. He stopped shaking his leg. It was the first time he’d spoken in what felt like hours, and yet his tone sounded so clear. “In time, the air will cool. There will be 
  
    plenty
  
   of opportunity to rest and recuperate once your act is complete.”
  This was a lie.
  To Jhin, you were an instrument. One carved meticulously by him, capable of 
  
    so
  
   much when held by the right musician. Malleable enough for his use, and yet headstrong enough for the narrative he sought to craft. It only felt right for a virtuoso such as him to bring you to your full potential, to give you a 
  
    fitting
  
   end.
  The trap had been sewn into your personal supplies when you weren’t looking – your clothing. The exact robe he planned for you to wear today, aware of how fond you were of it. This, you also knew. His work with a needle left something to be desired, you thought to yourself as your fingers ran over the frayed seam. This was hours ago, though, and 
  
    now
  
   was 
  
    now.
  
   To Jhin, you remained blissfully unaware, playing into this plan he considered you too unintuitive to catch onto.
  He planned to kill you.
  To Jhin, this was the ultimate act of love. For you, for himself, for anyone lucky enough to witness what would become of you. You would blossom into something far larger, far greater than yourself, and you would be permanently etched into the history of the 
  
    Golden Demon’s
  
   work.
  A part of you didn’t mind that idea, but you knew better than to blindly follow Death’s lead.
  “It’s 
  
    sweltering,”
  
   you complained, and understandably so. You knew not to whine too much, as it would aggravate Jhin far more than it was worth — for a man with high standards, you supposed it made sense for him to be 
  
    terribly
  
   picky with the people he worked with. “Could we at least… close the doors, maybe? Give us some more shade? We don’t have to work until well after sundown, any–”
  Jhin’s temper was a curious thing. You watched observantly as he stood up, crossing the room into the oppressive rays of sun. His hands gripped iron-tight onto the handles of the doors, and he 
  
    slammed 
  
  them both shut in the way a child might make a point of stomping up a flight of stairs. With the way his skin hit the sun, you could tell he was sweating too.
  He didn’t like when things didn’t fall in line with his mental plan, you came to find. It was cute, if not frustrating.
  
    “Better?” 
  
  Jhin strained out, turning back to offer you a glimpse of his face.
  The paneling of the door, now only offering slivers of light through wooden beams, framed his silhouette well. You were one of very few living in Runeterra

With each step getting heavier, he stepped on the porch, and his already clenched fist lingered in the air before the hesitation stopped him. What was he even going to say? Was he ready to face Kyle? Those stupid thoughts invaded his mind once again. "Get it together, Stan. This is your best friend. It's now or never," he reminded himself. Another steamy huff escaped his lips and he finally knocked on the door. The answer didn't take too long.
"Hello there, sweetheart," Sheila greeted as she appeared in the doorway.
"Uh, hello, Mrs. Broflovski," Stan replied, fidgeting with the laces of his coat. "Can I talk to Kyle?"
"Of course! He's in his room," Kyle's mother said and stepped back to let Stan in.
Stan walked in further and got rid of his shoes without bothering to take his jacket off. As he approached the stairs, he could catch a glimpse of familiar red hair that quickly disappeared behind the door. With another deep breath, he took careful steps up the stairs. He passed various family photos he had seen countless times, but one picture caught his eye.
It was a picture of him and Kyle on their first school day. They looked so silly as kids, both smiling nervously but also incredibly thrilled with the new path ahead of them. But it was long in the past; they were no longer little first graders. The boys had grown up and had to face another path, which seemed rather terrifying now.
Not letting the nagging doubts get to him, Stan walked up further until he reached Kyle's room. He knocked on the door softly and turned the knob without waiting for a reply.
"Hey, dude," said Stan, offering his best friend a small smile.
"Hey," Kyle replied shortly; his arms were crossed and he seemed guarded.
Stan stepped closer to him and noticed the faint tear stains on his cheeks. "Were you crying?" He asked and reached out to brush his finger against Kyle's cheek.
But Kyle swatted his hand immediately and muttered, "Shut up.. Must be some allergy." After those words, he rubbed his eye to dry his lashes before turning his head to look out of the window.
Stan frowned; he didn't like how his friend was behaving at all. He had a feeling that there was more than the sulky boy let on. His gaze lingered on the sight outside the window, watching the snowfall together with Kyle, before sitting down on his bed.
"So.."
"So, what did you come for?" They both spoke at the same time.
An awkward pause followed with Stan breaking it by clearing his throat. "Come on, man... Am I not allowed to hang out with my best buddy anymore?" He asked somewhat teasingly. It was true, though; he was supposed to leave in a few months.
Kyle grimaced at Stan's words, but a moment later, his expression changed into a one of acceptance, and he sat down next to Stan.
"Are you excited? For college." Kyle asked, not meeting Stan's gaze.
"Kind of... But I'm hella nervous, too," Stan remarked with a chuckle.
"Yeah, a whole different city," Kyle nodded, "But you don't have to worry, you know... I'm sure you'll be alright and... You'll meet new people, make new friends..." he then trailed off.
Stan picked up on the change in Kyle's tone and the way each word got quieter. "Hey, you know... You can visit me anytime," Stan tried to reassure his best friend.
"No, yeah, I know, but..." Kyle trailed off again, "I don't want to burden you."
"What?" the older one exclaimed, "That's bullshit. We're stuck together, remember?"
"Well, yeah, but..." Kyle was about to continue when Stan cut him off.
"No buts," he stated firmly and threw an arm around Kyle's shoulders, "you're stuck with me, and that's it."
Kyle stared at Stan with his eyebrows furrowed, but then couldn't help but chuckle softly.
"Dork..." Kyle let out without any actual bite.
Stan chuckled along and kept his arm around his best friend, squeezing his shoulder, “I may be a dork, but I'm  your  dork.”
Kyle shot Stan a glare but cracked a smile anyway, “Seriously, stop being so corny…” He then shrugged Stan's arm off his shoulders.
“Come on, you gotta cheer up a little!” Stan insisted. Then, he put his hand on his friend’s knee.
After a moment of hesitation, Kyle spoke again, “Are you sure you won't forget about South Park once you move to the city?”
“Oh,  please . How could anyone forget this hellhole? I'll never forget Kenny's dirty jokes and Cartman’s antics. And…”, Stan trailed off, his grip on Kyle's knee tightening slightly.
“What about Wendy?”
“What about her?” Stan frowned confusedly.
“Are you…”
“I don't care about her. Right now, I want to talk to you about you. About us.” Stan cut him off.
Now it was Kyle's turn to look confused, “About us..?”
“Yes. You've been my best friend for… As long as I can remember. I could never forget about our friendship...”
“Stan…” Kyle tried to get his friend's attention

It does not know which one is real and which is a mere illusion. Leona doesn’t cry, after all. It can’t, not since it was a small kid.A shudder shakes its body. Leona grits its teeth, and forces its body to relax.It takes a long, long time before Leona becomes aware of its surroundings again. There is a familiar scent in the air. It has nothing to do with sand and blot, and everything to do with dragon fire and sweet vanilla.Ah. That’s right. This is Diasomnia. Vi brought over the steaming bowls of oatmeal to the table for the whole family to eat. One might not think oatmeal was all that special, but Vi had her ways of turning it into one of her morning specialties. She always caramelized some apples to add to it, practically turning it into an appropriate version of apple pie for breakfast.
  However, Caitlyn was green around the gills as she contemplated it, even as one of her favorite meals. It made Vi think back to those days with no shred of fondness to speak of. Those early weeks were difficult, but Caitlyn had overcome a great deal to be in this position.
  Two reconstructive surgeries after seeking a second and third opinion, and multiple failed attempts to conceive, but she’d finally gotten what they fought so hard for. Their second little baby, this time with Vi’s egg, was nestled safely in Caitlyn’s womb, and even through her sickly pallor, she was glowing something fierce.
  They knew this pregnancy would be more complicated. Caitlyn was automatically considered high risk with her medical history. They already knew she would automatically get a C-section to lower any chance of bad outcomes posed by a natural delivery. This pregnancy was so different from Vi’s, but Caitlyn was 
  
    so
  
   happy. She had wanted to carry their first, but was told it could never happen. Vi had gladly taken on the task, but knowing Caitlyn got to fulfill this dream of hers and prove those first doctors wrong was a hard-won reward. It made Vi happy beyond belief just watching her with this little secret she carried with her every day.
  It was almost enough to have made Vi forget about breakfast altogether until it finally registered that Callie had just finished proclaiming how excited she was that Santa would come soon, and how determined she was to see him with her very own eyes this year.
  “That brings up a great question, Callie,” Vi said, looking down at their daughter, who turned to her with the sweetest smile, with cinnamon glaze wiped along her face. That’s when Vi noticed remnants of it on her sleeve. And those were a fresh set of pajamas. Oh well. “What do you want for Christmas this year?”
  “I know!” she said so excitedly. “I wished for it for my birthday.”
  Her third one, in fact, that only happened a week earlier.
  “Did you now? You know… usually, you’re not supposed to tell anyone what you wish for when you blow out the candles, but I think if you tell it to Santa, it’s okay. We’ll write him a letter later, so that means it’s okay if you tell us, too, because we have to help you.”
  “Okay.”
  “So, what did you wish for, sweetie?”
  “A baby!”
  Vi’s eyes shot open wide, immediately going to Caitlyn’s. Never in her wildest dreams had she expected that to work out so perfectly.
  “Wait,” Vi said, her eyes going straight back to Callie. “Do you mean like a doll, or…?”
  “No. A brother or sister.”
  Caitlyn had to hide her smile by resting her chin on her hand as she covered her mouth and looked away. Vi had a feeling Callie couldn’t read those context clues, anyway, but she couldn’t blame Caitlyn for wanting to hide away from it either. It was surprisingly hard not to spill the beans early with this admission.
  As it was, Caitlyn would be far enough along by Christmas to have her first sonogram and her blood tests done, so it was the perfect time to make their announcement to the family, with even more perfect timing to let Calliope open a present, telling her she was getting exactly what she wanted.
  “Well, we’ll be sure to write that letter to Santa just as soon as you finish your breakfast. Then we’ll have to wait a few weeks and see what happens, huh?”
  “Yay!”
  Caitlyn clearly had no appetite, leaving her food untouched, but she looked thrilled beyond belief, like the cost of everything to get here was well worth it. This was sure looking to be one of their best Christmases yet, perhaps only to be outperformed by the next.
